summary: Kephale’s constellation has mysteriously lit up, and one by one, the constellations of the remaining Titans follow suit, leaving the Heirs in confusion and unrest, with no answers to be found. Mydei, tormented by strange and disturbing dreams, is desperate to understand the unfolding chaos. Meanwhile, Phainon, always present and unnervingly calm, draws closer, offering reassurance that teeters on the edge of reverence. In a world spiraling out of control, at least Mydei has Phainon to lean on, right?

chapters.title: Devouring the Self
chapters.html:
The sun sank behind the stone walls of Okhema, its final rays casting the city in a warm, golden glow. Mydei paused just beyond the gates, taking in the familiar sights of the bustling square. Merchants packed up their stalls for the evening, their voices blending with the clang of hammers from distant forges and the faint laughter of children. It was the same as always —life in motion, a fragile rhythm in a world teetering on the edge of chaos.

He exhaled slowly, letting the cool air fill his lungs. The mission had been successful. He’d spoken to those scattered villages, the ones closest to the black tide, and convinced them to seek refuge in Okhema. It wasn’t easy— not for him. Mydei had a soldier’s pride and a prince’s bearing, traits that earned respect on the battlefield but offered little comfort to frightened priests. That was Phainon’s strength, not his. Phainon could charm anyone with that easy smile, the way he always knew just what to say to make others feel safe.

But this time, it had been Mydei’s task. He had taken the reins, and while he had done what was necessary, there was no denying the strain. The weight of expectation was something he bore in silence, even as the whispers of his past followed him wherever he went.

The people of Okhema had accepted him, but not without reservation. He could feel it now as he moved through the square, the subtle shift in the air when he passed—a tension, like the faintest crack in an otherwise smooth surface. Mydei ignored it, as he always did. Their doubts didn’t matter. What mattered was their safety, the walls of Okhema shielding them from the black tide creeping closer every day.

His boots clicked softly against the stone as he entered the central hall, the familiar warmth of the space easing the stiffness in his shoulders. But the moment he stepped inside, Mydei stilled.

Aglaea was there.

She stood near the center of the room, her golden threads shimmering faintly in the dim light. They flowed around her like liquid light, tracing invisible patterns in the air. Mydei couldn’t see their purpose—only Aglaea truly understood the web she wove—but he could feel their weight. The threads seemed to hum with life, carrying a knowledge far beyond his grasp.

Though her gaze was turned toward the window, Mydei knew she couldn’t see the city beyond it. Her blindness had never hindered her, not when the threads revealed all she needed to know. There was an otherworldly quality to her presence, an unshakable stillness that made it impossible to forget she was more than human.

“Aglaea,” he said, his voice steady but quieter than usual. He inclined his head slightly, a gesture of respect.

“You’ve returned.” Her voice was soft, yet it carried a weight that filled the space between them. The golden threads shifted, twisting and curling as if they were listening. “And you’ve done what was asked of you.”

“Yes.” He approached, keeping his movements slow and deliberate. “The villagers will arrive within the week. They’ll be safe here.”

Aglaea tilted her head slightly, her threads weaving tighter around her like a cocoon. “Safe for now.” She turned to face him fully, though her unseeing eyes didn’t meet his. “The tide presses closer every day. We cannot afford delays.”

Mydei nodded, though her words lingered like a shadow over his thoughts. Aglaea had always been singular in her focus, her devotion to the mission unwavering. She spoke in absolutes, her blind eyes fixed on a vision only she could see.

“There’s something else,” she continued, her voice dropping to a near whisper. “The threads tell me… there is a fracture. A shift.”

“A fracture?” Mydei frowned, his mind already racing through the possibilities. “Do you know what it is?”

Her threads shimmered, their glow intensifying for a moment before dimming again. “Not yet. But it draws closer. You’ll feel it soon enough.”

The way she said it—calm, certain—made the hairs on the back of Mydei’s neck stand on end. He straightened, his expression hardening into the stoic mask he wore so well. “Whatever it is, we’ll face it. Like we always do.”

Aglaea’s lips curved into the faintest of smiles, though it held no warmth. “I hope you’re right, Mydei. For all our sakes.”

She turned back toward the window, her golden threads swirling around her in slow, deliberate patterns. Mydei lingered for a moment, watching her. There was something unsettling about her words, the way they seemed to settle in his chest like a stone. But he pushed the feeling aside. There was no use in dwelling on what couldn’t yet be understood.

For now, the mission was complete. That was enough.

Or so he told himself.

The sun sank behind the stone walls of Okhema, its final rays casting the city in a warm, golden glow. Mydei stood at the edge of the highest rooftop, his gaze steady as he surveyed the sprawling city below. The rooftops, the narrow streets, and the distant horizon—all of it was part of the world he had come to protect.

For a long moment, he simply stood there, taking in the familiar sights, allowing himself a rare moment of quiet. The mission had been successful. He had spoken to those people, convinced them to seek refuge in Okhema, and, in doing so, kept them safe from the black tide that threatened their existence. It hadn’t been easy, but it was necessary. Still, Mydei couldn’t shake the weight of the task. There was something in the quiet moments between each mission that always seemed to linger longer than it should.

Okhema, despite the steady pace of life, had its own quiet tensions, most of them swirling around him. He was the former prince of Kremnos, after all, and even now there were people in the city who couldn’t completely shake the rumors of his past—of betrayal, of a kingdom lost. The murmurs had faded over time, but the shadow remained, hovering just out of reach.

But Mydei didn’t focus on the whispers. He had made a choice to be here. To serve Okhema and protect the people who had given him a second chance. And that was enough for him.

He took a slow, steady breath, the evening air cool on his skin. Okhema had come to feel like home, but there was a certain weight to it—the constant hum of movement, of people depending on the Heirs, on him. He couldn’t help but feel the burden of that weight on his shoulders, even now.

A noise from behind him broke his thoughts. Soft footsteps on the stone rooftop. Mydei didn’t have to turn to know who it was. He’d been expecting Phainon. The man’s presence had always been a constant, even in moments like this, when everything else around him was still.

Phainon didn’t speak at first, simply standing a few feet away, letting the quiet settle between them. The evening’s calmness seemed to wash over them both, the city still below, alive but distant.

“I thought I might find you up here,” Phainon said at last, his voice quiet but warm. It was a typical greeting, but the way he spoke it held something else—something unspoken. Phainon always had that way of making his presence known, not just through words, but through his very being.

Mydei glanced at him over his shoulder, offering a small nod. “It’s peaceful here,” he said simply, his tone measured, avoiding anything more. The words felt familiar, but not too heavy. He wasn’t sure how to explain it, but Phainon’s presence often felt like an anchor, a grounding force in the ever-shifting world they moved through.

Phainon took a step closer, his gaze drifting out toward the horizon. He didn’t press Mydei, didn’t ask too many questions. That was how Phainon always was—observing, understanding, and giving space when needed. It was one of the things that made him so easy to be around.

For a while, neither of them spoke. Mydei’s thoughts wandered, but he kept them guarded. It wasn’t as though he was uncomfortable with Phainon’s company—it was more that sometimes, in these moments of stillness, the weight of everything else came crashing down.

Finally, Phainon broke the silence. “You did well out there,” he said quietly, his voice steady. “The new recruits will be safe here.”

Mydei offered a small, almost imperceptible rare smile, though it didn’t quite reach his eyes. “They’ll be safe, yes,” he agreed, his voice neutral. “It’s all we can do, really.”

Phainon looked over at him, and for a moment, Mydei caught the faintest glimmer of something in his expression—something soft, but it was gone before Mydei could fully understand it.

“I’m glad you’re back,” Phainon said, his words simple, but there was a sincerity in them that Mydei felt more deeply than he let on.

Mydei nodded, his smile faltering for a second. “It was necessary,” he said, the weight of those words hanging in the air between them. “But we can’t stop now.”

The silence between them stretched again, but this time it felt comfortable —neither of them needing to speak. They both understood the weight of their roles, of the unspoken responsibility that came with being part of the Heirs. There was no need for further words, not in this moment.

“Deliverer,” Mydei said after a moment, his tone quieter, lacking the biting edge it usually has. “you’ve been distant lately.”

Phainon’s gaze flickered for a moment, but his expression remained calm. “I’m fine, Mydei. Just… thinking.”

There was something in his words that didn’t quite match the calmness of his demeanor. Mydei caught it, but he chose not to press further. Not yet. If Phainon wanted to talk, he would. If not, Mydei could wait.

“I’m here if you need me,” Mydei said simply, his voice calm and steady as ever. “You know that.”

Phainon offered a small, genuine smile, his eyes meeting Mydei’s. “I know.”

And with that, the two of them stood side by side, the city of Okhema stretching out before them, its life continuing undisturbed beneath their feet. The weight of their thoughts hung heavy, but neither spoke of it—at least, not yet.

Mydei stepped away from the edge of the rooftop, his fingers trailing along the stone railing. The city sprawled below him, familiar and constant, its quiet hum settling into his bones. As he descended from the rooftop, the weight of the mission he had completed felt both lighter and heavier in equal measure. The recruits were safe for now, their journey toward Okhema secured. He had done his duty, and yet, a strange feeling lingered in the back of his mind, something unnameable but pressing.

His thoughts wandered back to the day’s events—the quiet faces of the villagers he had met, those who still hesitated at the gates of Okhema. He knew why. Kremnos was his past, a past he couldn’t escape. The name still haunted him, despite all he had done. He wasn’t blind to the way the people of Okhema watched him, the way their voices hushed when he passed. There were those who respected him, yes, but there were always whispers, always the sting of doubt that clung to him like a second skin.

Yet despite all that, Mydei couldn’t bring himself to care. Not in the way they thought. He wasn’t here for their acceptance. He had his purpose now, and that was enough. He had learned long ago that there was no use in chasing approval that would never come. The people of Okhema needed protection, and that was what he could give them. What he had chosen to give them.

He made his way through the quiet streets, taking in the familiar sights—the soft glow of lamps lighting the paths, the distant clang of the blacksmith’s hammer, the lull of voices as people finished their day’s work. Okhema was thriving, despite everything. Despite the black tide, despite the constant strain of their mission. There was a kind of life here, something that felt worth fighting for.

As he walked through the city, Mydei could feel the weight of the day’s success slowly ebbing away. There was always more to be done, but for now, the quiet was a comfort. He paused in the square, watching as the last of the market vendors packed up their goods. It was a simple scene, but it reminded him of why he had come to Okhema in the first place. To protect this. To protect the simple moments, the ones that held everything together.

He leaned against the stone wall of one of the buildings, his arms folded across his chest, the quiet of the city settling around him. For a brief moment, Mydei allowed himself to relax, to just be here. His thoughts lingered on the faces of the new recruits, the lives he had just saved. He could see them in his mind—nervous, uncertain, but ultimately grateful.

A sound behind him broke the calm, and Mydei straightened. His gaze flickered over his shoulder, but there was no tension in his posture. The footsteps were too soft to belong to anyone else.

It was Phainon again, he’d followed him. Mydei didn’t turn around at first, letting Phainon approach without interruption. He was used to the quiet comfort of their shared silences. Phainon stood by him now, a slight distance away, but still close enough that Mydei could feel the subtle shift in the air when he was near.

“Is everything alright?” Phainon asked, his voice steady and calm, as it always was.

Mydei nodded, not bothering to explain further. “It’s fine. I was just thinking.”

Phainon’s gaze softened, though he didn’t press. “It’s good to think. Sometimes it’s the only way to clear your head.”

Mydei met his eyes for a moment, his gaze steady. Phainon’s presence was always reassuring, his quiet confidence a balm to Mydei’s more turbulent thoughts. The city was safe for now, and despite everything, Mydei was certain of his place here. There was no doubt in him, not now. Not anymore.

“I’ll join the others soon,” Mydei said, pushing himself off the stone wall, his posture shifting back into his usual resolute stance. “But for now, this moment is enough.”

Phainon didn’t respond at first, but Mydei could feel the unspoken understanding between them. They both knew the weight of their responsibilities, the endless mission they carried. It would never stop, not until the black tide was gone, and Okhema was safe. But even now, in these quiet moments, Mydei found a kind of peace.

After a few beats of silence, Phainon nodded, his gaze moving to the horizon. “I’ll walk with you,” he said softly, as if that were all that was needed.

And so, they walked side by side through the streets of Okhema, the city’s steady hum surrounding them. There was no urgency in their steps, no need for words. The city was safe, for now. That was enough.

As Mydei and Phainon continued their quiet walk, the air shifted once again. It wasn’t the normal pulse of the city, but something deeper— something that made the hairs on the back of Mydei’s neck stand up. He could feel the pull, the growing sense of purpose that had always guided him. Phainon, sensing the change, stopped and turned toward him, his expression unreadable.

“Time to go,” Phainon said, his voice steady. “They’re waiting for us.”

And just like that, the moment of normalcy slipped away, replaced by a heavy weight. “Lets go.” Mydei murmured, walking past Phainon.

The Vortex of Genesis had grown quieter as more of the Heirs arrived. Mydei stood slightly apart from the group, watching the steady weaving of Aglaea’s golden threads and the quiet, confident presence of Tribbie. There was an unspoken understanding among them all—though they hadn’t yet spoken of it, everyone could feel the shift in the air.

Castorice was there too, standing in her usual quiet manner, her presence somehow both unsettling and reassuring in its stillness. Mydei had always known she embodied death itself, and though he, as an immortal, would never experience it the way others did, there was something about Castorice that reminded him of the children from Kremnos—the ones who had lived despite the harshness of their world.

It wasn’t the fear of death that Mydei felt around her, but the deep understanding of loss. Death wasn’t a stranger to him—it was something he had witnessed firsthand in countless battles, in the fall of his kingdom, in the lives lost every day to the black tide. But with Castorice, it was different. There was no fear in her, only an unwavering, quiet reverence for what had to be. The way she kept her distance from him, though she never meant to isolate him, felt like a silent respect for the lives they had lived.

As the others spoke in hushed tones, Castorice approached Mydei, her presence as soft as the whisper of a breeze. She didn’t say anything at first, simply standing a few feet away, as if waiting for the right moment. Mydei turned slightly, acknowledging her without words.

“Sir Mydei,” Castorice’s voice was soft, but there was no hesitation in her words. She spoke with the same respect she gave everyone. “You’ve been quiet today.”

Mydei met her gaze, his eyes searching hers. Though her blindfold obscured her vision, there was something in her posture that suggested a deeper awareness, an understanding that didn’t need sight to perceive. She knew.

“I’ve been thinking,” he replied slowly, his voice steady but more reflective than usual. “About what we’re facing. The news we’re about to get, it’s bound to be unsettling.”

Castorice nodded, though her face remained unreadable, as it always did. “The threads are tangled. Too many strands are pulling in different directions. But we will face it together, as we always have.”

There was an odd comfort in her words, simple as they were. Mydei could feel the quiet reassurance in her presence. It wasn’t just her words—it was the calm certainty with which she spoke them. Even if death was her domain, Castorice seemed more at peace with it than anyone else in the room.

He exhaled slowly, letting her words sink in. “I know,” he said softly. “But sometimes… it’s hard to see what’s ahead.”

The corners of Castorice’s lips quirked upward ever so slightly, as if understanding his sentiment. “None of us can see it, Sir Mydei. But we will face it. You are not alone.”

He nodded slowly, his voice quieter now. “Thank you, Castorice.”

She offered him a nod, her head tilting slightly as if acknowledging his words without the need for further explanation. “It is nothing, Sir Mydei.”

And with that, she stepped back, keeping her respectful distance once more, as was her way. Mydei watched her go, the quiet weight of her presence lingering in the air. For all her power, for all the mystery she held, there was something human about her. It was a reminder that even in the face of death, one could find peace, even if it was just for a moment.

The silence that followed was almost suffocating as Aglaea and Tribbie stepped forward. The golden threads that flowed from Aglaea’s fingertips seemed to hum, the air thick with tension as the news was about to be delivered. Tribbie’s gaze swept over the room, sharp and calculated, her focus unwavering.

“We’ve been waiting,” she said, her voice low but firm. “It’s time.”

Mydei’s chest tightened, his heart beating faster with the weight of the words they were about to speak. The unease that had settled in his stomach only deepened.

“The constellation of Kephale has been lit,” Aglaea’s voice echoed, the finality of her words striking him like a thunderclap. “The Titan of Creation is no more. His flame has been taken.”

A wave of shock rippled through the group, but Mydei stood still, his gaze unwavering. The room fell into a stunned silence. Kephale—the God of Creation—had fallen. The implications were far-reaching, and yet, all Mydei could think about was the question that hung in the air:

Who had done it?

The air in the Vortex of Genesis had grown thick with tension after the announcement of Kephale’s fall. The Heirs stood in uneasy silence, their minds racing with the implications. Kephale had been one of the ancient Titans, a force of creation itself, and the idea that someone had defeated him was unsettling enough. But the fact that they had no idea who had done it— or worse, why—was more than troubling.

Phainon stood at the edge of the group, his usual composure masking the thoughts swirling in his mind. The Heirs exchanged quiet words, some speaking in hushed tones while others stood still, lost in thought. They all knew that whoever had done this had to have been close to them, someone who knew their identities, their weaknesses, yet chose not to join their cause. The thought gnawed at Mydei’s chest as he stood in the center of the group, feeling the weight of the unknown pressing on him.

Trianne spoke first, her voice sharp but tinged with doubt. “Whoever did this, they knew us. They knew what we were fighting for. Kephale’s fall— it’s no accident.”

Trinnon, usually silent but ever vigilant, nodded grimly. “Someone wanted to destroy what we’ve built. It doesn’t make sense. Why would they choose to take down a Titan, and yet refuse to join us? It’s… deliberate.”

Tribbie’s eyes narrowed, her arms crossed as she scanned the room. “It doesn’t feel right. Whoever did this is playing a game. They know who we are. They know what we’re trying to protect, and yet they chose to destroy Kephale. The Titan of Creation—gone, just like that. But why?”

Aglaea remained silent for a moment, her golden threads flickering around her as if listening to the whispers in the room. Finally, she spoke, her voice low and calm. “The threads tell me nothing, only that the balance is shifting. This is not just a victory, but a disruption. Whoever has taken Kephale’s flame… they’re a threat we don’t fully understand yet.”

Mydei couldn’t help but feel the weight of her words. It was clear now— this wasn’t just about victory. It was about someone making a statement. Someone had taken Kephale’s flame, but the reasons behind it were still shrouded in mystery. Whoever had done it was out there, and they were coming for them.

“Mydei?” Phainon’s voice broke through his thoughts. “Are you all right?”

Mydei’s gaze snapped to Phainon, his features hardening for a moment. “I’m fine,” he muttered, but the edge in his voice was unmistakable. He knew Phainon’s presence was meant to offer comfort, but in that moment, it felt like an intrusion. The weight of the situation was heavy enough without having to explain himself.

Phainon’s eyes softened, though he remained silent. He seemed to sense the growing tension in Mydei, but said nothing, waiting for him to speak, to act, to lead. As the Heirs continued to discuss their options, Mydei found himself withdrawing, his thoughts turning inward.

He didn’t respond, he needed time to think alone. That’s right—The bath houses.

Mydei’s footsteps echoed softly on the stone floor as he made his way to the private bathhouse. The hallways were quiet, a welcome silence after the clamor of the Vortex. His mind churned with thoughts, a growing sense of unease gnawing at him. The news of Kephale’s fall still lingered in his mind, but there was something else—something that had been building steadily over the past few days.

He didn’t like it. He didn’t like it at all. The tension in the air was thick enough to slice through, and the uncertainty was eating away at him. The very fact that one of their own had defeated a Titan—someone who knew them, yet chose to remain outside their ranks—bothered him. It should’ve been straightforward, but it wasn’t. He couldn’t shake the feeling that the world was about to tip, and none of them were prepared for it.

Pushing open the door to the bathhouse, he let out a quiet breath, the warm air soothing the tightness in his shoulders. The steam rising from the water felt like a brief escape, a chance to center himself, even if only for a moment.

But as he stepped in, his gaze snapped to the door. There, standing in the shadows, was Phainon. How did he even get here so fast? He could’ve sworn Phainon had been behind him a moment ago.

Phainon’s calm demeanor unsettled him. He wasn’t surprised to see him, but the fact that Phainon was just standing there—silent, watching, unnervingly still—didn’t sit right with Mydei. His posture was unnaturally relaxed, too controlled, like he didn’t have a care in the world. The slight tilt of his head, the almost serene expression—there was something about it that felt off.

“What the hell are you doing here?” Mydei said, his tone sharp and biting as he crossed his arms, a flicker of annoyance rising in his chest. “You know, for someone who acts like he’s too busy to help, you sure spend a lot of time lurking around, don’t you?”

Phainon didn’t flinch. In fact, he seemed almost… pleased. A faint smile tugged at his lips, though it was subtle, more like a quiet amusement.

“I thought you might need company,” Phainon replied, his voice unnervingly calm. Too calm.

Mydei raised an eyebrow, the unease in his gut growing. “Company?” he repeated, taking a step closer. “You’ve got to be joking. You’re the last person I’d want company from. You’re way too—”

He trailed off, his words hanging in the air as he finally let himself get a better look at Phainon. The way Phainon’s eyes didn’t leave him, the almost reverent focus he had—it was strange. Too focused. Mydei frowned, pushing the feeling of discomfort aside. This wasn’t like Phainon. He was always composed, sure, but this was something different.

“You’re… unnervingly calm,” Mydei finally said, his voice laced with disbelief.

Phainon’s smile widened slightly, though there was an odd tenderness in it, an intensity that felt too much. “I’m just here to keep you company, Mydei. If that’s alright with you.” His words were soft, but they carried a weight that Mydei couldn’t quite place.

Mydei’s eyes narrowed, something in his chest tightening at the casualness with which Phainon spoke. “You’re weird,” he spat, a hint of derision in his voice. “You never act like this. Did you hit your head, Deliverer ?”

Phainon didn’t respond to the mockery, his gaze fixed on Mydei with an unsettling intensity. “You’re always so tense,” Phainon said, taking a step closer, his voice still too calm, too smooth. “I thought you’d enjoy a little company. You deserve it.”

Mydei instinctively took a step back, his body bristling with unease. “What the hell is going on with you?” he asked, his voice harder now, tinged with a sharp edge. “You’re not acting like yourself. What’s the game?”

Phainon’s smile didn’t falter, but his presence seemed to grow more imposing, the air around him thick with something Mydei couldn’t quite understand. It wasn’t anger. It wasn’t even annoyance. It was something darker, more… unsettling.

“No game,” Phainon replied softly, his voice dropping to almost a whisper. “Just… a little bit of peace. Don’t you want that, Mydei? To just be… understood?”

Mydei stared at him, unable to shake the feeling that Phainon was getting too close. This wasn’t right. Phainon had never been this forward. They were allies, yes, and rivals, but this… this was different.

“You’re getting way too close for comfort,” Mydei said sharply, his patience thinning. “If you’re looking for something, you’re wasting your time.”

Phainon’s smile remained, but now there was something in his eyes— something that sent a cold shiver down Mydei’s spine. “I’m not looking for anything, Mydei,” he murmured, his voice low and almost reverent. “I’m just here… for you.”

Before Mydei could respond, the door creaked open slightly, and Phainon stepped forward again, the distance between them closing faster than Mydei was prepared for. Phainon’s presence was suffocating now, too close, too intense.

“I’m always here,” Phainon said, his voice soft and steady, yet carrying an unnerving edge. “I won’t leave you, Mydei. You can’t push me away.”

Mydei felt his heartbeat quicken, his instincts screaming at him to step back. But he held his ground, eyes narrowing. “What’s wrong with you, you damn bastard?”

But Phainon didn’t even flinch. His gaze softened, the hint of something almost worshipful in his eyes, as he leaned closer still. “I’m not leaving. You’ll see.”

Mydei stepped back quickly, his heart pounding as he finally broke the tension. “Get out, Phainon,” he said, forgoing his title, his voice tight with anger and discomfort. “Just… leave me alone.”

Phainon’s expression flickered, but he didn’t push any further. With a final, lingering glance, he turned and left the bathhouse, the door swinging shut behind him.

Mydei was left standing in the quiet, the strange feeling lingering in the air. He didn’t know what was happening, but something inside him told him this wasn’t over. Whatever was growing between them, whatever strange pull had settled into the air between him and Phainon, was far from normal. He sank into the warm water, letting the heat seep into his bones. The quiet of the room was a welcome escape, the only sound the soft trickle of water as it splashed gently against the stone.

Everything is fine. Everything has to be fine.

But as he sat there, the weight of the world pressing on his shoulders, he couldn’t shake the feeling that it was all slipping through his fingers. There was so much wrong with everything. The deaths. The betrayals. The growing unrest.

And then there was Phainon.

Mydei closed his eyes, letting the water surround him as his mind raced. It was easy to dismiss the tension between them, to pretend it didn’t exist. But it was there. It’s always been there.

He didn’t know why Phainon’s words seemed to haunt him. Maybe because, for the first time, someone really saw him. The vulnerability he tried so hard to hide—it was there, open and raw. Phainon knew that. Phainon always knew.

The door opened behind him with a soft creak. Mydei didn’t need to turn around to know who it was.

Phainon stepped inside, his presence like a shadow in the dim light.

“You’re still here,” Mydei said, trying to sound unaffected. But his voice was thick with something he couldn’t name.

“I said I’d be here if you needed someone,” Phainon replied, his voice low, almost a whisper.

Mydei wanted to push him away. He wanted to tell Phainon to leave, to stop intruding on his solitude. But he didn’t.

“Just don’t,” Mydei muttered, his head dropping into his hands.

Phainon didn’t press. Instead, he stood by the edge of the bath, watching him with an unreadable expression.

It wasn’t until Mydei finally lifted his head that Phainon spoke again, his voice softer this time.

“I don’t expect you to say anything you’re not ready for,” Phainon said quietly. “But I’m not going anywhere, Mydei. Whatever this is… we’ll face it together.”

Mydei felt his chest tighten at the words. He wanted to brush them off, to tell Phainon it didn’t matter, but… God, it mattered.

nd still racing, but the warmth of the bath started to work its calming magic. The steam curled around him, soothing the tightness in his chest. The longer he sat there, the more the silence seemed to press in, not suffocating, but oddly comforting.

He closed his eyes again, trying to force the noise in his mind to quiet, but the faintest sound of movement drew him back to the present.

When he opened his eyes, Phainon was standing there, looking down at him.

“Mydei,” Phainon said, his voice softer than usual. “I’m not leaving.”

Mydei said nothing in response, but he didn’t ask Phainon to leave, either.

Without another word, Phainon undressed and slowly eased into the water, his movements quiet but deliberate. There was something oddly peaceful about it—the way he slid in, his presence filling the space without needing to dominate it.

Phainon sat beside him, the heat of the water rising between them. For a moment, nothing was said. Just the sound of water shifting as they both settled into the bath.

Mydei let the silence stretch longer, feeling the pull of exhaustion but refusing to give in. Something in him wanted to keep fighting—to stay awake, to hold onto control. But then, just as he thought he might break, Phainon leaned toward him, his head slowly finding its place on Mydei’s shoulder.

Mydei tensed, just for a moment. His heart raced, expecting that pang of annoyance, the urge to shove him away, to remind Phainon of their unspoken boundaries. But instead, the feeling was different this time.

He didn’t push him away.

He didn’t say anything either.

He just let Phainon rest against him, his head light on Mydei’s shoulder, as the heat of the water surrounded them both. For some reason, the weight of Phainon’s head there felt right —like a steady anchor in the chaos of everything else.

Mydei’s heart thudded against his chest. He could feel Phainon’s breath slow, and in turn, his own pulse seemed to settle. For once, he didn’t feel the need to push away. He didn’t feel the tension building, didn’t feel like he had to maintain distance.

Just for a moment, he allowed himself to just be there—present, in this shared space.

Neither of them spoke. There was no need for words. Mydei didn’t know what it meant, but something inside of him—something quiet and aching— relaxed in the stillness. He wasn’t sure if it was a fleeting comfort or something deeper, but in that instant, it didn’t matter.

The weight of the world was still there, pressing down on him, but for a few moments, it wasn’t suffocating.

He wasn’t alone.

A few weeks had passed since Castorice’s death, and the air in Okhema felt heavier. The city, with its familiar rhythm of life, seemed untouched by the monumental shifts that had just occurred. But to Mydei, it was as if the world had been tilted, and no matter how he tried, he couldn’t find his footing again.

The death of Castorice, the fall of Thanatos’s constellation—he had seen it coming, in some strange way. But that didn’t make it easier to bear. The loss had hit him harder than he expected, though he refused to show it. His mind still raced with questions that had no answers. How had it happened? Who was behind it all? The Heirs had been left with so many unanswered questions, yet they couldn’t afford to dwell. Every day brought another challenge, another problem to solve.

Still, Mydei found himself reflecting, sitting alone in his chambers as the sun dipped lower behind the stone walls of Okhema. The silence weighed on him more than anything. He let his gaze fall to the window, watching as the city faded into shadows.

A cold breeze slipped through the cracks, making the candles flicker, and Mydei’s thoughts drifted back to the events of the past few weeks. He had kept his distance from the others, burying himself in tasks and reports, avoiding any deep conversations about what had happened. What could he say? He had lost so many already—he had to keep moving forward.

But sometimes, in the quiet moments like this, the melancholy crept in. He didn’t want to admit it, but the absence of Castorice lingered in the back of his mind, like an open wound. And with each passing day, more constellations flickered in and out, and the heaviness in his chest only grew.

He turned from the window, the room around him feeling colder as he pushed the thoughts away. There was no room for sentiment. He was Mydei, a soldier, a protector of Okhema. He didn’t have time for weakness.

Yet, even as he tried to steel himself, his mind kept drifting to Phainon.

Phainon had been with him more often recently, in ways that Mydei hadn’t quite expected. The Deliverer, his greatest foe, yet also his friend, had become a fixture in Mydei’s life. At first, it was just small things—an offer of help, a word of reassurance. But now, it was different. Phainon was there, lingering, his presence constant and undeniable.

Mydei had never thought much of it at first. But now? Now it was becoming harder to ignore. Phainon’s support, his unwavering attention—it felt… comforting, in a way. But that thought unsettled him.

Stop, Mydei told himself sharply. He couldn’t afford to go down that road. There was no time for distractions, no time for feelings. Not now. Not when Okhema was so fragile, so vulnerable. He couldn’t let himself fall into that trap.

Yet, despite his best efforts, his mind kept returning to the same thought: Phainon. What did this mean? What was he supposed to do with this feeling that had no name?

He clenched his fists, shaking his head to rid himself of the thought. There was no place for this. Not with everything going on. Not when they were all in danger when the Titans were falling one by one.

The room fell silent again, the only sound the flicker of candlelight and the distant hum of Okhema outside. Mydei stood from his seat, moving toward the window once more. The city was so still tonight, almost as if it, too, was holding its breath.

Focus, he reminded himself. You’re not the same person you were before. You must fulfill. Don’t lose sight of it.

With a deep breath, Mydei turned from the window and walked toward the door, ready to step back into the world outside. There were no more quiet moments for him. Not now. Not while the world seemed to be crumbling around him.

And yet, even as he left his chambers, the feeling remained. Phainon. Just the thought of him brought a tightness in his chest, a pull he couldn’t explain. But Mydei kept walking, knowing that distractions, feelings, all of it would have to wait.

There was more at stake now. There always was. And he couldn’t afford to falter. Not for anyone.

Not even for Phainon.

The sun hung low in the sky as Mydei made his way through the streets, the day’s duties finally drawing to a close. His steps were slow, the weight of the hours spent running errands and coordinating the city’s defenses pressing on him. It had been a long day, one that had passed in a blur of faces and voices, all of them asking for his attention.

Just as he thought he could finally enjoy some solitude, a familiar voice broke through the bustling sounds of the street.

“Mydei!”

He turned to see Phainon, standing beneath a nearby tree, looking up at something with a mixture of frustration and happiness at seeing him. Mydei raised an eyebrow, curious.

As he stepped closer, the reason for Phainon’s distraction became clear. A small, fluffy cat was perched high in the branches, looking down with wide eyes. Below the tree, a young girl, no older than five or six, clutched at Phainon’s shirt, her face a mix of distress and hope.

“My cat, my cat’s stuck…!” she cried, her voice trembling with desperation.

Mydei couldn’t help but smile—well, more like a smirk—as he watched Phainon attempt to coax the cat down. Phainon was shifting from foot to foot, clearly trying to figure out the best way to reach the tree’s highest branch.

“Need a hand, Phainon?” Mydei called, amused.

Phainon looked down at him, his face breaking into that characteristic, charming grin. “You’d think after everything, a cat would be the least I could manage,” he said, his tone light, though Mydei could hear the hint of frustration beneath it.

Mydei’s lips twitched upward, the fondness in his tone clear even if his words were meant to be mocking. “I never thought I’d see the day where the great Deliverer struggles with a cat.”

Phainon laughed, shaking his head. “You’re not the only one.”

With a final stretch, Phainon finally managed to reach the cat, coaxing it down with surprising ease. It mewed contentedly as Phainon lowered it to the ground, handing it back to the girl with a soft smile on his face.

“There you go,” Phainon said, his voice warm. He patted the girl gently on the head, his expression softening even more. “Just be careful next time, alright?”

The girl smiled brightly, hugging her cat to her chest. “Thank you, Mister!” she exclaimed before scampering off, cat in tow.

Mydei watched the exchange, something stirring in his chest that he couldn’t quite place. Moments like these—when Phainon let his guard down, even just a little—made Mydei feel something more . A flicker of something deeper.

“Of course, you’d have a soft spot for children.” Mydei said, unsurprised.

Phainon chuckled and turned to face him, clearly not minding the mockery. “Everyone has their soft spots, Mydei. Even you.”

Mydei shook his head, his lips twitching upwards as a small smile formed on his face. “Maybe.”

It wasn’t long before Phainon swept him back into the whirlwind of work once again. There was always something to do, some task that needed attention, and Phainon wasted no time in dragging Mydei through every corner of the city. Mydei had expected to find some quiet space to think, to reflect, but it seemed Phainon had other plans.

The people of Okhema, as they always did, greeted Phainon with warmth and respect. His easy smile, his calm presence—he was a beacon in the chaos. Mydei, on the other hand, often found himself met with hesitant glances. Some recognized him, others didn’t, but the whispers about his past were never far behind. He had once been the prince of Kremnos, and no matter how hard he tried, that shadow would always follow him.

It was in these moments that the contrast between him and Phainon became painfully clear. Where Phainon was accepted without question, Mydei was met with a cool distance, even when he worked tirelessly beside the people to protect them.

They stopped by a vendor selling fresh bread, and Phainon exchanged a few words with the merchant, laughing softly. The vendor smiled warmly at him, nodding, but when the merchant turned to Mydei, it was a more formal acknowledgment, a polite nod rather than the friendliness Phainon had received.

Phainon noticed the difference, but he didn’t comment. Instead, he patted Mydei on the shoulder as they moved on.

“You’re doing fine, Mydei,” Phainon said, his tone soothing but with that underlying sincerity that always seemed to soften Mydei’s sharp edges. “The people are grateful for your work. Don’t forget that.”

Mydei gritted his teeth, pushing the thought aside. “I know,” he said, his voice a little harsher than he intended.

They continued their rounds, moving from one task to the next, the day slipping away faster than Mydei had expected. Despite his internal conflict, there was a part of him that didn’t mind Phainon’s constant presence. It was easy, almost comfortable in a way he couldn’t quite explain.

The day had bled into twilight, painting the sky in hues of burnt orange and deep indigo. Mydei stood in the courtyard of Okhema, his posture still and deliberate, as if the weariness in his body wasn’t there. The faint hum of the bustling city was distant now, replaced by the quieter murmurs of wind through the old trees and cracked stone walls.

Phainon stood a few paces away, leaning lazily against the remnants of a fountain. His gaze, sharp and unwavering, lingered on Mydei as though watching him was its own form of meditation. The silence between them stretched—not uncomfortable, but unspoken words weighed heavy in the air.

“You didn’t have to stick around,” Mydei said finally, his voice calm, and low. He glanced over his shoulder at Phainon, his expression unreadable.

Phainon straightened, pushing off the fountain with a fluid movement. “And leave you to your brooding?” he said lightly, though the warmth in his tone

softened the jab. “You’d work yourself into an early grave if you weren’t… well, immortal.”

Mydei huffed quietly, the closest thing to a laugh he’d allow. “That’s not a concern for me, but you should rest.”

Phainon walked closer, closing the space between them until he stood at Mydei’s side. His presence wasn’t overwhelming, it felt natural. “I’m resting right now,” he said, gesturing vaguely. “In my own way.”

Mydei shook his head but didn’t press the matter. His gaze turned back toward the horizon, the last vestiges of sunlight sinking below the edge of the world. For a while, neither of them spoke, the silence settling in comfortably.

“I’ve noticed you’ve been more…constant,” no maybe that wasn’t the right word,

“No, absent lately,” Mydei said, his words slow, measured. “It’s unusual.”

Phainon gave a small, half-smile, tilting his head slightly. “Is that your way of saying you’ve missed me?”

“No,” Mydei said flatly, but his tone lacked bite. “It’s just an observation.”

Phainon chuckled softly, the sound low and warm. “You’re welcome, by the way. For all my efforts.”

“Efforts?” Mydei raised a brow.

“Keeping you alive, keeping you sane… the usual,” Phainon replied, his smile widening. “You’d be lost without me.” It sounded like teasing.

This time, Mydei didn’t respond. His expression was distant, thoughtful as if weighing something in his mind. He shifted his weight slightly, his hand brushing against the hilt of his blade out of habit. Finally, he glanced at Phainon, his eyes steady.

“You’re a good person,” he said quietly, the words slipping out almost like an afterthought.

Phainon froze for half a heartbeat, his sharp features softening in an instant. For all his confidence, the sincerity of the statement hit him like a blade to the chest.

“You… think so?” Phainon asked, his voice quieter now, more genuine.

“I know you are,” Mydei replied, his gaze steady. There was no humor in his tone, no attempt to mask the truth of what he said. “It’s not a matter of opinion.”

The simplicity of the statement lingered in the air, more impactful for its honesty. Mydei turned his head away, his focus shifting back to the horizon. “That’s all I meant to say.”

He began to walk off, his figure cutting a stark silhouette against the fading light.

Phainon stood frozen, watching him leave, his heart racing in a way that felt unfamiliar—unsettling, even. Mydei’s words echoed in his mind, over and over, louder than anything else around him.

You’re a good person.

A faint smile curved Phainon’s lips, but it wasn’t his usual smirk. It was something smaller, quieter, but infinitely more uncanny.

He was going to make sure Mydei never had a reason to doubt that.

Phainon now stood alone in the courtyard, the last light of day slowly fading into night. He exhaled, and for a brief moment, his chest felt tight— almost like something had lodged itself deep inside him, unwilling to leave. You’re a good person, Mydei’s voice echoed in his mind.

It was strange, how those words had hit him. Not the usual words of admiration or praise he was accustomed to hearing, but something rawer.

Something that felt too real, too vulnerable. Phainon chuckled softly under his breath, the sound hollow in the silence.

You’re a good person.

He repeated the words, rolling them around in his mind like they were some kind of puzzle to solve. Mydei’s voice lingered, just as clear as when he had spoken them, but Phainon felt the weight of them differently now. His chest tightened again, the sensation growing heavier with each passing second.

Is that what I am? Phainon thought, his fingers idly playing with the edges of his sleeve. A good person? Or am I just pretending to be?

His eyes dropped to his hand, and he noticed the golden butterfly that had perched there. The delicate creature, a nymph from Aglaea, fluttered its wings gently, unaware of the dark thoughts swirling in Phainon’s mind. It was beautiful in its fragility, a soft glimmer of gold in the growing dark.

You’re fragile too, he thought, his thumb brushing over the nymph’s wings with the slightest pressure. Just like Mydei. So beautiful. So fragile.

For a moment, he let himself imagine what it would be like to protect it. To guard that fragile beauty. But then the thought shifted, twisting into something darker.

What if I could be the one to break it?

The idea surfaced so suddenly, like a sharp, cold breath. Phainon paused, his fingers hovering over the butterfly’s delicate wings. Could I be his soft spot? He thought about Mydei again— always guarded, always distant . But that wasn’t enough for Phainon, was it? No. He didn’t want to be just the constant . He didn’t want to be a comfort . He wanted to be the one to shatter him, just enough to claim him entirely.

A soft laugh escaped him, low and unsettling. He glanced down at the butterfly again, its tiny legs scrambling, trying to regain its balance on his hand. His breath hitched, just for a second, as if the mere thought of breaking that delicate form had caused something inside him to tremble.

But it was weak —that’s what he told himself. Fragile. Weak. He couldn’t help but feel the need to control it, to hold it, to claim it for himself.

Phainon’s fingers tightened around the butterfly slowly, just a little at first, testing its response. It squirmed, but it didn’t fly away. No, it was stuck. Stuck with him.

He leaned down, his voice barely a whisper, a soft murmur just for the butterfly. “I wonder if I could make you my soft spot,” he whispered, his voice laced with both curiosity and something worse, something more possessive. “I wonder if I could make you need me… just like I need you.”

The butterfly twitched again, its tiny form shuddering against the increasing pressure. Phainon’s grip didn’t loosen; instead, he applied just a little more force, feeling its wings buckle beneath his fingers.

So fragile, he thought again, the words tasting bitter in his mouth. I could crush you, just like that. You’d never be able to escape me.

He held it for a moment longer, letting the sensation of its life beneath his hand pulse through him. His chest tightened again, but this time, he didn’t fight it. He didn’t want to. He wanted the feeling to last, to stretch out, to savor the power he had over this little creature, this fragile thing that couldn’t possibly escape him.

But the butterfly’s movements became slower, weaker. It was breaking. It couldn’t hold on for much longer.

Without another thought, Phainon squeezed harder, just enough to feel the frail body snap under his touch. The delicate sound of crushed wings filled the air, but the butterfly didn’t die. It fluttered weakly, still breathing, still alive .

A low chuckle rumbled from Phainon’s chest. He didn’t release it. Instead, he held it in his palm as it gasped for air, its movements strained, broken. His fingers curled around it like a cage, keeping it just alive enough for him to watch.

“I’m still here, though, aren’t I? I’ll stay with you till the end because I’m a good person , ” Phainon muttered to the butterfly, his voice taking on a strange tenderness. He was gentle now, holding the broken creature with a tenderness that betrayed the violence he’d just enacted. “You don’t get to escape. Not yet.”

The nymph’s wings flapped weakly, but there was no strength left in its body. It was dying, struggling for breath in Phainon’s hand, and he watched it, the twisted, agonizing fascination holding him captive.

He thought of Mydei again— strong, but so fragile . How long before Phainon could make him his? How long before Mydei would need him as much as he needed Mydei?

With a soft, almost reverent sigh, Phainon closed his hand completely, feeling the last of the butterfly’s tremors fade. He held it like that for a few more seconds, savoring the sensation of its struggle, before he finally opened his palm to let it fall.

The nymph crumpled, its tiny golden body still and lifeless. Phainon didn’t flinch. He simply looked at it, his mind already drifting back to thoughts of Mydei, wondering just how long it would take before the man would be just as broken, just as lost to him.

I will be everything to you, Phainon thought, his eyes narrowing, his heart beating faster with each passing second. And when you need me, when you’re completely in my grasp… I will never let you go.

With one last, quiet glance at the butterfly, Phainon turned and walked away, the quiet weight of his obsession—love, growing bit by bit. .

.
