The world was dim, drenched in an ethereal twilight that flickered between reality and something other . Mydei stood amidst shifting shadows, the

ground beneath him unsteady, as though it could slip away at any moment.

He knew this was a dream.

And yet, the air felt too heavy, thick with something he could neither name nor shake.

The sky above was vast and empty—no stars, no constellations, only an endless black void that pressed down upon him like a weight. The silence here was unnatural, humming with an absence that made his pulse quicken.

Then— a flicker.

Three figures stood ahead of him, their forms wavering as if they were barely clinging to existence.

The Triplets.

Tribbie. Trianne. Trinnon.

At first, they were fused together, their three faces overlapping in an eerie, seamless blend—one entity, three minds, held together by something unseen. Their presence felt familiar yet foreign, as though they weren’t supposed to be here , like this.

But as Mydei watched, something began to change.

The force binding them started to slip. A crack split through their unified form, jagged and unnatural, spreading like fractures in glass. Slowly, agonizingly, the Triplets began to tear apart .

Tribbie clutched at her head, her fingers digging into her scalp as if trying to hold herself together. Trianne staggered backward, her body flickering, edges curling inward like paper catching fire. Trinnon simply stood still, her eyes hollow, expression unreadable, but Mydei could feel it—the unraveling, the losing.

They are breaking.

A feeling of unease coiled in his chest, something deep and unspoken. He wanted to move, to step forward, to stop this. But his body would not obey.

The crack deepened.

Trianne let out a strangled gasp, her form flickering violently, as though something was being pulled out of her . Her lips moved, but no sound came. Her fingers stretched toward Mydei, desperate, reaching.

Trinnon’s expression didn’t change, but her body collapsed inward , folding into herself like a dying star.

And then there was Tribbie, the last one standing. She turned to Mydei, her eyes locking onto his, pleading but filled with something else.

Resignation .

Her form trembled. The force holding her in place was slipping, leaking out like light through shattered glass. And in that moment, Mydei understood— she was not trying to hold herself together.

She was trying to hold them together.

But it was too late.

A sharp, agonizing crack echoed through the void.

And then, they were gone.

Nothing remained but empty space.

And the whisper.

Faint, curling through the still air, slipping past the void to nestle itself into Mydei’s mind.

“What is left… when the binding fails?”

The words slithered against his thoughts, slipping beneath his skin, cold and final.

The emptiness stretched before him, vast and unending. His breath came slow and shallow, the weight of the silence pressing into his chest.

Then—

A new presence.

Something behind him.

He turned.

And woke up.

.

.

.

The dim light of the early morning filtered through the cracks in the walls, soft and pale. Mydei sat upright, his chest rising and falling in a steady rhythm, but his eyes were wide open, fixed on a point in the room that didn’t exist.

He didn’t move.

The dream lingered, etched into his mind like a fresh wound. The image of the Triplets breaking apart played on an endless loop in his head, each crack, each flicker, as vivid as if it had just happened before him.

But Mydei didn’t panic.

His breathing remained even, controlled, though his hands rested tensely on the fabric of the bedding beneath him, fingers curling ever so slightly.

The whisper echoed faintly in the back of his mind.

“ What is left… when the binding fails?”

It didn’t fade, nor did it deepen. It simply lingered, heavy and quiet, like a storm cloud refusing to break.

Minutes passed. Then an hour.

Mydei stayed exactly where he was, his body rigid but calm, his mind caught in the stillness between denial and acceptance. He didn’t try to make sense of it—not yet. He simply let the silence settle over him, matching its weight to the one pressing down inside him.

Eventually, his fingers loosened, the faintest tremble in their release.

His gaze shifted for the first time, falling to the floor by his bedside. His lips parted slightly, but no words came. There was no one to say them to.

Not yet.

He ran a hand over his face, the touch grounding him back into his surroundings. The faint ache in his chest remained, as though his heart had been clutched too tightly in the grip of something unseen.

Only then did Mydei stand, his movements deliberate, his expression guarded. But beneath the surface, the unease coiled and writhed, a quiet promise that the dream would not be forgotten.

He had questions.

But for now, Mydei stayed silent.

Mydei found Tribbie in the meadow near the colonnade ruins, twirling in circles as if the world itself were her dance floor. Her white robes fanned out as she spun, and she giggled softly to herself, the ornaments on her dress jingling with each step.

“Do you ever sit still?” Mydei asked, his voice low as he approached.

She stopped mid-spin, balancing on one foot like a child caught misbehaving. Her wide, playful grin softened when she saw him. She tilted her head, her hair tumbling like spun silver.

“We wondered when you would come to us!” she said, clasping her hands behind her back and rocking on her heels.

Mydei’s lips twitched faintly, the closest he’d come to a smile. “You’re more cryptic than usual,” he said.

She gasped, her expression fake offended. “ We are always clear. You’re just bad at listening!”

He sighed, rubbing a hand over his face. “Right. Well, listen to me, then. I need your help.”

Tribbie immediately brightened, bouncing closer. “You do? Finally! We were getting bored waiting for you to ask!” She clasped his hand between hers, looking up at him with wide, eager eyes. “So, what is it? Did something spooky happen? Did you see something weird? Tell us, tell us!”

He hesitated, but her sincerity—innocent and honest as it seemed—wore him down. Slowly, he relayed his dream. The splitting of the Tribios. The force that bound them came undone. The whisper that still clawed at his mind.

Tribbie listened intently, her antics momentarily subdued. She nodded along as if she understood every word, her golden eyes shimmering with something unreadable.

When he finished, she took a deep breath, her expression thoughtful.

“We know dreams can feel scary,” she said, her tone surprisingly gentle. “But they’re like puzzles De, you know? You just need to figure out what the pieces mean. And the whisper…” She trailed off, tapping a finger against her lips. “The whisper sounds important .”

“You think I don’t know that?” Mydei muttered, crossing his arms. “I need more than vague encouragement.”

Tribbie frowned, puffing out her cheeks. “ We’re not being vague! You just need to pay more attention! Dreams aren’t answers, Mydei—they’re clues!” She poked him in the chest for emphasis, her voice growing more animated. “Maybe you’re supposed to follow what’s coming undone. Maybe that’s the whole point!”

He stared at her, unamused. “You have no idea what it means either, do you?”

Her pout deepened. “Rude.” She turned away, arms crossed, before glancing back over her shoulder with a sly grin. “But fine. Think whatever you want. We still think you’re scared. That’s why you’re asking . ”

Mydei didn’t respond immediately. Her words hit closer than he wanted to admit, but he kept his expression neutral. After a long pause, he said, “If you’re so wise, tell me one thing. Is the dream a warning or a promise?”

Tribbie blinked, her grin softening into something faintly bittersweet. She reached up, brushing a strand of silver hair behind her ear.

“Both,” she said simply. “A warning is a promise if you don’t figure it out quickly.”

That was all she gave him.

Mydei stared at her, the cryptic reply sinking into his chest like a stone. Finally, he nodded once, turning to leave without another word.

Behind him, Tribbie cupped her hands to her mouth and called out playfully, “Don’t forget— we’re always right!”

As Mydei disappeared into the shadows, Tribbie’s smile lingered. She lowered her hands, her gaze softening as she murmured to herself, “The bindings are fraying… just like we knew they would.”

She spun again, her laughter trailing into the breeze, as though the heaviness of the moment hadn’t touched her at all.

Sighing, Mydei left.

As Mydei rounded the corner, he almost collided with someone, his steps halting just in time to avoid the contact. His eyes flicked up to meet Anaxa’s, the scholar’s usual distant expression unchanged, though Mydei couldn’t shake the odd sensation that prickled down his spine.

“Watch where you’re going,” Anaxa muttered, adjusting his papers, though his tone was far from irritating. He simply had the air of someone who’d right now prefer to avoid confrontation

Mydei hesitated for a moment, the sense of foreboding still lingering, but he pushed it down. “You’re distracted,” he said flatly, scanning Anaxa’s face for any hint of something unusual, though there was none.

Anaxa looked even more unamused. “Considering the situation, I don’t think that’s surprising.”

“I suppose so.” Mydei paused, the uneasy feeling pressing against his chest like an invisible weight. “You’re heading somewhere important?” He asked indifferently, though he couldn’t quite shake the feeling that something wasn’t right.

Anaxa glanced up from his papers, a brief flicker of something in his expression. “I’m always heading somewhere important, but that’s none of your concern.”

Mydei kept his gaze steady, neither pressing nor backing down. “I’ll walk with you, then.”

The two continued in silence, Mydei’s steps slightly faster than Anaxa’s, his mind still distracted by the strange foreboding sensation. He didn’t know why he felt compelled to follow the scholar, but the nagging feeling that something was wrong didn’t ease, and he couldn’t quite shake it off.

When they reached the point where Anaxa’s path veered off, Mydei stopped, his eyes lingering on the scholar for a moment longer than necessary. “Be careful,” Mydei muttered, his tone flat but not without an edge of concern, though his face didn’t betray it.

Anaxa raised a brow but said nothing, simply turning away with a slight incline of his head. “It’s just a walk, Mydei. Don’t waste your time.”

Without responding, Mydei turned and left, his steps quick and decisive. He didn’t look back, but the air felt different somehow, thicker, as though something was shifting just beyond his awareness. He kept his gaze straight ahead, trying to ignore the nagging feeling that had settled at the back of his mind.

As he passed through the winding paths, the city was quieter now, the sounds of distant chatter and footsteps fading as he walked deeper into the shadows. The usual weight of things pressing on him—the unease, the heavy burden of recent events—seemed to lift slightly, but not entirely. There was still something gnawing at him, something unresolved.

It was when he rounded a corner and saw Phainon that it returned. The man stood still, his posture tense, and there was no smile, no usual energy in the way he carried himself. Phainon simply raised a hand, offering a brief wave before turning away, and walking off without another word.

It was strange. Mydei felt the familiar pulse of discomfort in his chest— something was off. It wasn’t like Phainon to be so quiet, so detached. But Mydei didn’t have time to dwell on it. There were too many other things pressing on his mind, too many unanswered questions.

He shook the feeling away and moved on.

Minutes turned into an hour as Mydei walked alone, the city now a quiet backdrop to his swirling thoughts. His footsteps echoed faintly in the empty streets, the weight of silence wrapping around him like a heavy blanket.

And then, suddenly, something changed.

At first, it was subtle—a shifting in the air, a slight blur around the edges of his vision. But it grew, pulling his senses away from the world around him, drawing his attention inward. He couldn’t understand it at first. The feeling was intense, sharp, like a jolt of electricity. But his body didn’t react the way it should. He didn’t jump, didn’t flinch. Instead, he felt… disoriented.

And then, as though a veil had been pulled away, Mydei’s surroundings began to distort. His body went rigid, the world around him fracturing, splitting, as though it was no longer solid. The pulse of his heartbeat thudded loudly in his ears, so strong that it felt like it was reverberating through his very bones.

Mydei’s breath caught in his throat, but before he could react, something else invaded his senses—a vision. And this wasn’t like a dream. This was real. This was happening, bleeding into his reality like a poisoned ink spilling into water.

The vision hit him hard, and in that instant, he understood: It wasn’t just a vision of Anaxa. It was his pain . He felt it—the sharp, unbearable pain searing through his skull as though his brain was being twisted apart. He could hear the crack of bone, the sickening squelch of blood, the thumping of his own heart going wild in his chest.

And it was Anaxa .

His brain—Anaxa’s brain—felt like it was cracking under pressure, the force of it too intense to comprehend. There was a strange pressure building in Mydei’s own head, as if his mind were being stretched to its limits. His body reacted instinctively, his knees buckling beneath him, but he couldn’t move. He couldn’t escape it. The vision gripped him, holding him in place, forcing him to experience everything Anaxa felt.

He gasped as if it were his own pain, his body trembling. The vision twisted, warping his perception. The sense of Anaxa’s mind fracturing was almost unbearable—each pulse of agony was like a jolt of electricity running through Mydei’s own body. His breath quickened, shallow, desperate to escape the suffocating reality he was trapped in.

The pressure intensified.

And then, through the agonizing haze, a whisper cut through the madness, a voice that didn’t belong to anyone Mydei knew. “It’s not what you think. It’s never what you think.”

The words sent a chill down his spine, but they only made the pain worse, twisting his thoughts and his body further into a knot of confusion and terror.

No… Mydei thought, struggling against the vision. No, I can’t…

But it was too much.

Anaxa’s mind continued to fracture, the pain—his pain—becoming unbearable. Mydei’s head felt as though it were splitting in two. His vision blurred, his body burning with the heat of what should have been impossible.

It felt like dying. The pain, the horror, the brokenness of the vision—it felt like a second death. His breath came in ragged gasps as if he were drowning, suffocating under the weight of it all. His entire body trembled violently, unable to escape the chaos in his mind.

And then, just as suddenly as it began, the vision shattered, the grip on his mind snapping away with a violent force.

Mydei fell to the ground, his palms scraping against the cold stone beneath him. He gasped, each breath painful and shallow, as if he had just returned to life. His heart was still racing, the aftershocks of the vision leaving him trembling, sweat beading on his forehead.

But the image of Anaxa remained—his fractured, broken mind, and the whisper that would not leave.

It took Mydei a long moment to regain his bearings, his body aching from the force of the vision, his head still throbbing with the remnants of the

pain. When he finally stood, his legs unsteady beneath him, he couldn’t shake the feeling that something was wrong.

Whatever this was—whatever it meant—Mydei knew he couldn’t ignore it.

The unease that had settled in his chest grew heavier. He had to find Anaxa. There was no choice. Something was coming, and Mydei didn’t know how much time they had left, and he wasn’t willing to find out.

Mydei’s feet hammered against the cold stone floor, his heart pounding erratically in his chest. He barreled through the halls, the world around him a blur of shadows and distant voices. The usual noise of Okhema, its hum of life and energy, felt miles away, drowned out by the roar of his thoughts. He needed to find Anaxa. He had to.

It didn’t matter that the citizens were staring, their eyes widening as he pushed past them. The disapproving looks, the murmurs behind hands, the way people stepped aside and gave him wide berths—it didn’t matter. None of it mattered. He barely noticed, his focus razor-sharp as he continued searching every room, every hallway, every alley, demanding to know if anyone had seen him.

The sense of urgency clawed at him, the sinking feeling deep in his chest refusing to relent. He couldn’t shake the feeling that something was wrong. That something had already happened.

Time blurred as Mydei darted from one place to the next, his breath coming quicker, his movements sharper. His mind raced, but there were no answers. No clues.

He was about to give up, the ache of failure already gnawing at him when he noticed it—just the faintest streak of golden blood splattered across the wall. His breath caught in his throat, the gold gleaming in the dim light like some kind of sick beacon.

Golden blood.

His hands clenched into fists, and without thinking, he took off again, following the trail. His legs moved on instinct, propelled by something primal, the gnawing feeling of dread growing stronger with each step.

The trail of blood led him to a narrow corridor, the stone walls cracked and weathered. At the end, a door was slightly ajar, creaking faintly in the stillness. Mydei pushed it open without hesitation, his eyes immediately drawn to the horror that awaited him.

Anaxa’s body lay crumpled in the middle of the room. The once-dignified scholar was sprawled on the floor, unmoving, his face contorted in an expression of unimaginable pain. The blood around him—the golden blood —had already started to pool around his head, shimmering sickly in the light. The most jarring sight, however, was the deep, jagged gash that ran through the very center of his skull, cleaving it in two.

It was brutal. It was grotesque.

The cut was so clean, so deep, that it seemed as if someone had sliced through him with a blade honed for the sole purpose of destroying his mind. Mydei’s vision swam as he took in the details—the blood that stained the floor, the cracked stone around Anaxa’s body, and the hollow emptiness where his once-intelligent eyes would have looked. His skull, split in half like an overripe fruit, stared up at the ceiling, a final testament to the violence that had taken his life.

Mydei’s stomach twisted violently at the sight, his mouth dry, his legs shaking. He had to force himself to stay upright. He couldn’t— couldn’t — let his body react to this, couldn’t give in to the horror that threatened to overwhelm him. But it was hard. Harder than anything, any death, he’d experienced before. He pressed his palm against the wall, willing himself not to throw up, to stay in control. The stench of blood and death clawed at him.

For a long moment, he stood there in stunned silence, staring down at Anaxa’s shattered body. It wasn’t real. It couldn’t be. This wasn’t supposed to happen. Not like this.

But the blood was real. The broken skull was real. The unnatural stillness of Anaxa’s body was real.

And so was the pain that shot through Mydei’s chest, the hollow ache of losing someone yet again.

The days that followed were nothing short of a blur.

Just like Castorice, news of Anaxa’s death spread quickly through Okhema, and it wasn’t long before whispers began to circulate about Mydei’s involvement. He had been the last person seen with both Anaxa and Castorice. The suspicion was palpable, the eyes of the city fixed on him with a mixture of fear and accusation.

The citizens, once warm and welcoming, or as much as they could be to Mydei, now seemed to keep their distance even more. Their glances were sharp and wary. It was no secret that Mydei was different—he always had been—but now, with two deaths on his hands, his mere presence made them uneasy. They didn’t know what to believe, but they believed the worst. And it didn’t matter to Mydei. He didn’t care.

The weight of their stares barely registered. He was lost, his mind swimming with the death of Anaxa, the violence, the brutal way it had happened. He was a mess, his usual calm demeanor shredded by the grief and guilt gnawing at his insides. He didn’t have the energy to feign normalcy and didn’t care to maintain his usual detached facade. It felt… meaningless.

He wandered the halls, his head heavy with thoughts, until the news of Anaxa’s death reached the ears of the other heirs. It was a quick gathering, an urgent meeting held under the heavy weight of grief and suspicion. The heirs all looked at him—at Mydei—with a mix of concern and wariness, but no one dared speak directly to him. They, too, felt the heat of the rumors swirling around him.

And still, Mydei remained silent, the weight of it all pressing down on him.

But he didn’t care about the heirs. He didn’t care about their questions or their doubts. He had lost Anaxa, and that was all that mattered right now.

For now, Mydei was alone again.

Mydei barely noticed the passing hours, his mind a chaotic storm, his heart a hollow pit of dread. The faces of the heirs blurred as they spoke, their voices rising and falling in the background like a muffled noise he couldn’t fully comprehend. He stood among them, unfeeling, disconnected, a silent observer to the grief of others that didn’t reach him. It didn’t matter. Anaxa was dead. Castorice was dead. It was all slipping through his fingers.

As he turned to leave the room, desperate to escape the weight of their looks and words, Phainon’s voice broke through the fog.

“Mydei.”

He froze. The mere sound of his name from Phainon’s lips sent an involuntary shiver down his spine. He didn’t want to deal with him right now—not in the midst of all this. His hands clenched, trying to quell the nausea rising in his stomach. He wanted space.

He didn’t look at Phainon, but the heavy hand on his shoulder made his breath hitch. He flinched.

“Don’t touch me,” Mydei spat, the words coming out rough and hollow, the tone all sharp edges. His body jerked as he tried to pull away, but Phainon didn’t let go. The gesture felt too familiar. Too warm.

Phainon didn’t respond right away. He simply held his ground, his fingers still pressing lightly against Mydei’s shoulder. Mydei felt the weight of his touch, the constant pressure in the air between them. He could feel Phainon’s gaze boring into him, but the mess in his chest refused to allow any response.

For a long moment, neither of them spoke. The tension thickened, stretching long enough that Mydei’s breaths became shallow. Something was wrong—he could feel it again. That same pull, that gnawing sensation

from earlier, when he had seen Anaxa’s death. The same feeling that had prompted him to search for him.

It was back.

His heart beat erratically. Panic gripped him, and he couldn’t shake the sudden overwhelming sense of urgency. This… this wasn’t just a feeling. It was something more.

Before he could stop himself, Mydei grabbed Phainon’s wrist, spinning him around with a force that left both of them breathless. The sudden movement felt wild, like the instinctive reaction of a creature trapped in its terror. Mydei’s eyes were wide, his pulse racing.

Phainon’s voice caught in his throat, confusion flashing across his features as Mydei pushed him back a few steps, slamming him against the wall. “What the hell—”

“Don’t leave,” Mydei’s voice was barely above a whisper, but it carried the weight of something deeper—an unspoken plea, a desperate wish buried beneath layers of cold detachment. His hand was trembling, his body coiled tight with an energy that didn’t make sense. The words were shaky, rough with barely contained fear. His throat burned, but his mind couldn’t stop racing. No, not him too. I can’t lose him.

Phainon stared at him, his eyes narrowing with confusion and concern, but there was something else there—something darker, an undercurrent of tension. The uncharacteristic urgency in Mydei’s voice made him hesitate, his breath catching for a split second. Mydei wasn’t the type to show weakness. Not like this.

“What’s wrong?” Phainon asked, his voice low, steady—despite the shock in his gaze. But there was something in his expression now, a flash of worry, of hesitation.

Mydei didn’t answer, his grip tightening on Phainon’s wrist. The vision, the feeling—something wasn’t right. He didn’t know what it was, but every

fiber of his being screamed that he couldn’t let Phainon leave. Not yet. Not with the way things had been going. I need to protect him.

But even then, his voice cracked a little. “Please… don’t go. Not yet.”

Phainon remained still, his hand hovering uncertainly over Mydei’s, but he didn’t pull away. The weight of the moment seemed to stretch endlessly between them, but Phainon said nothing, only watching him with a faint furrow in his brow.

Mydei’s hand shook again, his breath coming quick, the cold dread clinging to him. And for the first time in what felt like forever, he didn’t know what to do. He didn’t want to let go. But more than that, he didn’t want Phainon to slip through his grasp.

He wouldn’t let him.

Phainon’s pulse raced as Mydei’s hand tightened around his wrist, spinning him against the wall. The raw energy radiating from him sent a rush of excitement through Phainon’s veins—uncontrollable, intoxicating. Mydei was close, so close now, pressed against him with an almost tangible urgency. For a split second, Phainon felt the briefest flicker of confusion, his mind still trying to make sense of the situation, but it was immediately overridden by something much darker, much more thrilling.

Mydei’s breath hitched as he gripped Phainon’s wrist tighter, his fingers trembling—trembling. The tiny detail was enough to send a rush of heat to Phainon’s chest. The pressure between them, the frantic need in Mydei’s gaze, was too much to ignore. Phainon’s heart pounded faster. This—this was exactly what he had been waiting for.

For a moment, he could barely contain the elated smile tugging at the corners of his lips. His chest swelled with an almost manic joy as he let his body lean forward, closer to Mydei. He could feel the warmth of, the rhythmic rise and fall of his chest, the faint scent of him, intoxicating. Without thinking, his mouth brushed against the smooth skin of Mydei’s neck, a shiver running down his spine as he did so. He’d dreamed of this—

of touching him like this—of being this close, of feeling Mydei’s tension, his fear, his need.

He could taste it in the air—the rawness of the moment.

“Please… don’t go. Not yet,” Mydei’s voice trembled in his ear, low and almost broken.

Phainon’s hand tightened around his wrist, but his heart was racing differently now—this wasn’t fear. No, this was something far more dangerous, something deep, something that buzzed beneath his skin.

He was alive . Mydei had come to him, clinging to him with a desperation that was almost too much to bear.

Phainon’s lips hovered just a breath away from Mydei’s neck, the heat of his skin intoxicating. He inhaled deeply, the feeling of his breath against Mydei’s skin a rare privilege that made his heart race even faster. I’ve finally gotten this close, he thought, his fingers lightly brushing against the back of Mydei’s neck as if savoring the moment.

His mind screamed with the elation of the situation.

He’d taken what he needed. Anaxa and Castorice—they were simply in the way. They always were. All their talk of protecting Mydei, all their attention, made Phainon’s skin crawl. Mydei was his. He was always meant to be his.

But no one could understand. No one could see . He couldn’t let them stand in the way. He didn’t need them. Mydei didn’t need them. He only needed Phainon.

The jealousy that had driven him to kill them both now felt justified. They had been obstacles —but now, there was nothing between him and Mydei. Nothing to keep them apart. Phainon had worked tirelessly for this, biding his time. His devotion to Mydei—it was pure. It was righteous.

You don’t know what it’s like to be adored like this, Phainon thought, his chest tightening with the thought. They could never give you what I can. Mydei could never see it, not yet, but Phainon would make him. He would make him see, make him understand.

He knew Mydei could never be with someone who wasn’t as strong as him. But Phainon had that strength, that conviction. Mydei didn’t need to fight anymore— he’d protect him . He had proven that over and over. And if Mydei ever questioned it, well… Phainon would make sure those doubts didn’t linger. He would burn them away.

He could feel Mydei’s heartbeat under his fingers, pounding faster, and Phainon couldn’t help the elated smile that finally crept onto his lips. Mydei was here, clinging to him with an undeniable urgency. He’d made sure of it. Now, he was going to savor it.

Phainon slowly, almost reverently, let his lips graze Mydei’s neck again, the brief touch enough to send a thrill down his spine. You’ll understand soon enough, he thought, his mind spinning with all the possibilities, all the things he would do to make Mydei realize how right they were for each other.

The death of Castorice. The death of Anaxa. They were just the beginning.

For now, he let his fingers trace the lines of Mydei’s shoulder, his grip tightening just slightly. He could feel Mydei’s tremor under his touch, but it wasn’t fear—it was something else, something that drove him mad with need.

The only thing that mattered now was keeping him close, keeping him safe, keeping him for himself. And no one will take you from me, he promised silently.

At this moment, with Mydei so near, Phainon was complete. He could feel it in every nerve, every breath he took. The obsession—his obsession—had only just begun.

But it wasn’t enough. Not yet.

Phainon adjusted his grip ever so slightly, leading Mydei forward, careful not to move too quickly. Mydei followed, staying close, his wariness still present but softened by his exhaustion. Phainon didn’t speak at first, letting the silence stretch between them, a quiet thread of unspoken understanding. He played it slow, cautious. If he rushed, he’d shatter the moment.

Mydei’s gaze remained distant, barely seeing the path ahead, his thoughts clearly elsewhere. Phainon knew exactly where. He could feel it in the weight of Mydei’s steps, the tension in his fingers when they’d brushed against his wrist earlier.

Grief.

But grief could be a wonderful thing. It broke people down, made them vulnerable, malleable. And Phainon had every intention of ensuring Mydei turned to him in his weakness.

So he sighed, just loud enough for Mydei to hear, a breathy, almost regretful sound, as if the situation had finally settled in his chest like a heavy stone. “I should’ve been there,” he murmured. “If I had known…”

Mydei finally looked at him. The expression on his face sent something sharp through Phainon’s chest—a real reaction, direct, raw.

“Phainon,” Mydei said, voice quieter than before. Then, with a weight that could crush bones: “Anaxa is dead.”

The words hung between them, heavier than the sky itself.

Phainon could feel the moment shift, as if Mydei were forcing him to understand. The sheer loss. The gravity of it all.

Oh, Mydei. If only you knew how little I cared.

But Phainon didn’t let even a fraction of that thought show. Instead, his breath stilled, his lips parting just slightly as if struggling to find the words. Slowly, he lowered his gaze, let his body slacken just a bit, not enough to appear weak—no, never weak—but just enough to seem… affected.

“I know,” he said at last, voice quiet, controlled. “I know.”

He let his hand tremble.

A small, involuntary shake, subtle yet deliberate. Just enough.

It worked.

Without hesitation, Mydei grabbed his hand, fingers curling around it firmly. The warmth of his touch, the way he held on without thinking—it was intoxicating.

Phainon had to focus to keep from shuddering at the sheer intimacy of it.

“Why are you shaking?” Mydei asked, eyes searching his face.

For a fraction of a second, Phainon considered telling the truth—because you’re touching me, and I could die happy in this moment. But that wouldn’t do. That would break the illusion.

Instead, he swallowed, shifting his expression into something more conflicted, something Mydei would believe. “It’s nothing,” he said, voice hoarse, forcing himself to look away as if burdened by thoughts too heavy to voice.

He expected Mydei to let go.

But he didn’t.

Instead, his grip tightened, not painfully, but with purpose. A reassurance.

Phainon barely heard his next words, too focused on the sheer audacity of what was happening.

It wasn’t about Anaxa. It wasn’t about Castorice. Not to him.

No—this was about Mydei.

About how his fingers fit around Phainon’s own. How his thumb rested against his skin absentmindedly, a thoughtless comfort. How his eyes, so tired and lost, still softened just slightly when he looked at him.

It was working.

It was all working.

And Phainon, with all the patience in the world, would let it continue. He would let Mydei mourn. Let him reach for him in the dark, thinking it was his choice.

And then, when the time was right, Mydei wouldn’t even realize he had no one left but Phainon.

.

.

.

Year: Unknown

The constellation of Janus has gone dark.

Talanton, the Scale of Justice, and Oronyx, the Veil of Evernight, now burned brightly, casting a blazing glow across the sky.

Law and Order had descended into chaos.

Chapter Notes

Lowkey this is probably my least favorite chapter, but I hope you guys still enjoy it.

This wasn’t really planned in my original script so I had to improvise everything and basically bullshit it💀

Also how do you guys feel about a sports au Phaidei fic? Totally not asking this to see if I should finish writing my draft😢

The night was quiet, heavy with the unspoken words of all that had transpired. Mydei sat just a little apart from Phainon, watching as his companion slowly drifted into an almost unnatural stillness. The stars above shimmered, scattered fragments of light amidst the dark canvas of the sky, but his eyes were fixed on the figure beside him, as if seeking reassurance from the constellations themselves.

The day had passed slowly, one quiet moment folding into the next as if time itself had become aware of their fragile existence. They had spoken little, but the silence between them felt full—not of awkwardness, but of shared grief. For Phainon, perhaps even more so. He had his own way of carrying pain, a quiet sorrow that often hid behind the sharpness of his words or the easy smile that came too naturally. But Mydei had seen past that mask more times than he cared to admit.

That night, as they sat under the stars, Phainon had been unusually silent. His gaze would flick to Mydei occasionally, and then back to the distant stars, as if searching for answers in their cold, distant light. It was almost as if he were waiting for something—waiting for someone to tell him it was all going to be okay. Mydei couldn’t offer that kind of reassurance. Not now. Not when the world itself felt like it was tilting dangerously.

The weight of the day had finally caught up to Phainon. Mydei had been aware of the strain the events had placed on him—the death of Castorice and Anaxa, the entire city falling apart, the uncertainty hanging in the air like a storm that never quite broke. Phainon had insisted on pushing forward, as he always did, instead focusing on reassuring Mydei instead, but now, here in the stillness of the night, he had finally surrendered to the exhaustion of it all. Mydei watched as Phainon’s eyelids fluttered, the tension in his shoulders easing, until at last, he slumped against Mydei’s side, his breath evening out in the softest of exhales.

Phainon had fallen asleep, just like that.

At first, Mydei had tensed, instinctively pulling away from the warmth that seemed to seep into him from their proximity. The urge to distance himself, to leave this fragile moment behind, was almost overwhelming. He wasn’t good at this. Not good at letting people in, not good at holding someone so close and allowing them to lean on him when he was barely standing himself. The chaos of the day still clung to him like a thick fog, and the weight of it was suffocating.

But then he exhaled, letting the moment settle around him. He didn’t pull away. For once, he allowed himself to remain where he was, close to Phainon, feeling his warmth radiate through the thin layers of clothing they both wore.

There was something about the way Phainon had leaned against him, so vulnerable in his sleep. Mydei couldn’t quite put his finger on it. Maybe it was the way Phainon’s heart beat just a little too fast, the way he was always on the edge of breaking, despite the confidence he projected. Maybe it was the fact that Phainon would never let anyone see how fragile he was, how much of himself he buried under layers of charm and confidence, as if the world would crack him open if it saw the truth.

In that moment, Mydei allowed himself to feel something he rarely did: a strange, unexpected tenderness toward Phainon.

It wasn’t that Mydei wasn’t used to being alone—he had spent years living in solitude, detached from everyone and everything that mattered. He had

trained himself to be this way, to remain distant and untouchable, so that the world and its demands could never break him. But Phainon was an exception. And perhaps that was what terrified him the most.

For once, it wasn’t about the city falling apart or the looming darkness that seemed to hang over their lives. It was about Phainon’s heart, which Mydei feared was just as fragile as his own. He knew Phainon better than most— maybe even better than Phainon knew himself—and he could see the cracks in the other’s facade. He had seen the way Phainon’s eyes had softened whenever they spoke of those they had lost. He had seen the guilt, the self-blame that was written on Phainon’s face when he thought no one was looking.

So Mydei stayed there, with Phainon’s head resting gently against his shoulder. He let the warmth of his presence fill the space between them, just as much for Phainon as for himself. It was a small thing, really, a quiet act of support that no one else would have noticed, but to Mydei, it was everything. It was the only way he knew how to be there for the one person who had stood by him through everything, despite his own carefully built walls.

Phainon had always been the one to keep others at a distance, never fully allowing anyone to see past the surface. But Mydei had learned long ago that Phainon’s smiles, his easy jokes, and his confidence were just masks. Beneath it all was someone who cared too much, who carried the weight of the world on his shoulders, even when he pretended to shrug it off.

There.

someone—something—had just made sure he knew it.

Mydei had learned, long ago, to push the noise away, but even now, when all of Okhema seemed to be against him, he couldn’t shake the gnawing anger.

There were four things that kept him from being torn apart, literally and figuratively. The first was that, despite everything, he couldn’t die. Immortality was a gift—and a curse—he had grown to accept, though it did little to ease his pain. The second: he was an heir, and Okhema had no other choice but to keep him alive, despite the evidence against him. Third was Aglaea, whose influence had proven invaluable in keeping him out of immediate danger. She fought tooth and nail for him, a silent defender even when it put her own position at risk. And lastly, there was Phainon—his words a desperate plea that left Mydei numb with rage and guilt.

Phainon had threatened to end it all if anyone dared harm Mydei. The words hung in the air like an ultimatum, and though Mydei didn’t need saving, the idea of Phainon suffering for him ignited something ferocious inside. Mydei had given Phainon a brutal thrashing for even thinking of such a thing—how could he ever make such a sacrifice? Yet Phainon had only looked at him with those same unwavering eyes, his emotions buried beneath a shield of devotion.

Now, Mydei continued, not out of necessity but because he had no other choice. Time marched on, and so did he.

Mydei sat alone, hidden in the darkness, a secluded corner of Okhema that felt far removed from the chaos of the world. The stars above stretched endlessly, but his focus was on a single constellation: Kephale. The one that had begun it all. The first seed of the storm that had thrown his life into this unrelenting spiral. The events that followed felt like a dream, a nightmare, and now, they weighed on him like a crushing force.

He was tired. Too tired. Physically, mentally—he couldn’t summon the energy to feel anything anymore, let alone rage or guilt. The nightmare of the Tribios’s death played on a loop in his mind, and the only thing that kept him from falling apart completely was the cold, steady silence of the night.

But then, a sound. Soft footsteps, a familiar presence. His gaze shifted, but he didn’t move. He didn’t have the strength to. Phainon, the last person he expected to find him in this moment of despair, appeared on the edge of the roof, his figure silhouetted against the starlight.

Phainon waved, a gesture so simple and quiet that Mydei felt the weight of it more than any forceful attempt at comforting words. For a few moments, Phainon didn’t speak, just climbed up beside him with his usual grace, settling in without any fanfare.

“Hey,” Phainon’s voice broke the silence, so soft, so hesitant, it almost didn’t feel real.

The words hung between them like a fragile bridge, and for the first time in what felt like forever, Mydei allowed himself to acknowledge the presence next to him. He could feel the cracks in his hard shell, the walls he’d built after Tribbie’s death, starting to form, crumble. He didn’t look at Phainon, couldn’t—afraid of what he might see. Instead, he focused on the sky. Kephale, still burning bright in the night.

For what felt like an eternity, they sat there, neither speaking. Just the quiet hum of the world around them. The weight of the past pressing down on Mydei, but for the first time in what felt like forever, it wasn’t suffocating.

Kephale had been the start of everything, but Mydei felt nothing now. No anger, no vengeance—just an emptiness that had consumed him. He hadn’t known how to keep going, but Phainon’s presence, without needing to say anything, had somehow offered him the smallest sliver of peace. It was strange, unsettling even. But for now, it was enough.

Mydei didn’t speak. Not yet. Not while the quiet stretched between them, while the constellations watched from above. The quiet was just as much a comfort as it was a prison.

And in that stillness, Mydei couldn’t help but feel the unbearable pressure of everything that had been lost.

The silence between them was thick, but it was a kind of silence that felt almost necessary. Phainon sat next to Mydei, close enough that he could feel the subtle weight of his presence, but Mydei was still trapped in his own thoughts. His gaze remained fixed on Kephale, and though he wanted to retreat further into his mind, there was something about Phainon being there that kept him anchored, even if he didn’t want to admit it.

After what felt like an eternity of quiet, Phainon moved. His hand gently brushed Mydei’s cheek, the touch so light, so tender, that it startled him. Mydei stiffened, not expecting the contact. Phainon’s thumb traced the curve of his face as he spoke, his voice soft but with an undercurrent of

something more—a kind of pleading Mydei hadn’t expected. “Don’t cry, please.”

The words hit him like a punch to the gut. Something in him—something he hadn’t even known was there—shifted. It was ridiculous. He wasn’t weak. He couldn’t be. He couldn’t afford to be. His face burned with a sudden heat, and his heart stuttered in his chest. The very last thing he wanted was for Phainon to see him like this, exposed in some way he couldn’t control.

Without thinking, Mydei shoved Phainon’s hand away. His voice came out more forceful than he intended. “I’m not weak,” he muttered, refusing to look at him.

Phainon didn’t immediately respond. For a long moment, Mydei’s heart pounded in his ears as he tried to steady his breath, his thoughts in disarray. Phainon hesitated, his gaze lingering on Mydei before he slowly began to get up, perhaps sensing that the space between them needed to be respected.

But as Phainon moved to leave, something inside Mydei snapped. Fear, paranoia—he couldn’t tell. He couldn’t let Phainon leave. Not now. Not after everything that had happened.

In a single, fluid motion, Mydei grabbed Phainon’s hand, his grip tighter than intended. He didn’t care. He couldn’t let him go. He didn’t trust that the world would let him have anything—anyone—left.

Phainon turned to face him, an unreadable expression on his face, but Mydei didn’t look at him. He couldn’t. He was afraid of what he’d see in Phainon’s eyes, and even more afraid of what he might find in his own heart.

“Come with me,” Mydei said, his voice quieter now. It wasn’t a question. It wasn’t even a request. He didn’t want to be alone. Not anymore. Not with everything that was happening.

Phainon didn’t say anything right away, but after a moment, he simply nodded, as if he understood more than he could put into words. Mydei

pulled him along, silent and unsteady, but with a certainty he couldn’t explain.

As they walked, the world seemed to shift. The tension between them hung thick in the air. But for once, Mydei didn’t care. For once, he wasn’t thinking about the consequences. He just needed Phainon there—beside him, next to him. Even if he couldn’t protect himself, maybe, just maybe, he could protect Phainon.

And for a moment, everything else faded.

Hey,” Phainon said, breaking the silence. “You know, when this whole mess is over, I think we should get out of here for a while. Just… go somewhere quiet, far from all this.” His voice was light, but there was something deeper behind it, an undercurrent of care. “Maybe the southern coast. I heard it’s peaceful there. Sunsets are supposed to be incredible.”

Mydei glanced over at him, surprised by the sudden shift in tone. Phainon was trying to steer the conversation away from all the chaos, trying to keep things light. It was almost like Phainon couldn’t stand seeing him this way —distant, consumed by anger and, well for lack of a better word—tired. So tired.

Phainon continued, his voice steady. “I bet you’d look good in the sunlight there. Maybe even smile.”

Mydei found his lips quirking up at that, a fleeting thought that vanished as quickly as it came. He didn’t know why Phainon had to talk about something like that, but he didn’t mind. Maybe it was nice to think of something—anything—besides the endless turmoil surrounding them.

“Maybe,” Mydei said softly, though he wasn’t quite sure he could ever feel at peace again. Not after everything.

The conversation drifted after that, with Phainon bringing up lighter topics —places they could visit, odd places he’d heard of, food he’d tried that Mydei probably wouldn’t touch. For once, Mydei didn’t resist. He let

Phainon’s words wash over him, distracting him from the ever-looming dread that haunted his every step.

Phainon looked over at Mydei, his voice casual, though laced with a subtle curiosity. “So, where’s your earring?”

Mydei shifted slightly, feeling the absence where it once hung. He didn’t respond right away, his eyes flicking downward, as if the answer was suddenly heavy. Then, after a pause, he sighed, a mixture of resignation and indifference in his tone. “It was stolen.”

Phainon’s gaze softened, but a quiet question hung in the air. “How? You didn’t just… lose it, did you?”

Mydei hesitated for a moment, then finally spoke again, his words flowing out as if they didn’t matter to him at all. “I let it happen.”

The words hit the air like a stone dropped into still water, and for a moment, the world itself seemed to freeze. Phainon’s eyes locked onto Mydei with a stillness that made everything else feel distant. His gaze, once soft and understanding, now darkened for just a fraction of a second—sharp, like a knife being drawn from its sheath.

Mydei felt it—felt the shift in the air, the weight of the silence hanging between them. For that split second, Phainon’s usual composure faltered, and something deeply unsettling passed between them, something raw and almost dangerous.

Phainon’s fingers twitched just slightly, and Mydei’s stomach tightened, like a knot being pulled. He couldn’t pinpoint why, but the atmosphere around them suddenly felt much colder, sharper. Phainon didn’t say anything, but Mydei could feel the unspoken question hanging in the air— Why?

Then, as quickly as it happened, Phainon’s expression softened again, returning to its usual calm. He nodded, as if he hadn’t just looked into something dangerous, something dark inside of Mydei. “I see,” Phainon murmured, his tone gentle, almost soothing. “You did what you had to.”

But Mydei could feel it—the way the air had shifted, the fleeting darkness in Phainon’s eyes that he couldn’t quite forget. It was like a shadow lingering, just out of sight. The normalcy returned too quickly, too smoothly, but something in Mydei felt disturbed by the moment, as if it had cracked open something he wasn’t prepared to face.

Phainon continued as if nothing had changed, his voice light as he casually shifted the topic. “So, anyway, I heard the new shipments arrived in the market today. What do you think of the fabrics they brought in?”

Mydei could barely focus on the words, his mind lingering on that brief, intense moment. He wasn’t sure if it was Phainon’s gaze or his own internal storm, but something had changed. It wasn’t just about the earring anymore —it was about the way things could change so quickly between them.

And as Phainon spoke, Mydei couldn’t shake the feeling that, for a second, he’d seen too much.

Phainon had noticed his silence, his tiredness, his eyes scanning Mydei’s face as if trying to read him. The softness in his voice broke through the haze. “You’ve been going for days, haven’t you?” Phainon said, his tone quiet, but there was no mistaking the concern there.

Mydei didn’t answer right away, only looking away, his gaze lingering on the distant horizon. His jaw tightened. The truth was, he hadn’t slept in days, not since the Tribios’s deaths. Not since the nightmares had started. Not since everything had fallen apart.

He had tried to keep going, pretending he was fine, but he wasn’t. Not anymore.

Phainon shifted beside him, noticing the subtle shift in his posture. “You should rest, Mydei.”

“I can’t.” The words slipped out before Mydei could stop them, and he immediately regretted it, his throat going dry. He didn’t want to sound like a child, but the exhaustion—no, the desperation —seeped into his words. “I can’t… I need…” He trailed off, but Phainon didn’t push him to finish.

The silence stretched, and for a long moment, Mydei didn’t speak. Then, something inside him cracked. He didn’t want to admit it. He didn’t want to ask for something so… childish. But the words slipped out before he could stop them.

“Phainon,” Mydei started, his voice barely audible, “will you… will you stay with me tonight?”

He immediately regretted it. His cheeks flushed with embarrassment, and he immediately looked away, as if the words hadn’t even left his mouth. He felt stupid, childish, weak. He could feel his heart racing, his skin burning with shame. He wasn’t supposed to need anyone. Not like this.

For a long moment, he didn’t hear anything, only the distant sounds of the city below, the wind brushing through the trees. He almost thought Phainon hadn’t heard him. Or worse, that he’d laugh or brush it off as some whim Mydei would forget about in a second.

But then, Phainon’s hand gently touched his shoulder, a quiet, steadying presence. “You don’t need to be ashamed of that,” Phainon said, his voice soft but grounded, filled with an understanding that Mydei couldn’t quite grasp. “You don’t have to do this alone.”

The words made something inside Mydei snap—a sharp ache in his chest that he couldn’t explain. He felt something twist, something he didn’t want to acknowledge.

“I’m not weak,” Mydei muttered quickly, looking away. “I just… I just thought you might—”

He stopped himself, his words getting caught in his throat. He felt embarrassed, stupid, and so incredibly small in that moment. He wanted to take it back, wanted to bury the request somewhere deep and pretend it had never happened.

But before he could do anything else, Phainon gave a small, knowing smile. “You don’t have to explain yourself to me.”

Mydei’s chest tightened. His face burned. It didn’t matter how many times Phainon had said something like that before—it still felt like a weight was pressing down on him.

And yet, before Mydei could speak again, Phainon stood up, turning toward him with a small, reassuring smile that wasn’t soft or too understanding. It was gentle. “Come on. Let’s go.”

Mydei opened his mouth to protest, to maybe back out of it, but the words died on his tongue. Something inside him—something deep, something he hadn’t realized—made him reach out. His hand brushed against Phainon’s arm, hesitating for a moment before he spoke.

“Don’t leave me tonight,” Mydei said, his voice quieter now, barely a whisper.

Phainon turned back to him, his expression steady, his eyes soft. “I’m not going anywhere.”

Without waiting for a response, Phainon reached out, taking Mydei’s hand in his. Mydei didn’t pull away. He didn’t want to. He followed Phainon, not saying anything else, not wanting to say anything else.

But as they moved together, Mydei couldn’t shake the feeling that something had shifted. He had asked for something, and Phainon had given it freely. It wasn’t weakness. It wasn’t childish. It was… just necessary.

If his heart started beating faster after that, no one needed to know.

The first light of morning pierced through the curtains, casting soft beams across the room. Mydei’s eyes fluttered open, a weight on his chest that had nothing to do with sleep. He blinked, confused for a moment, before his gaze settled on the familiar figure beside him—Phainon, still asleep, his

features soft in the gentle morning light. There was a quiet warmth in the room, a strange, unspoken peace that felt almost fragile, like it could shatter if Mydei so much as breathed too loudly.

Last night felt distant already. The dreams had stopped the moment Phainon had fallen asleep beside him. It wasn’t just the absence of nightmares. It was the absence of everything —the weight of his responsibilities, the constant gnawing feeling of impending doom that had lingered ever since the Tribios’s deaths. It had been… just a night. A night with someone who didn’t ask for anything in return.

It was the first night in weeks where Mydei had let his guard down, even just for a moment.

He glanced at Phainon once more, his heart tugging with something he refused to acknowledge. Phainon had been there when he needed him most, offering not just comfort, but something else—something that Mydei couldn’t quite place. In a way, it was easier not to think about it too much. He had learned long ago that giving in to soft moments like these only led to weakness. Weakness, however, seemed a little less terrifying when Phainon was beside him.

With a reluctant sigh, Mydei pulled himself out of bed, careful not to wake Phainon. The air was cool, the smell of the city creeping in through the window. Mydei dressed in silence, gathering his thoughts, preparing himself for the day ahead. The past few days had been a blur of grief, pain, and endless searching. The weight of it was still there, but for now, it was easier to carry. It didn’t feel so suffocating anymore.

He left the room, quietly closing the door behind him, and found himself wandering the streets of Okhema. It wasn’t a conscious decision; he didn’t know where he was going, just that he needed to be out in the open. The city was waking up around him—people rushing to their daily routines, the distant calls of vendors selling their goods, and the hum of life still continuing regardless of…

Mydei was walking aimlessly through the city streets, the bustle of the market district swirling around him. He was tired. Tired of the rumors, tired

of the whispers, and most of all, tired of the unrelenting sense of dread that had been gnawing at his insides since the death of the Tribios. His thoughts were heavy, his body tired, and he longed for nothing more than some semblance of peace.

He didn’t even know where he was going. His feet simply carried him through the familiar streets, his eyes half-lidded in quiet contemplation, when something caught his attention. A shadow flitted past him in a blur—a child, small and lithe, darting through the crowd like a phantom. It was the same child.

The one who had taken his earring. Huh, what a coincidence.

Mydei’s first instinct was to ignore it. The child had already taken from him once, and Mydei was in no mood to make a scene. Maybe he’d just let it happen again. Maybe he’d sneak a few extra coins into the child’s pocket while they were at it—an unspoken bargain of sorts, one that didn’t require gratitude, just an understanding.

But when the child darted back into his path again, Mydei sighed, resigned. He knew the signs. The pride in their movements, the way their gaze flickered, like they were ready to steal, but didn’t want to admit it. Some kids could sense when they were being watched—when someone could offer a hand without pity. This one wasn’t ready for it.

So Mydei gave no more thought to it as the child snuck closer, his eyes lazily scanning the market again. A flicker of movement in his peripheral vision caught his attention—before the child’s nimble fingers slid into his coat pocket, swiping another piece of his jewelry.

It was in that moment, just before he realized the theft, that Mydei heard a sound. A sickening, wet snap.

His stomach lurched, and before he could react, a sharp, agonized scream split the air. Mydei turned sharply, instinctively reaching for his side as the sound cut through the bustle. The child had frozen, a look of utter horror flashing across their face, blood spurting in a thick, crimson arc.

The child’s hand was gone— severed.  The small arm that had been so nimble a moment before was now a jagged stump, the limb lying discarded in a pool of blood.

It was impossible. The child had been so quick—Mydei hadn’t even realized it until the damage was done. A blade had cleaved through the air with such force that it had severed the child’s hand at the wrist, leaving nothing but a mangled mess of flesh and bone.

The child’s scream echoed in the chaos, but it was cut short as they collapsed to the ground, their body convulsing in shock and pain. Blood poured from the stump, staining the street with dark crimson, and Mydei’s breath caught in his throat. He hadn’t seen it coming. He had barely processed what had happened.

He didn’t know what to do. The child’s panicked sobs, their cries for help, filled the air as their body shook, clutching at the remaining part of their arm, trying to stop the blood that poured like a flood.

People had started screaming now too, running in every direction as the chaos erupted around them. Mydei was frozen for a moment, caught between the brutal sight of the dismembered child and the instinctual horror that rose in him. His heart was pounding so loudly in his chest he could barely hear himself think. His eyes kept flickering between the child’s severed hand and their face—still twisted in agony.

It was like a nightmare. A nightmare he couldn’t wake from.

The smell of blood, coppery and sharp, filled his nostrils as he finally snapped to attention, rushing toward the child’s side. Someone else had already arrived—an older man, perhaps a shopkeeper, kneeling beside the child, trying desperately to stop the bleeding with nothing but his hands.

Mydei didn’t know what to do. What happened? One second everything was normal but now—his mind was blank. He should be helping now. But it was too late. The damage had been done.

The city seemed to move in slow motion around him as he staggered back. His legs were like lead. The world felt too big and too small at the same time. People were running, shouting, pulling away from the scene. Mydei stood there, frozen, staring at the mess. His fingers trembled, and his breath came in short, shallow bursts.

Before he realized it, he was being dragged away. He didn’t resist as he was pulled into the hospital—though he wasn’t sure how it had happened, or who had gotten him there. It was a blur, his mind too overloaded, too numb to process the details.

The sterile, cold air of the hospital did nothing to ease the sickening feeling in his stomach. They had tried to patch the kid up—hadn’t even bothered to check on Mydei for any injuries. His hands were still covered in blood, but they didn’t ask. They didn’t need to.

Mydei barely felt the passing of time. He was left alone in the quiet room, the sound of his ragged breathing the only thing that reminded him he was still alive.

The world outside the hospital window was calm. The sky was a pale blue, the sun creeping through the clouds as if it hadn’t noticed the darkness that had descended upon the streets.

He couldn’t get the image of the child out of his mind. Couldn’t stop thinking about the violence, about the severed hand, the life that had been forever changed in an instant. And it made something inside him twist, something dark and deep that he couldn’t quite name.

He stood up and left the room, slipping out into the hallway, though he had no destination in mind. He was suffocating.

Why.

It was one simple word.

Why?

Mydei staggered through the hospital halls, the faint smell of antiseptic mingling with the coppery scent of blood. The sight of the child—so innocent in their appearance but now lying broken, their stump raw and twitching where their arm used to be—was burned into his memory.

Impossible.

The air around him seemed to grow heavier, a pressure in his chest that didn’t come from the fear alone. It felt like the very atmosphere had been warped, like reality itself was holding its breath.

The world had changed. And Mydei could already feel himself losing his grip on it.

Erased.

just like what’s been happening.

He has no evidence. No proof. But he knows it to be true, deep in the marrow of his bones.

A chill settles in his chest, spreading outward like ice.

And then the final thought strikes him, stark and absolute:

He was being watched.
