The hairs on the back of Mydei’s neck stood straight, a cold, gnawing sensation crawling across his skin like a thousand unseen eyes. He had been watched before. He had known it. The sensation of being followed, of being studied, was nothing new. But this—this was different.

It wasn’t the usual subtle feeling of eyes trailing him from a distance. No, this was something else, something far more suffocating. It felt as if the very air around him was thick with presence, as if something—someone— was watching, waiting, observing his every move, down to the way his chest rose and fell with his shaky breaths.

Mydei slowed his pace, eyes darting across the street as his heartbeat quickened, the panic slowly creeping in. He tried to tell himself it was just his paranoia, just the residue of everything that had happened. But deep down, he knew. He knew something was wrong. A knot formed in his stomach, a cold, clammy feeling that made his body want to move in a frantic, erratic way. But he forced himself to stay calm, forcing his legs to walk as if nothing were out of the ordinary.

The moment he turned a corner, though, the sensation intensified. His hand twitched, as if compelled to reach for his blade, but the weight of it at his

side only reminded him of the fact that the feeling had nothing to do with a physical threat.

What’s going on?

The world around him felt still. Too still. Even the bustle of Ampherous’s streets seemed to have gone quieter, the normal hum of city life muted, as if everyone had been swallowed by the same eerie presence. The usual chatter of vendors, the footfalls of passersby—everything was drowned out, as if the very pulse of the city had been suppressed.

He kept walking, but each step felt heavier, as if the ground beneath him was pressing back. The tension in his chest continued to build, a constant pressure threatening to suffocate him. He could feel the gaze upon him now, almost tangible. It was like a phantom breath on the back of his neck.

His eyes flicked from side to side, scanning the shadows that clung to the narrow alleyways, the doorways, the corners. But there was nothing. No movement. No sound. No trace of the presence that was suffocating him. And yet, it was there—right in front of him, just beyond his line of sight.

Then, without warning, his pulse skipped.

There.

He caught a glimpse of something—no, someone—a figure standing in the distance. For a brief moment, it looked as if they had been watching him all along, standing motionless in the shadows. His heart stuttered, a cold dread curling up his spine as he froze, staring at the figure. It wasn’t clear, just a vague silhouette against the backdrop of Ampherous’s dimming light.

But that was enough.

His breath hitched in his throat.

Was it them?

The figure didn’t move. Didn’t speak. Didn’t even blink. It was almost as if it were… waiting.

He stepped forward, cautiously, his muscles tense as if poised to spring at the slightest provocation. But with each step he took toward the figure, something within him screamed to stop. This was wrong. There was something fundamentally wrong about the way this person—this thing— stood there, utterly still.

And that’s when Mydei realized it.

The figure wasn’t human. It was wrong in a way that was almost impossible to explain. The shape of its form seemed almost too smooth, too perfect in a way that his mind couldn’t quite comprehend. Like a shadow given life, its edges too sharp, too… fluid. The way it shifted, the way it loomed, was something unnatural, something that made his stomach churn and his skin crawl. The uncanny feeling of something other wasn’t just present—it was radiating from the figure.

His heart began to pound again, faster now, too fast, as the air seemed to grow colder. He took a step back, then another, before he realized his feet were moving quicker than he had intended. He spun around to run, but—

The world went black.

A sudden, overwhelming force washed over him, and for a split second, he couldn’t breathe. Couldn’t move. Everything froze in place. His limbs turned to lead, his throat constricting as he gasped for air that didn’t seem to come. His eyes widened, but he couldn’t blink, couldn’t look away.

Then, the sensation was gone, and he was left standing in the same spot. Alone.

Mydei’s breath came in shallow gasps, his chest heaving as he slowly, cautiously, turned around. The figure was gone. Vanished, as though it had never been there at all. But the feeling of its presence lingered, still pressing in on him, something he couldn’t shake.

He shook his head, trying to clear the fog from his thoughts. His heartbeat hammered in his ears, the frantic rush of blood making everything else sound distant, muffled.

Was it a hallucination?

He couldn’t know. Couldn’t be sure. The only thing he did know was that whatever that thing was, whatever they were, it wasn’t something he could ignore. The hairs on his neck prickled again, his body still on high alert as his mind scrambled to make sense of what had just happened.

And then, the thought hit him.

It wasn’t just the figure. It wasn’t just the presence. It was everything—the way he couldn’t shake the feeling that he was always being watched. That someone, somewhere, was pulling the strings. And the more he thought about it, the more he realized it wasn’t just paranoia.

No, this was something far more sinister. Something that reached far beyond anything he had ever known.

Something was watching him.

And it wasn’t just watching— it was controlling.

He stumbled, his legs unsteady as the realization smacked into him. He had been too distracted. Too absorbed in the immediate threats, the loss of the Titans. But now, now he understood.

They were being controlled. Every movement, every decision, was being manipulated, and this unseen force was pulling the strings, controlling the rules of the very world he had once thought to understand.

In that moment, Mydei didn’t know whether he was still safe or if the world around him was already slipping through his fingers. But one thing was clear.

The shadows were closing in.

Mydei stood frozen in place, his breath caught in his chest as his pulse quickened, the silence around him suddenly deafening. The air was heavy, thick with something he couldn’t quite put a name to. It felt like the world itself had shifted just out of his reach, like the shadows were no longer

simply dark corners of the city but living, breathing things. Watching. Waiting.

His heart hammered against his ribs, frantic, as his eyes flicked wildly from shadow to shadow, desperate to catch a glimpse of whatever lurked in the dark corners of his mind. Every sound—every creak of the stone beneath his boots, the rustle of wind through the dead trees—sounded too loud. Too close. His breath came in sharp, shallow gasps, each exhale more desperate than the last as if he could push the feeling away with just the force of his will.

It’s just your mind playing tricks on you, he told himself, trying to calm his shaking hands. You’ve been through too much. It’s the stress. It’s just paranoia.

But the feeling of being watched… that didn’t feel like paranoia. The hairs on the back of his neck stood on end, his skin crawling with the prickling sensation of eyes that weren’t there—yet.

His gaze darted again, scanning the shadows, willing himself to see nothing. Nothing but the empty streets, the quiet city, but the longer he stared, the more it felt like the silence had turned against him. The space around him seemed too still, too suffocating, like something was waiting for the right moment to pounce.

His breathing became erratic, his chest tightening as if the world itself was slowly closing in on him. He could feel it then—something, the presence pressing down on him like the weight of a thousand unseen hands. The air felt colder, darker. Closer.

Where are you? His thoughts were frantic, each one slamming into his mind in an avalanche of raw fear. He wanted to move, to run, but his legs felt like stone. He couldn’t feel the ground beneath him. The weight in his chest was unbearable.

No. No, not now.

He tried to take a step, but his legs wouldn’t obey. The world felt like it was tilting, spinning on its axis as the shadows around him seemed to grow, stretching, folding in on themselves. The oppressive feeling of being watched deepened, sinking into his bones until it was all he could feel. They’re here. They’re real.

He jerked his head toward the sound of a distant footstep, the sound so sharp it felt like it was echoing in his skull. His chest tightened even more, suffocating under the feeling of the dread that clung to him. He couldn’t take it anymore. He wanted to scream. He wanted to run.

But then the sound stopped. The silence was all-consuming again. His heart pounded in his ears, each beat reverberating in his skull until it felt like the walls were closing in around him.

Please. Please, let it end.

And then—crack.

The sound shattered the silence like a thunderclap. Mydei spun around, eyes wide, fists raised, ready to strike, but there was nothing there. Only darkness. Only empty streets that seemed to stretch on endlessly, mocking him, trapping him in this world where nothing felt real. The sound was gone, but the presence remained. It lingered, like an icy breath down his spine, freezing him in place.

His stomach churned, bile rising in his throat, but he fought it back. His body trembled, sweat beading on his forehead, as he tried to make sense of it all. It’s in my head. It has to be.

But then the whisper came.

It—that soft, mocking whisper that seemed to brush against his ears, as though it were inside his mind. The voice was no longer a distant murmur. It was close. Too close.

“You’re running out of time, Mydei.”

The words slithered through him like poison, sinking deep into his heart, twisting it in knots. His eyes scanned the shadows again, searching for the source, but it was always just out of sight. Always just behind the veil. Closer. Always closer.

His hands clenched into fists at his sides, his knuckles white, nails biting into his skin as he tried to ground himself. It’s not real. It’s not real.

But the sound—the whispering—was back, louder now. It echoed around him, bouncing off the walls of his mind, getting louder, closer, until it was all he could hear.

“Do you feel it?”

“They’re coming.”

“You can’t hide.”

The voice pulsed with a mocking, hollow laugh that curled like smoke in his veins, stealing the air from his lungs. He gasped, trying to pull in a breath, but the air felt like it was thickening around him, turning to tar, pulling him deeper into the suffocating darkness. He was drowning, suffocating, trapped in this nightmare where nothing made sense, where the world was shifting around him, warping in ways he couldn’t understand.

His mind reeled, each thought slipping away, the pressure building, overwhelming, suffocating. His heart pounded harder, faster, as the sounds grew louder, more insistent. The ground beneath him seemed to tremble, and in the back of his mind, something was whispering, laughing. Mocking.

What is it? What’s happening?

The answer never came.

The pressure mounted until Mydei couldn’t hold it anymore. He screamed —once, twice, until his throat burned with the effort, until his lungs begged for release. But it was as if the scream was swallowed whole by the dark. There was no escape.

And then, just as suddenly as it began, it all stopped.

The silence was deafening, a vacuum of stillness. The weight lifted. The shadows receded. His lungs burned for air as he collapsed to his knees, gasping, hands clutching at his chest, his body shaking uncontrollably. Was it a hallucination? A dream? He couldn’t tell. The world seemed so wrong.

The presence was gone. But the dread lingered, thick and heavy in the air around him, as if something had left its mark. His body trembled, cold sweat clinging to his skin as he fought to steady himself, to calm the frantic beat of his heart.

I’m not safe, he thought. None of us are.

Mydei didn’t think. He just moved.

His legs carried him forward on instinct, his body acting before his mind could catch up. He needed to be anywhere but here. The empty streets felt suffocating, the lingering dread gnawing at his bones. His heart pounded as he pushed himself forward, his hands trembling at his sides, his breaths coming too fast, too uneven. He was dizzy, wrong, the world around him twisting in ways he couldn’t fully grasp.

The voice was gone, but its absence was worse. It was like a stain on the back of his mind, something watching him from just beyond the edge of awareness. No matter how far he went, it felt like it was still there. A presence curling around the corners of his thoughts, waiting.

He swallowed hard, forcing himself to focus on his surroundings. He’d wandered further than he realized. The city streets had given way to a quiet, secluded garden—a place tucked away from the world, untouched by the chaos that brewed beyond its walls. The scent of damp earth and crushed petals filled his lungs as he stumbled forward, his legs finally giving out beneath him.

He sank onto a low stone bench, his hands pressing into his temples as he tried to still his racing thoughts.

You’re running out of time, Mydei.

The whisper slithered through his mind again, unbidden, unwelcome. He sucked in a sharp breath, fingers digging into his scalp as if he could claw the thought away. The knowledge of what had just happened pressed down on him like a hand against his throat. His mind was no longer his own. His thoughts—his suspicions, his curiosity—had been turned against him. Something had stripped him of the right to even think freely.

How many times had this happened before?

How many times had he been close to an answer, only to be erased?

A sickening realization churned in his gut. How much has already been taken from me?

The nausea rose again, thick and choking, but he forced it down. He clenched his jaw, digging his nails into the stone bench beneath him, grounding himself in the rough texture. He couldn’t let this consume him. He needed to think. To find a way around this.

But if his thoughts weren’t safe, then what was?

A flicker of movement caught his eye.

Mydei’s head snapped up, his body tensing on instinct. His breath hitched as he spotted a figure just beyond the hedges, moving toward him with careful, measured steps. The moment his eyes focused, his stomach twisted into knots.

Phainon.

The sight of him should’ve been grounding—should’ve been familiar, something solid in this unraveling nightmare. But all Mydei could feel was suspicion. A deep, gnawing unease coiled in his gut, colder than anything he’d felt before.

Phainon had always been an enigma, a puzzle with pieces that never quite fit together. Mydei had let it slide before, let himself believe that Phainon’s

presence, his attentiveness, was nothing more than what it seemed. But now… Now, everything felt wrong.

Phainon’s gaze softened the moment he saw him. “There you are,” he murmured, as if relieved. “I’ve been looking for you.”

Mydei didn’t respond.

Phainon approached slowly, his steps cautious, like he was trying not to startle a wounded animal. “Are you all right?” he asked, voice low, carefully measured. “You look pale.”

Mydei’s eyes flickered over him, searching—for what, he didn’t know. His mind screamed at him to pay attention, to watch closely.

His fingers curled against the stone. “How did you find me?”

Phainon blinked, tilting his head slightly. “You always come here when you need to think.”

It was an easy answer. A reasonable one. Mydei had sat in this garden countless times before, had sought its quiet solace more than once. But the unease only deepened.

Something in Phainon’s expression was too careful. Too controlled.

Mydei swallowed the bitterness rising in his throat. “And what exactly do you think I need to think about?”

Phainon hesitated. It was brief—so brief that anyone else might have missed it. But Mydei didn’t.

His breath stilled.

He narrowed his eyes, leaning forward just slightly. “Go on,” he said softly. “Tell me.”

Phainon’s gaze flickered, just for a second. The shift was almost imperceptible—the kind of mistake only made when someone thought they

weren’t being watched.

Mydei was watching.

And then, too quickly, Phainon smiled. It was gentle, reassuring—wrong. “I only meant that you’ve been through a lot. Anyone would need time to process things.”

Liar.

Mydei’s hands curled into fists. “Is that all you meant?”

Something passed through Phainon’s expression, something fleeting but sharp. He held Mydei’s gaze, unwavering, as if he could will him into believing. “Of course.”

Mydei didn’t breathe.

He felt it then—that deep, sickening drop in his stomach. There it is. There it is.

Phainon had slipped.

It was small, subtle, but wrong. Like a single crack in a flawless mirror.

And Mydei knew.

His pulse quickened, rage and dread twisting together in his chest, his suspicion sharpening into something more dangerous. He had been right to be wary. Right to watch.

Phainon wasn’t just here by chance. He knew. He had known something.

Mydei’s voice was low, sharp as a blade. “You’re lying to me.”

Phainon’s smile didn’t falter, but Mydei could see the shift—the way his muscles tensed just slightly, the way his fingers twitched as if resisting the urge to move.

“Mydei,” Phainon said evenly, “you’re not making sense.”

The gaslighting was immediate.

Mydei’s jaw clenched so tightly it ached. “Don’t do that.”

Phainon’s brows furrowed in concern—false concern, Mydei realized with a sickening certainty. “Do what?”

His voice was too soft. Too understanding. It made Mydei’s skin crawl.

“You know what.” His voice was shaking now, his anger barely held in check. “You let something slip. I heard it. You knew.”

Phainon didn’t speak.

The silence stretched between them, tense and electric.

And then, slowly—too slowly—Phainon’s expression shifted.

The concern melted away, giving way to something quieter. Sharper.

He took a step closer. “You’re paranoid,” he murmured.

The way he said it, so gently, so certainly, made Mydei’s blood run cold.

Because for the briefest moment, he almost believed him.

Mydei’s breath was tight in his chest, a cold sweat gathering on the back of his neck. The more he pressed, the more he could feel the suffocating tension in the air. The flicker of unease in Phainon’s gaze was subtle, but it was enough to make the hairs on Mydei’s arms stand on end.

“I know you know something,” Mydei said, his voice low and sharp. “You’ve been too careful. Too predictable.”

Phainon gave a soft, almost disbelieving laugh, but it didn’t reach his eyes. “Predictable? Mydei, you’re not making any sense.”

You’re lying. You’re lying, and I can see it.

The thought surged in Mydei’s mind, but the moment he let his suspicion settle, his pulse picked up again. Why? Why would Phainon—of all people —be involved? But the more he looked at him, the more he noticed the little things. The way Phainon’s shoulders tensed when Mydei spoke too frankly. The slight hitch in his breath whenever the conversation veered too close to something real.

“You’re deflecting,” Mydei said, his voice quieter but no less forceful. His fingers gripped the edge of the bench, knuckles white with the force of it. “Stop trying to sidestep the question. You know more than you’re letting on.”

Phainon’s expression shifted, just slightly, the calm mask cracking at the edges. For a second, there was something flickering behind his eyes— something that wasn’t quite human. But as fast as it appeared, it was gone, replaced by that same patient, concerned expression.

“Mydei,” he said, and there was a softness in his voice now, almost too soft. “You’re stressed. You’re reading into things.”

It was like a knife to Mydei’s chest, that gentle tone. It felt wrong, too wrong. Phainon was too smooth, too perfect in his manipulation. But that didn’t stop the crack in his composure from showing, just a flicker of something deeper—something more sinister—beneath the surface.

“No,” Mydei pressed, his voice rising a little. “No, I’m not. You know something. You’re hiding something from me. And it’s not just a slip-up. You’ve been hiding it for a while now.”

Phainon’s face tightened, just the smallest twitch in his jaw. “Mydei, please,” he said, stepping forward just enough to close the gap. “This isn’t the time for this. You’re not in the right frame of mind.”

Mydei’s pulse thrummed in his ears. This isn’t right. I know this isn’t right. But even as the nagging voice inside his mind tried to piece everything

together, another part of him—the real part of him, the part that should have been clouded by the strange forces—held on.

It wasn’t working.

Phainon was trying to get to him, trying to disarm him, to make him doubt himself, but it wasn’t working. Mydei’s suspicions were still there.

“You’re not convincing me,” Mydei muttered under his breath. His words hung in the air, thick and heavy. “You’ve been playing me for so long, Phainon.”

The shift was barely noticeable. One second, Phainon’s expression was just shy of worried, the next, there was a tension in his stance—a flicker of something sharp, dangerous. For the briefest moment, Mydei saw it. Phainon’s lips parted, but the words didn’t come.

Then, his voice softened again, but now it was colder, more controlled. “You’ve been under a lot of pressure, Mydei. You’re letting your mind play tricks on you.”

“Shut up,” Mydei hissed, his eyes narrowing, muscles coiling with anger and suspicion. “I’m not crazy.”

Phainon’s calm facade cracked again—just enough to make Mydei’s blood run cold. His eyes widened for a split second, an almost imperceptible flash of something beneath the surface. Mydei caught it. That’s when he realized —this was the lie. Phainon was trying to hide the truth behind the mask of sympathy, pretending he didn’t know what was really going on.

But Mydei saw through it.

The silence stretched between them, thick and unbearable. Mydei was sure now. He was almost certain. Whatever was happening, whatever Phainon was hiding, it was tied to the darkness, to the twisted forces that were pulling at the fabric of his reality.

Phainon was involved. He was part of it. And he had been all along.

But the question remained: How?

“Mydei…” Phainon’s voice was barely a whisper now, an attempt to regain control, to smooth over the crack. “This isn’t healthy. You need to rest. Think about this with a clear mind. You don’t know what you’re saying.”

But Mydei didn’t listen. He couldn’t. He knew, deep down, that if he didn’t press now, if he didn’t expose the truth, then he might never get another chance.

“You know something, Phainon,” Mydei said, every word like a dagger. He leaned in, his face cold and sharp. “And you’re not fooling me anymore.”

The deflection was clear, but it didn’t matter.

Phainon’s smile faltered just a fraction, the edge of his patience wearing thin. There was something darker behind those eyes now—something that wanted to break free, but it was contained, locked behind a smile that was just a little too tight.

Mydei’s fingers trembled, but he didn’t look away. He wouldn’t. “You’re hiding something from me,” he repeated, voice like steel. “And I will find out what it is.”

Phainon’s expression tightened, but he said nothing more.

Mydei’s heart pounded in his chest, his mind racing. For a moment, just a fleeting moment, he thought he could see through Phainon’s calm facade, but the next, it was gone.

Mydei stood from the bench, his eyes still fixed on Phainon. His suspicion was absolute.

But he still didn’t know the truth. And that was the only thing that kept him from going over the edge.

Phainon remained silent, watching him with that soft, unreadable expression.

It wasn’t over. Not yet.

The tension between them had broken, and now Mydei was all rage. Every word Phainon refused to speak, every evasive glance he cast, only fed Mydei’s fury. He couldn’t let it go. He couldn’t.

“Tell me, Phainon,” Mydei snarled, his voice low and guttural, barely containing the fury that surged beneath the surface. “What is it you’re hiding from me? What is it you know?”

Phainon’s lips parted as if to answer, but no words came. The silence between them stretched longer than it should have, thick with unspoken tension. Phainon just stared at him, eyes defiant, cold, unafraid.

Mydei snapped.

With a brutal motion, he threw Phainon to the ground, slamming him against the dirt so hard that Phainon’s breath was knocked out of him. Before he could recover, Mydei was on top of him, hands curling into fists around his throat.

“Answer me!” Mydei roared, his eyes wild with fury. The words were like poison, laced with accusation. His fingers tightened around Phainon’s throat, but not enough to choke—just enough to force compliance. Just enough to make him feel the threat.

But Phainon still said nothing, still didn’t fight back. He simply looked at Mydei with that same detached, almost amused expression.

It was maddening.

Mydei’s anger surged again, and before Phainon could even react, he grabbed the nearest weapon—Phainon’s own sword—and drew it free from its sheath. The cold, sharp steel glinted in the dim light, its edge gleaming with the promise of violence.

Phainon’s eyes widened ever so slightly, but still, no fight. No resistance. No fear. It made Mydei’s blood boil even more.

“Mydei,” Phainon’s voice was calm, unnervingly so, even with Mydei’s grip tightening. “This is beneath you.”

The words hit Mydei like a slap, and his anger only deepened. His grip on Phainon’s hair tightened painfully, yanking his head back. The gauntlets on his hands dug into Phainon’s scalp, the pressure enough to pull the skin taut, a sharp burn of discomfort that made Phainon wince, but he didn’t cry out.

Mydei’s rage was at the breaking point. With a snarl, he pressed the sword against Phainon’s neck, just hard enough to draw blood. The thin line of red welled up, staining Phainon’s skin. Mydei’s fingers were still tangled in his hair, pulling hard enough to make Phainon’s neck arch painfully back.

“You don’t get to stay silent anymore,” Mydei growled. His voice was hoarse, the edges of it cracking with the anger of his frustration. “You’ll talk now. Now. Or I’ll make you.”

Phainon coughed, a strangled sound that made his chest tremble. Blood spattered onto the ground, and he winced at the pain, but his eyes never left Mydei’s face. There was no fear in them. No desperation. Only that same expression of passive amusement, like a cat watching a mouse squirm in its claws.

Phainon coughed again, this time harder, the blood dripping from his lips.

“You’re hurting me, Mydei,” Phainon whispered, his voice laced with a softness that was almost mocking. “This isn’t like you.”

Mydei’s grip tightened on Phainon’s hair, pulling harder, forcing Phainon to look up at him. The sword pressed into his skin, the sharp edge biting deeper now. Blood spilled down his neck in steady rivulets, but Phainon didn’t make a sound. He just stared back at Mydei, unblinking, as though Mydei’s violence were nothing more than a trivial inconvenience.

The silence stretched, suffocating, and Mydei’s hand trembled with the effort it took to stay in control. The words were bubbling up, his mouth dry, his throat tight.

“Why aren’t you fighting back?” Mydei hissed, his voice cracking with the sheer intensity of his fury. “Why aren’t you—” He broke off, his breath coming in ragged gasps.

Phainon coughed again, blood splattering onto Mydei’s gauntlet, but still, he said nothing. He let the blood drip from his mouth as if it didn’t matter, as if Mydei’s rage was just another thing to be endured. And that calm, that resignation, only made Mydei angrier.

With a roar of frustration, Mydei moved the sword up and shoved it deeper against Phainon’s shoulder, the tip slicing into the tender flesh, the blood flowing more freely now. His gauntleted hand pulled Phainon’s hair with a violent tug, forcing Phainon’s face upward as if trying to break him open.

The sound of the blood dripping onto the ground was deafening in the otherwise silent space.

“Tell me what I need to know!” Mydei shouted, his voice shaking. “Why are you hiding this from me? You think I can’t see it? You think I can’t tell when something’s wrong? Who are you working with, Phainon? Who the hell is pulling your strings?”

Phainon’s eyes met his, calm, collected, and full of an emotion Mydei couldn’t quite place.

And then Phainon spoke, the words just loud enough to make Mydei’s breath catch.

“You’re the one who’s wrong, Mydei,” he said softly. “You’re the one who can’t stop. You’ve already made up your mind, haven’t you?”

Mydei’s anger boiled over. With a shout, he slammed Phainon’s head against the ground, the force of it shaking the dirt beneath them. He stood over him, chest heaving, sweat dripping from his brow, as the sword slipped from Phainon’s neck.

For a long moment, the only sound in the air was the ragged breathing of the two of them, and the wet, sickening sound of Phainon’s blood dripping

onto the earth.

Phainon didn’t move, didn’t even flinch. He just looked up at Mydei with an almost curious expression, as though he were waiting for something.

But Mydei wasn’t going to let up. Not yet. He wanted answers. And he was going to get them—no matter what it took.

Mydei stood over Phainon, chest heaving, his hands trembling slightly from the intensity of his own actions. The sword, now coated in blood, slipped from his grasp as his grip faltered. His breath was ragged, uneven, like a beast on the edge of collapse. His body was tense with adrenaline, every fiber of him still strung taut from the violence, the need for answers.

Phainon’s face was a twisted mess of cuts, bruises, and blood. His once-pristine skin was marred, eyes half-lidded and unfocused, struggling to stay conscious beneath the weight of Mydei’s blows. Blood pooled around him, staining the ground, yet he hadn’t moved. Not once had he fought back.

Mydei’s pulse throbbed in his ears, the adrenaline still pumping through his veins. For a moment, he couldn’t understand what had just happened. His hands were shaking, his heart pounding in his chest like a drum of war.

The moment he sat down, he knew he couldn’t stand again. His body felt like it had been hollowed out, drained of everything. He let himself collapse into the nearest chair, his back slumping with the heaviness of it all. His armor—still caked with dirt and blood—felt like it was part of him now, each strap digging into his skin, each piece pressing into him as if trying to remind him that he couldn’t escape this.

His eyes fluttered, closing for just a moment, just long enough for the room to spin around him, the sounds of the world outside fading into the background. He tried to resist it, to hold on for just a bit longer, but his body had other plans.

The weight of his own eyelids, the pull of sleep, was irresistible. He didn’t even bother to remove his armor. He barely had the energy to take off his boots before he let himself fall forward, his face hitting the table with a dull thud. His breath came in uneven gasps, shallow and labored, as if each inhale were a struggle, each exhale a victory.

And then, as the room seemed to spin around him, he let go.

The pain, the fear, the grief—they were all drowned out by the merciful pull of unconsciousness. Mydei’s body finally surrendered, and the weight of the world no longer mattered.

It was just him and the darkness.

The world shifted. There was no sound, no air—just the oppressive hum of golden threads stretching infinitely into a darkness that swallowed everything. They twisted and pulsed like living veins, thick as ropes, their glow seeping into his very soul.

Mydei wasn’t standing on solid ground anymore. His feet sank into the threads, each step dragging him deeper into their suffocating grip. The threads tightened around his legs, biting into his flesh, pulling him forward with an unnatural force. His heart thudded violently in his chest, the beat ringing through his body like a death knell, but there was something else— something wrong.

He had to keep moving. This was a dream, he reminded himself, struggling against the pull of the golden strands. It was all a nightmare, a reflection of his fears, and he couldn’t let himself get caught in it. But every step felt heavier than the last, each movement more painful, like his body was being torn apart from the inside out.

But despite the terror clenching his chest, the pressure in his mind, there was a gnawing thread of clarity—he knew. He knew this was a dream. This wasn’t real.

Yet, somehow, the pain felt real. It cut deep into him as the threads wound around his body, digging into his flesh like talons. His breath hitched, his

throat raw as the threads constricted tighter and tighter. He could feel his muscles burning, straining against the unnatural weight of the dream.

And then—she appeared.

Aglaea.

Her form shimmered in the distance, twisted and caught in the golden threads that snaked through the air, like a puppet trapped in its own strings. She was struggling, her body trembling as the threads wound around her, suffocating her. Her once regal figure was bent, her hair tangled and matted, her eyes wild with fear, desperation.

Mydei’s heart cracked. This wasn’t real, he reminded himself again. She couldn’t truly be here—she couldn’t truly be suffering—but as he moved toward her, his legs trembling beneath him, the feeling of inevitability sunk into his chest.

He could barely walk. His feet dragged through the threads, each movement a struggle. His body screamed, muscles burning with pain, but still—he pushed forward, because he had to get to her.

Her cries were muffled, swallowed by the hum of the threads, but he could see her lips moving, feel the rawness of her agony in the air. Her eyes locked on him, pleading with him, asking him to save her, to free her from whatever nightmare they were both trapped in.

But Mydei knew this was no salvation.

The threads—they were killing her.

They had burrowed into her skin, ripping her apart from the inside out. Her blood—her golden blood—spilled from her wounds, dripping onto the floor below her, pooling like liquid light. The sight was nauseating. The air was thick with the stench of death.

“Aglaea,” Mydei whispered, voice trembling, though he knew it wouldn’t reach her. It couldn’t.

And yet, his body moved as if of its own volition. The dagger appeared in his hands, cold steel, foreign in his palms. It felt wrong, but his fingers wrapped around it with sickening familiarity. It was too heavy, too cold.

This isn’t real. He tried to tell himself again, but the dagger didn’t feel like a dream anymore. It felt like something he could feel, something that was anchored in this twisted nightmare.

Aglaea’s hands reached out, her fingers shaking as they brushed against his chest, her eyes still wide with shock. She knew. She knew what was happening. Her mouth moved, but no sound came. Her eyes—those golden, all-knowing eyes—looked at him, full of regret, full of pleading.

And then, before he could stop it, before he could scream, his hand lifted, the dagger in his grasp, the cold steel reflecting the dim glow of the threads.

Her eyes widened as the steel sunk into her chest.

The world froze.

The blade drove through her flesh, deep, too deep, and Mydei could feel the sickening warmth of her blood as it sprayed across his hands, his face. He could hear the sound—the wet, sickening sound—of the steel cutting through her. Her body jerked, her mouth opened, but no sound came. Only blood.

Golden blood.

It gushed from her wound, hot and thick, coating his hands, staining the threads, covering him completely. The sensation of it, the heat of her life draining into him, was enough to make him gag, to make him want to scream—except his voice had been stolen.

She was still staring at him. Those eyes. They were still full of disbelief. Why? The word hung in the air like a poison, but it never escaped her lips. She reached for him again, but it was too late. The light in her eyes flickered, dimmed, and then—she was gone.

Her body collapsed, her head tilting back as the last of her life drained away, mixing with the golden threads beneath her. And then—the world began to collapse.

This is a dream, Mydei thought, but his chest constricted with guilt, with horror, as his hands trembled violently, the dagger still clutched tightly in his grasp. His legs buckled beneath him, his body giving way to the agony that was no longer a dream.

But it was too late.

As her blood soaked into the threads, and the last of her essence faded into nothingness, Mydei’s heart shattered. He knew what he had done. There was no escape from it now. Ut was a dream, only a figment of his imagination, but fuck if that still didn’t hurt him.

And in her final moments, Aglaea’s lips moved again.

His name.

But it wasn’t enough. She was already gone.

And Mydei was left in the dark.

-

The smell of salt in the air was soothing, grounding. Mydei inhaled deeply, the familiar scent bringing him a brief sense of comfort. For a moment, he felt like everything was okay, like the chaos of the world outside had been nothing but a dream, a terrible, nightmare-like distraction. It had to have been. Everything had felt so surreal, too sharp, too heavy. But as the fog of sleep faded from his mind, reality began to tug at him, gently at first.

He was back in the safehouse. He had to be. He could still feel the warmth of the fire crackling somewhere in the distance. The sheets beneath him were soft, familiar, and the air—yes, the air was normal. No golden blood. No cold, lifeless body in his arms. Just the usual quiet hum of the house, the peaceful stillness of safety.

Just a dream.

He let out a shaky breath, closing his eyes again, willing himself to push the nightmare away. It was just a dream. He was fine. The chaos, the death—it wasn’t real. He wasn’t holding her. She wasn’t dead in his arms. He wasn’t drowning in the guilt of his own hands.

A sharp breath caught in his throat. His eyes snapped open, wide with panic, but the room around him remained undisturbed, the flickering warmth of firelight dancing across the walls. He had to get a hold of himself. This wasn’t real. He was in the safehouse, just like before.

But something felt off. The blood.

His hands were sticky, his fingers coated with something slick, warm. He looked down, still half believing it was a trick of his mind, a ghost of the dream.

Golden blood.

The thought slapped him awake with brutal force. He blinked rapidly, his mind struggling to comprehend. His breath caught in his chest as he looked down to see the source, and there she was—Aglaea.

No.

It was impossible. No.

Her body was limp in his arms, her pale face marred by the blood that stained the skin beneath her, as if the color had been drained from her completely. His hands were soaked in it—golden blood, just like before. But this time, there was no escaping it. His heart thudded painfully in his chest, his breath shallow and ragged.

No.

The air grew thick and oppressive as the weight of her body, lifeless in his arms, became an unbearable presence. He tried to make sense of it, to reconcile what he was seeing with what his mind told him should be true.

She couldn’t be dead. She couldn’t be in his arms, bleeding out with his hands soaked in her life.

This is a dream. His thoughts trembled, disjointed. I just have to wake up.

But the weight of her was too real, too heavy. The warm slickness of her blood against his skin grounded him, each drop an undeniable truth. His chest tightened as he tried to move, to get away from the suffocating weight of it. He wanted to wake up, to force himself back into the safehouse, into the lies. Please let it be a dream.

But it wasn’t. The blood wouldn’t stop. It flowed from her wound, staining his arms, his clothes, his soul. He couldn’t breathe. The pain in his chest was suffocating, not from the physical weight of her body, but from the weight of the reality that he had done this.

I killed her.

The words felt alien on his tongue, distant as they reverberated in his mind, but they wouldn’t leave. The guilt gnawed at him, sinking its teeth into the marrow of his bones. Her lifeless eyes stared back at him, the softness in them gone, replaced by a cold emptiness. Her body was still, and there was no undoing it.

The desperation in his chest tightened, pulling at the very core of his being. He needed to wake up. He needed to escape. He didn’t want this. He didn’t want her in his arms like this, dead in his arms.

With trembling hands, he reached up to his neck, feeling the pulse of his own heartbeat, trying to ground himself, trying to make the reality slip back into a dream. He needed the pain. He needed to feel something. Anything that would make him feel alive again, something to snap him out of this nightmare that had become too real.

His fingers dug into his skin, sharp nails pressing into the flesh, but the sensation didn’t reach him. It was nothing. Nothing like the terror, the coldness, the grief that was flooding his mind. He could feel the blood beneath his nails, but it didn’t matter. It was too much. He needed more.

His mind screamed at him, This is a dream. This isn’t real. But his body betrayed him. The pain that he inflicted on himself only brought him further into despair, deeper into the nightmare he couldn’t escape. It wasn’t enough to erase what he’d done, to erase the life he’d stolen. He dug harder, the raw sting of the pain spreading up his neck, the crimson flowing from the cuts, but still, the tears came.

And with them, the truth.

He had killed her.

The reality of it shattered him. His breath hitched, his chest constricting tighter than before. He couldn’t stop the flood of tears that came after that— real tears, tears that came with the realization that this was no longer a dream. He wasn’t waking up. This wasn’t a nightmare he could run from.

This was his reality.

The golden blood soaked into his skin, the warmth of it growing colder with each passing second. He could feel it on him, all around him, filling the cracks of his brokenness.

Aglaea’s body grew colder in his arms, and as his tears continued to fall, his heart broke a little more with each drop, each breath that rattled in his chest.

The terror didn’t end. It couldn’t.

This was real.

Mydei’s body shook, each breath coming in jagged, gasping sobs. The reality of it was crashing in on him with a force he couldn’t contain, couldn’t escape. He could feel her—Aglaea—so cold and lifeless in his arms, her blood still seeping out onto his skin, soaking through the fabric of his clothes. The golden liquid had long since turned darker, a sickening shade of crimson pooling beneath her, and every drop felt like a weight on his chest.

He couldn’t move. He couldn’t think. The truth was sinking in, and there was no turning away from it. I did this. The words were like a broken record, playing over and over in his mind, louder each time. His hands, shaking and trembling, refused to let go of her. His fingers were locked around her, gripping her as though if he just held on long enough, the nightmare would end. But it didn’t. The weight of her body, the coldness spreading through her veins, was a stark reminder that it was real.

She was gone.

And it was his fault.

His stomach twisted as his mind tried to force some semblance of logic, something to save him from the crushing weight of guilt. But it was no use. There was no justification. No reason. He had struck the fatal blow. He had chosen to end her suffering, but in doing so, he had destroyed everything that had ever mattered.

I killed her. I killed Aglaea.

The realization hit him like a hammer to the skull, and his entire body recoiled in horror. A guttural, animalistic cry tore from his throat as he collapsed against her, his face buried in the coldness of her neck. His hands gripped her tighter, as though by some miracle, he could pull her back, reverse the damage. But nothing could undo it.

The world outside—every voice, every scream, every ounce of pain—faded into a blur. The only thing that existed now was Aglaea’s lifeless body and the overwhelming truth of his responsibility. The tears came in waves, but they weren’t enough. Nothing was enough. It wasn’t enough to wash the blood from his hands. He couldn’t escape the horror.

He couldn’t stop the sobs. They tore through him like a relentless storm, shaking his body violently as he curled into himself, clutching her like a lifeline even though she was already gone. His chest was tight, as if the very air around him had become too thick to breathe, every breath stolen by the grief that consumed him.

I did this. It kept repeating, louder, clearer. I did this. I killed her.

His throat was raw, his chest heaving with the force of his cries. The tears didn’t stop. They kept falling, endless, a torrent that wouldn’t end. The sobs wracked his body, sharp and desperate, as if he were trying to expel the guilt, to somehow rid himself of the horror he’d unleashed. But it only made it worse. The more he cried, the more the weight of it pressed down on him.

Aglaea’s body was cold. So cold.

It felt like hours had passed. How long had he been sitting there with her? Hours? Days? His mind couldn’t keep up. Time had lost all meaning. There was nothing but the suffocating reality of her death and his role in it.

He tried to pull himself together, to pull away, to stop, but he couldn’t. His fingers refused to release her, as if the act of letting go would make it all more real. And so, he held her—held her in silence as his sobs filled the empty space around them. The only sound in the world was his heart breaking, over and over again.

Eventually, the tears ran dry, leaving only the aching emptiness. His face was blotchy and raw, his eyes swollen and red, but still, his chest heaved with the weight of the grief. His mind was numb, broken in ways he couldn’t understand, but the knowledge of what he’d done never left.

I killed her. The words, empty and hollow, echoed through his mind like a death sentence. There was nothing left. He had nothing left.

The world outside was fading, distant and irrelevant. All that mattered was the emptiness inside him, the hole that Aglaea’s death had left in his heart. He didn’t know what to do with himself anymore. He didn’t know how to exist in a world where he had taken her life.

He wanted to die. He wanted it all to end. But he couldn’t. Not when the world had already taken so much from him.

Mydei’s arms grew weak. His chest, already tight, felt as though it was collapsing under the sheer amount his guilt. His body ached, but it was a hollow pain. He wanted to sleep, to escape, but there was no escaping this.

I killed her.

The tears came again, softer now, but endless. The realization was a slow burn, sinking deeper into him, making him wish he could simply vanish into the air. But he couldn’t. He was here. Still here.

And nothing would ever be the same again.

The hours stretched, turning into a day. Mydei didn’t move.

The world outside Okhema continued, the city pulsing with life beyond the temple walls, but to him, it may as well have been a distant dream. He had not spoken. He had not eaten. He had not moved from where he sat, Aglaea’s lifeless body cradled against him, golden blood long dried in sickly patches across his arms, his chest, his face.

He didn’t even register time anymore. His mind had been on the edge of breaking for hours, each second pulling at the frayed edges of his sanity. There was nothing left in him. He had screamed until his throat was raw, cried until his body physically could not shed another tear. He had tried everything—digging his nails into his own skin, dragging a blade across his arm just to feel something, anything, that wasn’t this. It hadn’t worked. The pain wasn’t enough. It was never enough.

But he couldn’t leave. He couldn’t. Not even to clean the blood from his hands, to clear the haze from his mind. He had killed her. If he left, then it would be real. If he left, then he would have to accept what he had done.

The doors creaked open.

Mydei didn’t react.

He could hear the low murmurs of voices, the cautious, hesitant footsteps. Elders. They must have come for their usual business with Aglaea, unaware

that she was no longer capable of meeting them. He barely noticed. They didn’t matter.

Then—gasping. Quick, hurried whispers, panicked scrambling of feet. The unmistakable sound of someone tripping over themselves in a desperate attempt to flee.

Mydei barely turned his head, just enough to catch the sight of the elders bolting out of the room as if they had seen death itself.

Or rather—him.

A pause. The rush of footsteps. Then a voice.

“Mydei?”

At first, he didn’t register it. His mind was so fogged over with exhaustion and grief that the voice didn’t even feel real. But then—again, closer this time, laced with something that made Mydei’s stomach churn.

“Mydei—what have you done?”

The words should have struck something in him. Should have sparked a reaction, a defense, something. But all Mydei could do was stare down at Aglaea’s lifeless body, blankly, like he had long since become disconnected from himself. His thoughts were empty. He had no response. There was nothing left to say.

Phainon stepped forward.

Mydei wanted to feel something at the sight of him. Relief, maybe. A flicker of hope that Phainon—who always had something to say, always had some way to lighten the weight on his shoulders—would do something. But when he finally looked up, when he finally saw Phainon’s expression—

His heart shattered all over again.

Phainon was terrified.

Not just at the sight of Aglaea’s body. Not just at the blood smeared across the floor, the walls, Mydei himself. But at him.

For the first time, Phainon looked at him with fear in his eyes.

The way Phainon stiffened, the way his throat bobbed as he swallowed down his nerves, the way he hesitated, visibly fighting some deep-rooted instinct to take a step back instead of forward—Mydei felt it. He felt the shift, and once again everything a about it pressing down on his already fragile mind.

Phainon was afraid of him.

The realization hit like a blade to the gut.

Mydei’s breathing grew shallow, erratic, his hands curling into fists against Aglaea’s cold skin. He tried to say something, anything, but his throat was too dry, too raw, too broken to form words. He wanted Phainon to fix this. He wanted him to say something, to crack some stupid joke, to make light of the situation the way he always did.

But Phainon just stood there, struggling, like he didn’t even know what to do with him.

And that—that was what finally broke him.

The one person he had left. The one person he had still been clinging to, desperately hoping for even the smallest shred of reassurance—Phainon couldn’t even look at him the same way anymore.

A choked sound clawed its way up Mydei’s throat. A dry, pathetic half-sob, his body shaking violently as his fingers dug so hard into Aglaea’s skin that they might as well have broken through.

Phainon took another slow step forward, cautious, hesitant, like he was approaching a wounded animal. His expression flickered between fear and something deeper, something pained, something he was clearly trying to suppress.

“Mydei,” Phainon murmured, voice shaking just enough that it cut through the haze of Mydei’s mind. “Come here.”

But Mydei couldn’t move. He just shook his head, lips trembling, tears spilling again even though he thought he had none left to cry. His shoulders convulsed as he tried to breathe, but the air wouldn’t come, and for the first time since this nightmare had begun—

He wanted to die more than he ever had before.

But he couldn’t.

So instead, he just broke apart completely, curling in on himself as the sobs overtook him once more. Every tear was a manifestation of the pain that cut through him, but it was also a release—a futile attempt to rid himself of the agony that would never leave. He felt as though the world was collapsing around him, and in this fragile state, his mind could no longer hold onto the illusion that he was still alive, that he still mattered.

Phainon’s hand reached out, gently placing it on his shoulder, his grip firm but cautious. “Mydei…”

For a moment, Mydei didn’t respond. He didn’t even acknowledge Phainon’s touch. His world was too far gone, too broken to care. The only thing that remained was the unbearable weight of Aglaea’s death and his own unbearable guilt.

But Phainon, despite the trembling fear in his voice, didn’t let go. He stayed with him.

And that’s when Mydei realized—despite everything, despite all the horrors, Phainon was still here.

Phainon’s gaze flickered to Aglaea’s body, a somber look crossing his face as he watched Mydei clutch her tighter. His eyes softened for a fraction of a second, before the cold, calculated resolve took over. He knew this moment had to come—he just hadn’t anticipated how much he’d have to break through.

“Mydei…” Phainon’s voice was gentle, coaxing, but there was something else lurking beneath it—a quiet, unsettling tension. He reached for Aglaea’s body, fingers brushing lightly against Mydei’s arm.

The second his fingers made contact, Mydei’s head snapped up, eyes wide with desperation. He tightened his grip, his arms trembling. “No,” he whispered, a broken sob in his throat. “No, don’t take her. She… she’s not gone. She can’t be gone.”

Phainon’s face was unreadable, but there was an edge to his calm that made Mydei feel vulnerable, exposed in a way he hadn’t felt since before all this began. He didn’t understand why Phainon—why anyone—would want to take Aglaea from him, when she was the only thing that kept him tethered to what was left of his sanity.

“Let her go, Mydei.” Phainon’s voice was firm now, the kind of command that cut through the air. “We have to… we have to let her go.”

Mydei recoiled at the thought, clutching Aglaea’s corpse harder, his tears spilling anew. “I won’t let her go. I can’t… She’s… she’s mine.”

Phainon’s eye almost unnoticeably twitched when he’d said that, but other than that his hand hovered over Mydei’s, cold but steady. “You’re not alone in this anymore. You have to let her go.”

There was a pause—a long, heavy silence. Mydei’s breathing quickened, his chest tight, and for a moment, he almost thought Phainon would force him. But the tenderness in Phainon’s voice kept him from pushing away, as if the other man was pleading with him in the only way that didn’t make him feel like an intruder.

Slowly, agonizingly, Mydei’s grip loosened. His heart twisted as he pulled away, hands shaking uncontrollably as he let Aglaea’s body slip into Phainon’s embrace. Every inch of him recoiled from the motion, but he was too numb to fight it anymore.

let it end please.

-

Time passed in a blur. The funeral was held in the sacred halls beneath Okhema, where the air was thick with incense and grief. The procession was silent, filled with tight-lipped elders and weary onlookers who bowed their heads, but none of them mourned like Mydei.

Because no one else had killed her with their own hands.

He barely registered the words spoken, the rites performed. Aglaea’s body was laid to rest in golden wrappings, her features untouched by death, serene in a way that made Mydei’s stomach turn. Her blood, her golden blood, had long since been cleaned from his hands, but he still felt it there, caking under his nails, burning his skin. He stared at her, waiting for something—anything—to feel real again.

It never did.

She was lowered into the tomb with quiet reverence. Mydei didn’t cry. He didn’t move. He only watched, hollow, as the stone door slid into place, sealing her away forever.

And then there was nothing.

He should’ve left. Should’ve walked away, as the others did. But he stayed, standing before the tomb, staring at the carved engravings of Aglaea’s name until his vision blurred. His body swayed slightly, exhaustion gnawing at his bones, but he barely felt it.

He didn’t want to feel anything anymore.

Wouldn’t it be easier if he just—

Mydei exhaled sharply, pressing a trembling hand to his forehead. He was immortal. There was no escape for him, no matter how much he wanted it. Even if he burned, even if he shattered every bone in his body, he would wake up again. Every time. Over and over and over—

A sharp breath caught in his throat, and for the first time since the burial began, his fingers curled into fists. His shoulders trembled, and for a single, horrifying moment, he swore he could still feel the knife in his hands, feel the way Aglaea’s body had gone slack, how her blood had pooled around him like a golden sea—

A hand touched his shoulder.

Mydei flinched violently, nearly staggering backward. His head snapped up, eyes wild, only to meet familiar green ones staring back at him.

Phainon.

He didn’t say anything. Not at first. Just stood there, quiet, watching him with something unreadable in his expression. Then, carefully, gently, he guided Mydei down, pressing him to sit on the cold stone steps.

Mydei let him. He let Phainon press a hand against the back of his neck, grounding him, steadying him. He barely noticed the way Phainon’s grip was firm but deliberate, the way he handled him as though he were something fragile, something on the verge of shattering.

Because he was.

“You’re still here,” Phainon murmured, voice low.

Where else would he go? What else was left for him?

Mydei swallowed, throat tight, the words sticking there, too much, too heavy to say. He squeezed his eyes shut, shaking his head.

“I don’t know who I am anymore,” he whispered, voice hoarse.

For a moment, there was only silence. Then, Phainon’s voice, soft but unyielding:

“Then let me be your anchor.”

The words settled deep in his chest.

Mydei had nothing left. No reason to keep going, no future, no purpose. He was drowning in his own grief, his own mistakes. And yet Phainon stood before him, offering something steady. Something real.

For once, Mydei didn’t hesitate.

He nodded. Slowly, but without doubt.

And then—he moved.

Not away. Not to flee or fight or run. But toward Phainon, towards the only thing still standing in the wreckage of his world. His hands gripped Phainon’s sleeves, clutching tightly, shaking, as if afraid that if he let go, he would disappear entirely.

Phainon didn’t pull away. He let Mydei cling to him, let his body tremble against his own, let him bury his face in his shoulder like a broken man grasping at the last thing tethering him to existence.

It didn’t fix anything. It didn’t erase what had been done.

But Mydei believed him.

And for the first time in what felt like centuries—

Phainon truly smiled.

Just barely, just for a flicker of a second, before it melted into something softer, something crafted to be seen.

Mydei didn’t realize it, but in this moment, Phainon had won.

There was no more need for manipulation. No more need to nudge, to twist, to push Mydei into place.

He was already where he needed him.

Phainon buried the satisfaction under layers of concern, wrapping an arm around Mydei’s shoulders, holding him close. “I’ll help you,” he murmured.

“We’ll move forward, together.”

And Mydei, shattered and lost, believed him.

Because there was nothing else left.

And Phainon? He had never been happier.

The world had lost its color.

Days bled into nights, nights into days, but Mydei hardly noticed. Time moved around him like a slow-moving tide, pulling and receding, dragging him along without resistance. He did what was necessary—he protected what little remained of Okhema, shielded those who still clung to its broken remnants. That was all he had left.

The air always smelled of smoke and damp rot, the weight of the city’s slow decay pressing down on him with every breath. Ruin stretched across the streets, buildings hollowed out like carcasses, their bones left to crumble. The people were quieter now. The grief that once screamed had settled into a whisper, into vacant stares and shuffled steps. They were like ghosts haunting their own bodies. Mydei wasn’t sure when he had become one of them.

He moved where he was needed, fought when it was required. But he was hollow. Detached. The world was muted, blurred at the edges, as if he were

walking through a dream he couldn’t wake from. He felt neither hunger nor exhaustion, only a constant, quiet ache—a weight in his chest that never lifted. It didn’t matter. None of it did.

But then—Phainon.

Phainon was the only thing sharp in the haze, the only presence that cut through the numbness. He was steady, solid, there. Always there.

He simply existed alongside him, offering help where he could, easing the burdens Mydei refused to acknowledge.

When Mydei was too lost in his own head to eat, Phainon would place food near him, making some offhanded remark about how much weaker he looked. When Mydei moved through the streets like a shadow, Phainon was at his side, as if making sure he didn’t fade into nothing entirely. When the silence in his mind became too vast, Phainon filled it, speaking about things that didn’t matter—stories, observations, meaningless little things that, somehow, still kept Mydei tethered.

Phainon never pushed him to move on. Never told him to forget.

But he never let him slip away, either.

And Mydei, without realizing it, started letting him in.

The city had always been a cradle of fire and blood, but now it was a shell of what it had once been. Mydei was no different.

Sitting on the edge of a stone wall overseeing the outside world from Okhema, his hands clasped loosely in his lap, he gazed out over the wreckage that sprawled before him. Okhema was holding on by a thread, but everything else? Shattered. Not even worth mentioning. It was

everything he was, everything he had once been, crumbling to dust. He couldn’t feel it anymore. There was only the quiet hum of emptiness.

Behind him, Phainon’s footsteps were soft, purposeful. He didn’t intrude— never did—but his presence was undeniable, like a shadow falling over the smallest corner of Mydei’s world.

“Mydei,” Phainon’s voice, rich with concern, stirred the stillness, a gentle tug on the threads of Mydei’s consciousness. He glanced over his shoulder, meeting Phainon’s gaze.

Phainon’s expression was unreadable, but there was an undercurrent of worry there—so subtle, so quiet, that Mydei could have easily missed it if he wasn’t paying attention. The soft lines around his eyes, the way his posture had softened, the slight tremble in his usually steady hands—all of it spoke of a care that Mydei couldn’t quite fathom, couldn’t truly understand.

Phainon stepped closer, his movements slow and deliberate, as if trying not to disturb something fragile. “Would you like something to eat?” His voice was low, coaxing, as if testing the waters. “Or perhaps… some rest?”

There was no force in his tone—no demand. Just a soft invitation, a suggestion. He wasn’t trying to make Mydei feel anything he didn’t want to, but his words lingered in the air suffocating with a kind of unspoken plea.

For a long moment, Mydei said nothing. He didn’t even really acknowledge the offer, his gaze drifting back to the ruined skyline. He could feel Phainon’s eyes on him, watching him with a kind of intensity that shouldn’t have been so comforting, but somehow was.

Phainon took a step closer, just enough for Mydei to feel the warmth of his proximity. His next words were softer still, almost a whisper.

“I care about you, Mydei.” There was a pause, the weight of those words settling between them, unspoken yet understood. “Please… take care of yourself. At least for my sake.”

The way Phainon said it was… different. There was nothing like the cautious or poisonous conversations that had become their norm, nothing like the manipulation or the power games. This was something else. It was care—pure, genuine care—something Mydei hadn’t realized he needed until that very moment.

Mydei’s chest tightened, a dull ache blooming in the pit of his stomach. He tried to shove it down, to ignore it, but it wouldn’t go away. Phainon’s presence, his concern, was a kind of lifeline Mydei hadn’t known he was clinging to. And it terrified him.

He pulled in a breath, his throat dry. “I’m fine,” he said, his voice hoarse. It was a lie—he knew it. Phainon knew it too, but neither of them called it out.

Phainon didn’t respond at first. Instead, he just stood there, letting the silence stretch between them like a taut wire. The kind of silence that spoke louder than words ever could. Then, quietly, almost tenderly, Phainon placed a hand on Mydei’s shoulder. Not to command, but to offer something —comfort, support, maybe just the feeling that Mydei wasn’t alone in the dark.

“I don’t think you are,” Phainon said softly. His voice wasn’t accusing, wasn’t pushing—it was simply the truth. “But that’s alright. You don’t have to be. Not with me.”

Mydei swallowed hard. It was impossible to ignore how close Phainon was, how his warmth seeped through the thin fabric of clothes the other was wearing. He could feel the faint thrum of life in Phainon’s touch, steady and sure, something Mydei had forgotten how to be.

There was a long pause.

“I…” Mydei started, but the words caught in his throat. What could he say? How could he explain this… this strange vulnerability that Phainon had awakened in him without even trying?

“I’m not… ready,” he managed to say finally, his voice barely above a whisper.

Phainon’s eyes softened, the hint of a smile tugging at his lips, though it was laced with a sadness Mydei didn’t fully understand. He squeezed Mydei’s shoulder once, then let his hand fall away.

“That’s alright,” Phainon said, his voice still gentle, his tone unwavering. “Take your time. I’ll be here when you’re ready.”

Mydei didn’t know why, but the words stirred something in him. Something warm, something that made his chest tighten all over again. He wanted to pull away, to retreat back into the fortress he had built around himself. But instead, for just a moment, he stayed.

“Thanks,” Mydei muttered, more to himself than to Phainon.

Phainon’s gaze softened even more. “You don’t have to thank me.” He paused, then added, with a rare tenderness that sent a shiver down Mydei’s spine: “Mydei. Let me help.”

The words hung in the air, a silent promise, one Mydei wasn’t sure he was ready to accept but somehow couldn’t reject. Not now.

Time was something that slipped through Mydei’s fingers, no matter how hard he tried to hold onto it. The city—Okhema—still stood, but there was a palpable tension in the air, a constant shiver of instability beneath the surface. Phainon and the Elders had managed to keep the worst of it at bay, holding the city together, but Mydei knew better than to trust the calm. It felt like a breath held too long, waiting for a snap.

Some days, he would wake up, his body heavy with the weight of unspoken exhaustion, as though he hadn’t slept at all. He could feel the silence

pressing in from all sides, filling the empty spaces with echoes of things he’d long since forgotten how to name.

His breath was slow. Deep. But in the silence that followed, all he could hear was the faint hum of his heartbeat—steady, always. Unyielding. It was the only thing that wouldn’t let him go.

It wasn’t the first time he’d felt the overwhelming need to break the silence, to feel something sharp and real, to take a moment where he could focus on the sting of it, the way it would remind him that he was still here.

It wasn’t the first time he’d wondered if he should do it. But his skin—his cursed, eternal skin—wouldn’t let him. The immortal curse that kept him bound, bound to a world that felt too heavy and a heart that felt too cold. Nothing could end it.

Not even a knife.

The Elders and Phainon tried their best to keep him stable. They talked to him, sometimes. They tried to make him feel human again, though it was like trying to patch a cracked vase with tape. He squeezed his eyes shut, trying to shut it all out.

Focus. Focus on something else.

His heart thudded faster, an erratic pulse racing beneath his ribs. He could feel his pulse in his throat, the familiar ache of frustration building in his chest, pushing him toward the same restless place he’d been circling for weeks. For months.

It wasn’t real. It couldn’t be. There was no place for that kind of behavior in his life anymore. Not after everything that had happened.

The words still lingered, curling into his thoughts like smoke.

“Don’t leave.”

A sharp exhale hissed from his teeth as he shoved them aside. Not now. Not like this.

He ran his fingers through his hair, pulling at it almost violently, as though the act of doing so might purge him of the thoughts, of the soft, careful way Phainon spoke to him, as if Mydei still deserved kindness. He had to force it out, pushing the feeling away with every ounce of will he had left.

He didn’t need it. He didn’t want it. Not from him. Not anymore.

Blood spattered across his gauntlets, the warmth seeping into his skin as the body beneath his hands went still. He barely registered the gurgled final breath of the last enemy before he wrenched his gauntlets free, a sharp twist of his wrist ensuring the damage was irreparable. Another one down. The walk back was quiet—at least for a while. Mydei strode ahead, his pace unrelenting, his mind already locking itself back into the cold void he’d grown accustomed to.

“Mydei,” Phainon called from behind him, his tone firm but edged with something else. Concern.

He ignored him.

“Mydei,” Phainon said again, quickening his pace to catch up. “Stop. Talk to me.”

He heard the faint shift of movement before Phainon’s voice rose, not in anger, but in frustration.

“You think you can order me around?” Mydei’s voice was low, sharp, each word dripping with venom. “You think I owe you an explanation?”

He leaned in closer, his grip tightening ever so slightly.

Phainon’s lips parted slightly, his breath coming faster—but it wasn’t fear. It wasn’t even defiance.

It was something else entirely.

A kiss.

Not to his lips, but to his cheek.

Soft. Simple. Deliberate.

It sent a shock through his entire body, his grip on Phainon’s collar going slack, hesitatingly raising his arm to Phainon’s cheek.

His first instinct was to push away, to hit him, to snarl and snap and take back control of whatever this was, but—

He couldn’t.

His body refused to move, frozen in place as the warmth of Phainon’s lips lingered on his skin. His pulse roared in his ears, and for once, he was silent.

Phainon had known. Known he wasn’t ready, known anything more would have been too much, too close, and yet—

The realization struck hard and fast, and suddenly, Mydei couldn’t stand to be here anymore.

He released Phainon as if burned, taking a staggering step back. His breath came sharp and uneven, his hands clenched into fists at his sides.

Then, without another word, he turned on his heel and walked away.

Phainon didn’t stop him this time. But Mydei could hear his quiet footsteps trailing behind.

The walk back was silent. Phainon hadn’t said a word since that, and Mydei was fine with that. He needed the silence, needed to shove what happened deep into the recesses of his mind before it had a chance to sink its claws into him.

But something was off.

At first, he thought it was his own unease, but the more he focused, the clearer it became.

Phainon’s stride. It was slightly off-rhythm. A fraction slower. He still carried himself with that same languid ease, but there was a stiffness to his movements, a deliberate effort to conceal something.

He was hurt.

Mydei didn’t acknowledge it. He didn’t so much as look at Phainon. But he noted it, filed it away, and adjusted his pace accordingly.

And then—

A flicker of movement.

Subtle. Just beyond the broken remains of a nearby pillar.

He didn’t react. Didn’t let on that he’d noticed.

He only waited.

Phainon took another step, and the instant his foot hit the ground—

A figure lunged from the shadows.

A man. Human. A Follower of Strife.

It was rare to see humans among the god-tainted zealots, but Mydei didn’t waste time wondering why he was here. It didn’t matter.

What mattered was the blade in the man’s hand, the way it arced through the air, aimed straight for Phainon’s exposed side.

Phainon was fast. But Mydei was faster.

He moved in a blur, barely registering the snarl on the man’s face before he slammed into him, driving him back before the knife could connect. They hit the ground hard, dust and dirt scattering as Mydei straddled him, pinning him beneath his weight.

The man choked, but he wasn’t given time to struggle.

Mydei’s gauntleted hand came down swift and merciless, plunging straight into his chest.

Bone cracked. Flesh tore.

The man gasped, eyes going wide in disbelief as Mydei twisted the gauntlet deeper, making sure the damage was irreversible.

A human. He could feel the fragility of it—the way the body beneath him trembled, so easily breakable, so unlike the divine beings they usually fought.

He leaned in, voice quiet, emotionless.

“You should’ve run.”

The man shuddered. Then he stilled.

When Mydei pulled his hand free, the body slumped lifelessly beneath him.

Phainon was watching.

He hadn’t moved. Hadn’t said a word.

He only stood there, one hand pressed loosely to his side, fingers curling and uncurling as if weighing whether or not to acknowledge his own injury. His eyes flickered from the corpse at Mydei’s feet to the crimson staining his gauntlets, then to Mydei himself.

Something unreadable passed across his face.

Mydei scowled. “You’re lagging behind.”

Phainon blinked. Then—slowly, deliberately—he smiled.

“I see that,” he murmured.

A muscle in Mydei’s jaw tightened. “Then keep up.”

And yet, as they walked, it was Mydei who stayed a step behind, his eyes locked onto Phainon’s every movement.

Watching.

Guarding.

Ensuring no one dared try again.

Even if Phainon never said a word about it, even if he pretended he didn’t notice—

Mydei knew.

And he would make damn sure no one laid a hand on Phainon while he was still breathing.

He had expected something.

Anger. Rage. A curse spat through gritted teeth, a threat sharp enough to cut.

But not this.

Phainon lifted a hand to his cheek, fingers ghosting over the spot where Mydei’s hand had been just moments before. Not in violence. Not in fury. But in something hesitant, something trembling and fleeting before Mydei had ripped himself away, as if the moment itself had burned him.

And then he had fled.

Not out of hatred. Not out of disgust.

But because for the first time, Mydei had been confronted with something he couldn’t fight.

Phainon exhaled, slow and measured, though his pulse betrayed him.

Gods.

Gods.

He hadn’t been prepared for this. Hadn’t expected the heat curling in his gut, the sharp coil of want twisting tight, pulling, dragging him deeper into something he couldn’t name.

Not just desire. Not just amusement.

Something more. Something much more.

His lips parted, his breath uneven as he let the realization settle, let it take.

He wanted him.

Not just the Mydei who tore through enemies without hesitation, who painted the world in blood and ruin without blinking.

No—he wanted this Mydei. The one who flinched at kindness. The one who had no idea what to do when faced with something he couldn’t cut down.

The one who had unknowingly let Phainon in, just for a moment, before retreating in a way that had left Phainon aching for more.

His fingers curled, nails biting into his palm.

He would have him.

One way or another.

The walk back to Okhema felt longer than it should have.

Mydei kept his pace quick, his feet moving in almost mechanical precision, his thoughts scattered. The streets felt different now, colder, like the city itself had become more fragile. But that was something he couldn’t think about—not when his mind kept drifting back to that moment. The kiss.

The heat of it still lingered on his cheek, even though he’d tried to shake it off. The way Phainon’s lips had barely grazed his skin, like it was the most tender thing he’d ever done.

Why did it make his heart skip?

He didn’t want to care. Didn’t want to feel anything for Phainon—certainly not this. He was already too damaged, too broken. He couldn’t afford to let someone else in.

When he glanced over his shoulder, Phainon was walking a few steps behind him, his posture stiff. His eyes weren’t on the ground, but not quite

meeting Mydei’s either. It was a strange kind of silence between them now —uncomfortable, but gentle.

The door closed behind him, and he finally let out the breath he had been holding, the silence wrapping around him like a shroud.
