The heat from the water seeped into Mydei’s bones, but it was the warmth of Phainon’s body against his that made him feel more alive, more real than he’d felt in a long time. He wasn’t sure what had changed or why it felt different this time, but something in him shifted.

His voice, when it came, was low, as though he were speaking to himself more than to Phainon. “I never thought I’d have something… like this.”

Phainon didn’t say anything at first, just squeezed his hand. Mydei felt the weight of it, but it wasn’t a burden. It was steady, certain, and for once, it felt like there was someone who wasn’t going to let go.

Mydei’s gaze lifted, meeting Phainon’s eyes for the first time in what felt like forever. There was something in those eyes, something open, and for a moment, the world beyond them didn’t exist.

He could feel his heart beat a little faster, a little more uneven. For the first time in ages, it wasn’t because of fear, but because of something else. Something he can now name as affection.

Phainon leaned in, his lips brushing against Mydei’s temple, and Mydei didn’t pull away. He stayed there, the quiet of the room pressing in around them as if this moment were a breath, something to hold onto. Phainon’s hand shifted, trailing down to Mydei’s side, fingertips skimming over his skin in a way that made Mydei’s breath catch.

Phainon’s voice was soft but firm, his lips brushing Mydei’s ear. “I’ll stay with you.”

The words weren’t anything new, but they were different when Phainon said them. There was no promise of forever, no heavy meaning behind them. Just the truth, plain and simple.

Mydei closed his eyes, feeling the tension in his chest loosen, even if only for a moment. He leaned back slightly, resting his head on Phainon’s shoulder, his eyes still closed as the heat of the water and Phainon’s touch grounded him.

Phainon kissed the top of his head, his hand settling against Mydei’s back, pulling him in closer. It was familiar now, the way they fit together. There were no words, no grand declarations. Just the space they shared, the quiet understanding between them.

For once, Mydei felt like he didn’t have to fight. There was someone here who wasn’t going to leave him, even if everything else fell apart. And that was all it took.

-

Phainon watched Mydei, his body leaning slightly against him in the warm water, eyes half-closed in contentment. The quiet rhythm of his breathing filled the space between them, steady, predictable.

His fingers lightly traced the line of Mydei’s arm, then down to the curve of his ribs, still lingering where the steady pulse of his heart beat beneath the skin. The intimacy of the moment wasn’t lost on Phainon, but there was something else, something that tugged at the edges of his thoughts.

This… was almost too easy.

He could feel the way Mydei trusted him, the way his body relaxed under his touch, all the pieces falling into place without much effort on his part. There was no struggle, no hesitation. Just Mydei, so willing to give it all. The truth of it settled in his chest like a familiar, comfortable thing.

It wasn’t that he minded. No, far from it. But it was so simple, so easily achieved, that for a fleeting moment, Phainon wondered how much more he could pull from this.

But not now. Not yet.

He leaned back, letting the heat of the bath and the closeness of Mydei settle over him. A slight smile tugged at his lips, but it wasn’t for Mydei’s eyes. This was his to have for now and for as long as he wanted.

And Phainon wasn’t in a rush to make it anything else.

Chapter Notes

I am finishing this motherfucker before 3.1 whether anyone likes it or not, I have cried blood, sweat and tears while writing this trying to meet my quota of words but fuck if I don’t finish this by morning….

Mydei floated in a tranquil expanse, a dream state that felt light, almost ethereal. There was no pressure, no expectations—just the gentle sensation of being untethered. The world around him was a soft blend of colors, muted and warm, like a fading sunset. He felt at peace, embraced by the silence that enveloped him.

But as time drifted, that serenity began to warp. Shapes flickered at the edges of his vision, shadows twisting in the periphery. The warmth faded, replaced by a creeping chill that gnawed at his skin. The soft hues morphed into stark greys, an oppressive weight pressing down on his senses.

Suddenly, he stood in a graveyard, the air thick with an unshakable sense of foreboding. Tombstones jutted from the earth like jagged teeth, their inscriptions fading into obscurity. Mydei’s heart raced, not from fear but from an inexplicable understanding that something was very wrong. The stillness morphed into something uncanny, as if the world held its breath.

Then, faces emerged from the shadows, their expressions frozen in anguish, a collective sorrow that filled the air like a dense fog. Mydei stumbled back, confusion twisting in his gut. He turned, searching for escape, only to find that he was not alone. The graveyard pulsed with an unearthly energy, a sense of anticipation that made his skin crawl. And then, something eldritch, grotesque, began to materialize in the distance—a silhouette shifting against the backdrop of a waning moon.

His heart dropped as the figure loomed closer, its presence suffocating, an ancient hunger emanating from its very being. Just as abruptly, he was

thrust back into a different dream.

Now, he wandered the familiar streets of Okhema. Yet something was off— an unnatural silence gripped the city, and vibrant colors faded to muted tones, as if life itself had been drained. The buildings loomed overhead, their shadows elongated, but no one looked at him. Heads were bowed, bodies moving like puppets on strings, each step a mechanical dance devoid of emotion.

An unsettling chill wrapped around him as he walked. The streets, once bustling with life, now felt hollow. A growing sense of dread seeped into his bones, a realization that this dream was a reflection of something deeper, a cycle he couldn’t escape.

He approached an unmarked grave, its surface unremarkable against the backdrop of despair. But as he leaned closer, recognition struck him like a bolt of lightning. It was Aglaea’s grave, a cruel mockery of their fleeting connection.

Without warning, the faceless figures around him turned, their necks snapping in a synchronized motion, a grotesque display that sent ice through his veins. They bore no features, only an emptiness that echoed the hollow ache in his chest.

Mydei staggered back, fear rooting him in place as the reality of his situation washed over him. This was more than a dream; it was a haunting, a reminder of everything he had lost and everything that was yet to come. He could feel their vacant gazes piercing into him, a judgment as cold as the grave.

As he stood there, the air thickening with palpable dread, the world began to dissolve around him. The faces faded into darkness, and he felt his heart drop, as if severed from him completely. Everything vanished into nothingness, leaving him stranded in an unsettling void.

Mydei jolted awake, the remnants of the dream lingering like shadows at the edge of his consciousness. The familiar surroundings of his room came into focus, but they felt eerily distant, as if he were viewing them through a

glass pane. He lay still for a moment, holding his breath, the quiet pressing down around him like a heavy shroud.

Nothing surprised him anymore—no more shock at the surreal visions that haunted his nights. But today felt different. The air charged with a sense of foreboding, as if the very fabric of reality trembled in anticipation. Shifting slightly, he felt an unsettling twist in his chest, as if the dream had carved something new within him.

Sitting up, he raked a hand through his hair, a deep breath escaping him as he dissected the dream with a detached calm. The graveyard, the faceless figures, the eldritch presence—each element had its place in the mosaic of his mind, each a piece of a puzzle that hinted at something darker lurking beneath the surface of his reality.

The echoes of despair resonated within him. The dream had bared its teeth, and he couldn’t shake the sensation that it meant something profound—a warning wrapped in metaphor. Aglaea’s grave—why her? Did it signify a loss he hadn’t fully processed? Or was it a reminder of the life he once clung to, now slipping through his fingers?

Mydei stood, movements deliberate and almost methodical, as he paced the room. The walls felt as if they were closing in, the memories of those faceless figures pressing against his mind like a haunting melody. What did it mean to dream of an empty city, devoid of life? The absence of color mirrored his own fading hopes, a reflection of a world drained of vibrancy.

An itch of dread crawled up his spine as he recalled the eldritch figure that loomed at the edge of the graveyard. Its presence had been suffocating, an entity thriving in shadows, whispering of untold horrors. Was it a manifestation of his own fears? Or something more, a specter of fate that threatened to engulf him?

Every dream had come with a lesson, and he couldn’t ignore the chill gripping his heart. This was a warning, a sign that the fabric of his reality was fraying, that he was teetering on the edge of something monstrous.

He glanced out the window, early morning light filtering through the grime, illuminating the world outside. The streets of Okhema seemed deceptively calm, yet he felt an underlying tension, as if the city itself held its breath, waiting for something to unfold.

Mydei stepped back, leaning against the wall, his heart racing in sync with the pounding of dread in his chest. Something was coming—he could feel it in the marrow of his bones. The dream had stripped him bare, exposing his vulnerabilities, and he was left grappling with a chilling realization: the boundaries between his dreams and reality were blurring, and whatever had emerged from the depths of his mind would not be easily contained.

The weight of the dream lingered, but Mydei refused to let it unnerve him. Instead, he took a slow breath, grounding himself in the present. The edges of fear sharpened into something else—clarity.

These dreams weren’t just dreams. He had long since stopped doubting that. They meant something, left breadcrumbs, clues buried beneath layers of cryptic imagery. And this one… this one had been louder than the rest.

His fingers twitched at his side. The city drained of color. The faceless figures. The grave. And that thing that had watched him, that had felt real. It wasn’t just another nightmare. It was a message.

And messages could be deciphered.

He moved without hesitation now, dressing quickly, strapping on his shoes. The usual morning haze, the slow lull between sleep and waking, didn’t touch him today. There was no time for it. His mind was already working through the pieces.

Aglaea. Why had it been her grave? Was it a metaphor? A warning? He hadn’t thought about her in a long time—had forced himself not to. What was his mind trying to tell him now?

He left his room, steps steady, gaze sharp. The city outside stretched before him, bathed in early morning light, but something about it felt different today. He had seen it empty in his dream, its people silent, avoiding him.

Now, as he walked, he studied every passerby with scrutiny. Did they look at him differently? Did they know something he didn’t?

No, that was paranoia. He exhaled, pushing it down.

First, he needed information. He couldn’t afford to chase vague impressions. There were people who kept records—of deaths, of burials, of disappearances. Aglaea’s grave existed, marked somewhere.

And if it wasn’t?

Then that meant something too.

Either way, he was going to find out.

-

Mydei stepped into the cool morning air, the remnants of his dream clinging to him like a heavy fog. Today felt different—a restless compulsion pulled him toward Aglaea’s grave, a place where memories mingled with shadows of regret. He navigated the familiar streets of Okhema, each step a deliberate act to push past the echoes of his night terrors.

As he rounded a corner, he collided with a force that felt like sunlight cutting through the gloom. Phainon stood before him, effortlessly charming, an easy smile dancing on his lips. It had been two weeks since they had crossed that unspoken threshold, and Mydei’s heart twisted at the sight of him—comforting yet laced with an undercurrent of danger.

“Going somewhere?” Phainon asked, his voice teasing, a glint of mischief in his eyes.

Mydei raised an eyebrow, irritation flaring at the interruption. “Yeah, actually. I have things to do.” The words came out sharper than intended, but he couldn’t shake the feeling that the graveyard loomed in his mind. Confessing that felt like a betrayal.

“Things can wait.” Phainon stepped closer, his presence a tantalizing distraction. “You should take a break from all that brooding. The sun is

shining, and the city is alive. Why not enjoy it?”

“I said I have things to do.” Mydei’s voice was firmer, though he felt the warmth of Phainon’s presence tug at him. “This isn’t some idle stroll.”

Phainon brushed his fingers along Mydei’s forearm, a gesture that sent a jolt of awareness coursing through him. “What’s more important than sharing a moment with me?”

Mydei fought against the instinct to lean into the touch, aware of the precarious line he was treading. “I need to find something out,” he finally admitted, the words slipping out as if confessing a secret.

“Something?” Phainon feigned confusion, his eyes sparkling with playfulness. “What’s so pressing that it can’t wait for a stroll? The city isn’t going anywhere.” He gestured toward the vibrant life around them. “Come on, let’s walk. Just for a little while.”

Mydei felt his heart race, the tug of Phainon’s charm hard to resist. “Fine,” he relented, though he held onto his irritation like a shield. “Just for a moment.”

They walked side by side, the city buzzing with life, but Mydei’s thoughts remained anchored in the shadow of Aglaea’s grave. The ache in his chest tightened, memories tugging at him like persistent ghosts.

“You seem distant,” Phainon remarked, glancing sideways with a mix of curiosity and concern. “What’s on your mind?”

“Nothing.” Mydei’s tone was clipped, the warmth of Phainon’s attention feeling both invasive and comforting. “I’m just…thinking.”

“Thinking can be dangerous,” Phainon replied, teasing yet tinged with something deeper. “It’s far more enjoyable to simply be.” He leaned in closer, brushing against Mydei, their shoulders almost touching, igniting a tension he couldn’t ignore.

Mydei fought against the urge to pull away, the gentle pressure of Phainon’s body language urging him to stay. “Look, I’m not in the mood for distractions,” he said, trying to keep his tone steady, though he could feel the walls around his heart crack slightly.

“Come on, Mydei,” Phainon said softly, his voice a low invitation. “Let me show you something. Let’s forget about all the heavy thoughts for a moment.”

Mydei swallowed hard, the temptation clashing with the remnants of his irritation. “I don’t know…” he started, his resolve weakening.

“Trust me.” Phainon’s eyes locked onto his, earnest and captivating. “Just breathe. I promise I won’t let you fall.”

In that moment, Mydei felt ensnared, the tension in his chest unwinding slightly. He took a deep breath, surrendering to the moment, letting the warmth of Phainon’s presence envelop him. The journey to Aglaea’s grave faded into the background, obscured by the intimacy of their connection. The shadow loomed still, but it felt distant now, almost bearable.

For now, in this stolen moment, he chose to indulge in distraction, letting the weight of his worries slip away, if only for a while.

Phainon led him through the winding streets of Okhema with a casual ease, his hands tucked loosely behind his back, as if he had all the time in the world. Mydei followed, tense despite himself, scanning the city as they moved. The dream still clung to him like a damp fog, its weight pressing against his ribs. The faceless figures, the empty streets, Aglaea’s grave—all of it lingered in his mind, making every shadow feel sharper, every quiet moment too loud.

They passed through a market street, the air thick with the scent of spiced meats and the bite of citrus. The city was alive, buzzing with movement, vendors shouting their wares, coins clinking in fast exchanges. It was the kind of scene Mydei had walked through countless times, but today it felt… off. He couldn’t put his finger on it—just a feeling, an itch beneath his skin, as if the world around him wasn’t sitting quite right.

Phainon, however, seemed unbothered. If anything, he was reveling in the moment, smiling at passing merchants, plucking a dried fig from a vendor’s stall without hesitation. He tossed it to Mydei, who caught it on reflex, staring at the wrinkled fruit in his palm as if it might dissolve into ash.

“You’re brooding again,” Phainon remarked, biting into his own piece, voice laced with amusement. “I can practically see the storm cloud hanging over your head.”

“I’m thinking,” Mydei corrected, his tone clipped.

Phainon exhaled an exaggerated sigh. “Yes, and as I’ve said before, thinking too much is bad for your health.” He nudged Mydei’s shoulder, his touch brief, barely there, but enough to send a jolt through him. “Come on. I’m taking you somewhere.”

“I don’t need—”

“I wasn’t asking,” Phainon interrupted, his grin widening as he grabbed Mydei’s wrist and tugged him forward.

Mydei let out a quiet growl of irritation but didn’t pull away. He could have, easily. Phainon’s grip was firm but not unbreakable. Yet Mydei let himself be led, if only because arguing further felt like more effort than it was worth.

They weaved through the market and slipped into a quieter part of the city, where the stone streets grew narrower and the sounds of trade faded into the distance. Mydei’s shoulders remained stiff, his unease deepening with every step. The city wasn’t supposed to feel like this. He’d walked these streets before, and yet today, they felt unfamiliar in a way he couldn’t articulate.

Phainon finally stopped in front of a small terrace overlooking the city. A stone ledge framed the view, and beyond it, the rooftops of Okhema stretched into the horizon, bathed in warm, golden light. The sky above was a soft gradient of deepening blue, the first hints of evening creeping in.

Phainon leaned against the ledge, stretching his arms out as if embracing the air itself. “See? Peace. No nightmares here, just a city that’s too busy to care about whatever storm is brewing in your head.”

Mydei hovered near the edge, arms crossed tightly over his chest. He hated how easily Phainon peeled away his defenses, how effortlessly he pulled him into his rhythm. He shouldn’t be here, indulging in distractions when his dream still gnawed at him. And yet, as he took in the view, something inside him loosened, just a fraction.

But the itch beneath his skin remained.

The city below was alive, vibrant, and yet—wrong. His eyes flicked across the streets, searching, scanning. The way the people moved, the rhythm of it —it wasn’t… natural. It was too orderly. Too precise. As if they were all following some unseen pattern.

Phainon tilted his head, watching him with a knowing look. “You’re still doing it.”

“There’s something off,” Mydei muttered. “Can’t you feel it?”

Phainon hummed as if considering. “Or maybe you’re just looking for something to be wrong.”

Mydei’s jaw tightened. “That dream wasn’t just a dream.”

Phainon sighed, his teasing edge softening—just a little. “Maybe not. But you’re here, now.” He reached out, fingers grazing Mydei’s wrist again, grounding him. “Can’t you be here, just for a moment?”

Mydei exhaled sharply, looking away, unwilling to meet the warmth in Phainon’s gaze. The city stretched before him, pulsing with life, but that nagging sense of unease wouldn’t let him go.

Still, he didn’t move.

Phainon was patient. He always was, in his own way.

And Mydei, despite everything, despite the wrongness pressing at the edges of his senses—

He stayed.

Mydei leaned against the railing, his posture languid, arms crossed as he gazed down at the city. The tension in his shoulders had loosened, just slightly, though he wouldn’t admit it out loud. Beside him, Phainon shifted closer, not enough to touch but enough to be felt—a steady, warm presence.

“You’re quiet,” Phainon mused, his voice soft, lacking its usual teasing lilt. “That’s rare.”

Mydei scoffed but didn’t look at him. “You say that like I’m always running my mouth.”

Phainon hummed, tilting his head. “Not always. Just when you’re irritated.” He nudged him lightly with his shoulder. “And when you’re trying not to care about something.”

Mydei didn’t flinch away this time. He stayed still, watching as the wind carried the faint sounds of the city up to them. “And you’re always this insistent?”

“Only when it’s important.” Phainon’s voice was quieter now, sincere, slipping beneath Mydei’s skin. “I can tell something’s weighing on you.”

Mydei pressed his lips into a thin line. He could feel Phainon’s eyes on him, searching, waiting. It made something in his chest twist—something unfamiliar, like a thread being tugged loose. He wasn’t used to this, to someone seeing through him so easily.

“I had a dream,” he admitted, the words escaping before he could stop them. He sighed, rubbing a hand over his face. “It doesn’t matter.”

Phainon didn’t push. He didn’t demand details or tease him for it. Instead, he leaned forward against the railing, mirroring Mydei’s posture, his voice light but careful. “Sometimes dreams tell us things we don’t want to hear.”

Mydei turned his head slightly, just enough to catch the soft expression on Phainon’s face. It wasn’t pity—he wouldn’t have tolerated that. It was understanding. A quiet patience.

“Yeah,” Mydei murmured, looking away again. “I know.”

They stood there for a long moment, the silence between them comfortable, stretching out like something fragile but steady. Mydei didn’t realize how close they’d become until the warmth of Phainon’s arm brushed against his own.

He could have moved. Should have, maybe. But he didn’t.

Instead, he let himself stay there, eyes tracing the city below, his heart beating a little too loud in his ears.

Mydei lingered where Phainon had led him, resting an arm against the railing as he gazed out over the city. His posture was deceptively relaxed, his expression unreadable, but the weight of the morning—of the dream— still pressed against his thoughts. He didn’t want to talk about it. Especially not with Phainon, whose presence always made him feel too exposed, too seen.

Phainon, of course, wasn’t one to let things be. “You’re still so quiet, Mydei,” he mused, watching him. “That’s not like you.”

“I don’t feel like talking,” Mydei said flatly, they’d already gone through this, why’s he repeating his words?

Phainon hummed in amusement, undeterred. “Since when?”

Mydei shot him a sharp glance. “Since now.”

But Phainon didn’t step away. If anything, he drifted closer, his movements unhurried, deliberate. “You were heading somewhere before I stopped you,” he noted. “Something important?”

“Not particularly.” Mydei’s reply was smooth, but Phainon caught the slight tension in his jaw, the way his fingers curled subtly against the railing.

“Liar.”

Mydei exhaled through his nose, irritated but not surprised. He turned his gaze back to the horizon, willing the conversation to end there.

It didn’t.

Phainon took another step, closing the space between them, and Mydei— without thinking—edged back slightly. A mistake. The cool metal of the railing pressed against his lower back, and before he could adjust, Phainon braced his arms on either side of him, palms resting lightly against the railings. Not pinning him, not quite. But close. Close enough that Mydei became acutely aware of how little distance remained between them.

Phainon smiled, slow and knowing. “You’re acting like you have something to hide.”

“Or maybe I just don’t like being cornered.” Mydei’s voice was sharp, but there was a slight hitch in it, betraying his composure.

Phainon tilted his head, his breath warm against the space between them.

“Cornered?” he echoed, amusement threading through his tone. “You could push past me if you really wanted to.”

Mydei hated that he had a point. He could move—should move—but his body betrayed him, heat creeping up his neck, irritation mixing with something he refused to name. Phainon was too close. His eyes, gold in the morning light, held him in place, as if waiting for something.

Then—

“Mydei!”

The voice shattered the moment like glass. Mydei jerked his head toward the source, heart still hammering in his chest.

Phainon, to his credit, didn’t seem the least bit bothered. He sighed, stepping back as though nothing had happened, leaving Mydei with too

much space and not enough air.

“Well,” Phainon mused, glancing toward the interruption. “Saved just in time, I suppose.”

Mydei scowled, willing the heat in his face to subside. He was going to kill whoever had interrupted—right after he got a grip on himself.

As Mydei turned, he found himself face-to-face with a young Kremnos refugee—one of many who had fled with him after the fall of their homeland. The child’s cheeks were smudged with dust, but their eyes gleamed with unshaken excitement. Clutched tightly in their small hand was a frayed toy, a relic of the life they had left behind.

“Mydei! Mydei!” The child bounced on their heels, breathless. “Come see! I found something!”

He exhaled, irritation flickering at the edges of his composure. Not now. Not when Phainon was standing so close, not when the moment between them had been so precariously balanced. But the child was looking up at him, expectant, too bright-eyed to turn away.

“What is it?” Mydei asked, his voice steady, though the tension had yet to fully leave his body.

“A secret place! You’ll love it!”

Their excitement was infectious, their enthusiasm unwavering. Mydei hesitated, glancing over his shoulder. Phainon still leaned lazily against the railing, arms draped in a way that felt almost deliberately careless. That familiar smirk tugged at his lips—bemused, knowing. Mydei clenched his jaw at the sight of it. Always so damn sure of himself.

A small hand tugged at his sleeve. “Come on!”

He sighed. “Alright, alright,” he relented, straightening. A part of him felt like he was retreating—stepping away from something unspoken. He

wouldn’t acknowledge that. Instead, he focused on the child’s eager steps as they led him away, leaving behind the phantom heat of Phainon’s proximity.

Even as the city’s noise swallowed them, Mydei could still feel him watching.

The child wove through the streets, talking the entire way, their small voice filling the silence Mydei didn’t realize he’d been carrying. Eventually, they ducked into a narrow alley where the walls were worn with age, the murals upon them faded but still bursting with color. Sunlight pooled through the cracks in the stone, illuminating a small patch of wildflowers that had taken root despite everything.

“See?” The child turned to him, beaming. “They’re still growing!”

For a moment, Mydei simply stared. The flowers—delicate yet stubborn— stood defiantly in the light, their colors stark against the worn stone. Something in his chest tightened, not in pain but in something quieter, something he wasn’t sure he knew how to name.

“They’re beautiful,” he murmured, crouching to touch one of the petals.

“Just like you!” the child chirped.

He scoffed, shaking his head as he ruffled their hair. “You’ve got bad eyesight.”

The child laughed, utterly unconcerned, and Mydei let himself be drawn into it. For just a moment, the world felt smaller, simpler. He could almost forget the conversation left unfinished—the proximity of Phainon’s face, the way his arms had boxed him in against the railing. Almost.

But not quite.

-

Phainon remained where Mydei had left him, the last echoes of his presence still lingering in the space between breaths. The air was thinner without him, the city’s hum suddenly distant, as if dulled at the edges.

He tilted his head, exhaling slowly. So close. Mydei had been cornered, pressed back against the railing with nowhere left to go, his sharp tongue faltering for once. Phainon had seen the way his breath hitched, how his resolve wavered beneath the teasing. A single push, and perhaps he would’ve—

But then the child had called out. The moment shattered, slipping through his fingers like sand.

Phainon tapped his fingers against the railing, the motion unhurried, but something darker coiled beneath his skin. It wasn’t jealousy. No, that would be petty. It was something else entirely. Mydei had turned away too easily, his focus shifting like Phainon hadn’t just unraveled a thread of his defenses.

A low chuckle escaped him.

Mydei was still holding onto the illusion of choice. Of distance. But the truth was already settling in around them, slow and inevitable.

Phainon let his gaze drift toward the city, where somewhere beyond the winding streets, Mydei was caught in a fleeting moment of peace. Let him have it. Let him think he had pulled away.

Because in the end, Mydei always found his way back to him.

And soon, he wouldn’t be able to walk away at all.

-

Mydei returned to find Phainon where he’d left him, leaning against the railing with an air of idle amusement, as if he had never once doubted that Mydei would come back.

The sunset had deepened, staining the sky in hues of violet and crimson, casting long, flickering shadows across the city below. Phainon turned his head slightly at Mydei’s approach, his blue eyes gleaming in the fading light.

“You’re good with children,” Phainon mused, his voice light, conversational. But there was something beneath it, something illegible. “It suits you.”

Mydei tensed at the remark, a flicker of irritation rising in his chest. “It’s nothing,” he muttered, brushing past him. “They needed something to hold on to. That’s all.”

Phainon hummed in acknowledgment, pushing off the railing with easy grace. He fell into step beside Mydei as if it were the most natural thing in the world. “That’s what you do, isn’t it?” he said, casting Mydei a sidelong glance. “Give people something to hold on to. Even when you have nothing left for yourself.”

Mydei exhaled sharply, shaking his head. “Spare me the analysis,” he said, but the words lacked their usual bite. The moment with the child had softened something in him, made it harder to summon the same sharp-edged resistance.

Phainon didn’t press, only chuckled, the sound rich and knowing. “Come on. You look like you could use a distraction.”

“I’m fine.”

“Are you?” Phainon tilted his head, considering. Then, without waiting for an answer, he gestured toward the street ahead. “There’s a place not far from here. Good food, quiet atmosphere. Humor me.”

Mydei hesitated. He should say no. He should put distance between them, shake off whatever strange pull Phainon had over him. But he didn’t.

“Fine,” he relented. “Just for a little while.”

Phainon smiled, the kind of smile that felt like a victory, though Mydei couldn’t tell whose.

They walked side by side through the winding streets, the city settling into the lull between dusk and nightfall. Lamps flickered to life, casting warm

glows over the cobbled paths. The tension from before faded, replaced by something easier, something that almost felt normal.

Phainon let the silence linger for a time before speaking again. “You know, you don’t always have to carry everything alone.” His tone was softer now, almost gentle, like he was offering something real.

Mydei scoffed, but it wasn’t harsh. “And what, you’ll carry it for me?”

Phainon’s eyes flickered with something unreadable. “If you let me.”

Mydei looked away, pretending to be more interested in the dimly lit street than the weight of Phainon’s words. He didn’t have a response for that, not one that wouldn’t give too much away.

And Phainon, ever patient, didn’t push. He only smiled to himself as they continued walking, their steps falling in sync, the distance between them growing smaller with every moment.

They reached the quiet eatery Phainon had mentioned, a tucked-away place with lanterns casting soft, flickering light over polished wooden tables. It was quiet, just as promised, the hum of the city muffled by thick walls and heavy curtains. Mydei slid into his seat with the ease of someone who didn’t care for the pretense of decorum, stretching out his legs beneath the table.

Phainon sat across from him, watching with that same unreadable look from before, but something shifted in his posture when Mydei leaned back, settling in like he belonged there. Mydei tilted his head, eyeing Phainon as he picked up a glass of wine from the table between them. The way the dim light glowed against his skin made something stir in Mydei’s chest, but he ignored it in favor of something far more entertaining—the way Phainon’s fingers tightened ever so slightly around the stem of his own glass, his carefully maintained composure beginning to fray.

“Oh?” Mydei murmured, letting the sound roll off his tongue in lazy amusement. He turned the glass in his hand, taking a slow sip before meeting Phainon’s gaze. “Something on your mind?”

Phainon’s blue eyes narrowed slightly, his lips pressing together for a fraction of a second before curving into a smirk. “You tell me,” he countered smoothly, but there was something else now—a slight stiffness in his movements, a tell.

Mydei almost laughed.

Instead, he leaned forward, resting his chin in his palm, watching Phainon with the kind of look that could be mistaken for idle interest, but wasn’t. “You keep staring at me like that,” Mydei said, voice deceptively casual, “and I’ll start thinking you actually like me.” It was an obvious provocation, of course Phainon did, and likewise so did he.

But Phainon still went unnaturally still for half a heartbeat.

Then, he chuckled, shaking his head as he took a sip of his wine, but it wasn’t enough to mask the way his fingers flexed slightly around the glass. “And what if I do?”

“Oh?” Mydei said again, slower this time, watching as Phainon’s breath hitched, so subtle that anyone else wouldn’t have noticed.

It was a fascinating thing, seeing Phainon react to him like this.

So, Mydei pressed.

He leaned in further, resting his forearm on the table, bringing himself just close enough that Phainon had nowhere to look but at him. “Then I suppose I’d have to do something about it.” His voice dropped lower, softer, a brush of velvet over steel. “Wouldn’t I?”

Phainon had always been a master of self-restraint, but Mydei saw the slight parting of his lips, the way his throat moved when he swallowed, the flicker of something almost vulnerable before it was quickly masked.

It was intoxicating.

And Mydei, for once, was the one pushing Phainon’s buttons.

He let the silence stretch just long enough before he sat back again, exhaling as if he’d lost interest—though they both knew better. He picked up his glass, swirling the juice in it idly before taking another slow sip. “You’re quiet all of a sudden,” he mused. “Did I say something to fluster you?”

Phainon recovered fast, but not fast enough. His smirk returned, but the corner of his mouth twitched like he was holding back something more genuine. “Not at all,” he lied.

“Hmm.” Mydei pretended to believe him.

And then, just as he was about to lean in again, to push just a little more, the door to the restaurant creaked open. A waiter was asking for their order, breaking whatever had been thrumming between them.

Phainon exhaled through his nose, quiet, controlled, but Mydei didn’t miss the way his shoulders relaxed ever so slightly.

Well, Mydei thought, amused. This was going to be fun.

The waiter’s departure left a quiet stillness between them, the space charged yet unspoken. Mydei watched as Phainon lifted his glass again, his movements smooth, practiced—but there was a shift, barely perceptible. A touch more controlled, as if steadying himself.

Mydei let the silence breathe, idly turning his own glass between his fingers, watching how the candlelight caught in the wine, deep and rich, much like the way the lamplight flickered in Phainon’s eyes.

“You looked relieved just now,” he remarked, tilting his head slightly.

Phainon glanced up, looking at Mydei faintly. “Did I?”

Mydei hummed, neither confirming nor denying, only watching the way Phainon held himself a fraction too still. “Did I make you nervous?”

A pause. Just long enough to be telling.

Then Phainon exhaled softly through his nose, setting his glass down with careful precision. “You think quite highly of yourself.”

“You’re avoiding the question.” Mydei rested his chin against his knuckles, gaze unshaken. “Which is interesting.”

Phainon’s lips curved—not quite a smirk, but close. “And if I said no?”

“I might believe you.” Mydei took a slow sip, letting the words settle. “Or I might not.”

Phainon traced the rim of his glass, the motion absent, but Mydei caught the subtle tension in his wrist, the quiet restraint.

“You have a habit,” Phainon mused after a moment.

“Oh?”

“You prod,” he said, as if considering aloud. “Like you’re looking for something. A weak spot, maybe.” He lifted his gaze, meeting Mydei’s over the rim of his glass, blue eyes half-lidded, guarded. “Have you found one?”

Mydei smiled, just faintly. “Would it bother you if I had?”

Phainon’s smirk was measured, deliberate. “Not at all.”

Liar.

But Mydei let it pass, leaning back as the waiter returned with their meals. The interruption was brief, polite, yet by the time they were alone again, something between them had shifted. The conversation carried on, light and unhurried, but beneath it lingered the trace of something unresolved.

Mydei had no intention of settling it. Not yet.

As the evening stretched on, their conversation drifted between idle musings and sharp-edged remarks, circling the unspoken. Mydei played the part well—relaxed, engaged, entirely at ease. He let his amusement flicker

through, a half-smile here, a slow tilt of his head there, watching Phainon with a gaze just a little too steady. Just enough to make him wonder.

Phainon held himself well, as he always did, but Mydei noticed the way he reached for his glass more often, the measured pause before certain responses. How his fingers lingered at the stem just a fraction longer than necessary.

Leaning forward slightly, Mydei let his voice drop, just enough to shift the air between them. “You’ve been watching me all night.”

Phainon didn’t flinch, but his grip on the glass tightened—briefly, barely. “Observing,” he corrected, smoothly.

“Mm.” Mydei tilted his head, as if considering. “And what have you observed?”

Phainon met his gaze, composed, yet something about it felt more carefully placed than before. “That you enjoy pressing my limits.”

Mydei smiled, slow and knowing. “I like seeing what people do when pushed.” He tapped a finger against the rim of his glass, the sound light, almost absent. “You’re interesting.”

Phainon chuckled, low and indulgent. “Flattering.”

“I wasn’t trying to be.” Mydei’s voice remained even, but his gaze flickered lower, just once, just enough. When he looked back up, Phainon was already watching him, blue eyes sharpened, as if weighing something.

Mydei let the silence stretch before leaning back, an easy, effortless shift. “I think I like you like this,” he murmured, almost to himself.

Phainon raised a brow. “Like what?”

Mydei only smiled, finishing his drink with slow deliberation. Then he set his glass down and stood, the movement fluid, unrushed.

“I’ll let you wonder,” he said, voice light, but edged with something that stayed behind.

Then he turned, stepping past Phainon with the faintest brush of movement —just enough to be noticed. He could feel Phainon’s gaze on his back as he walked away, and he didn’t need to look to know he had left him thinking.

As they continued their silent walk together, Phainon moved to stand, adjusting his sleeve, but before he could step away, Mydei followed suit, cutting off his path with an almost absent motion. Close, but not imposing. Just there.

Phainon glanced at him questioningly. “Something else on your mind?”

Mydei hummed, as if considering, before reaching out—not with force, not with the urgency Phainon might have expected. No, this was different. His fingers barely brushed Phainon’s sleeve, and then—

A kiss.

Not on the lips. Not demanding, not searing, not the kind of thing that burned with all-consuming heat.

Just a press of warmth against his cheek, light, fleeting. A whisper of contact rather than a declaration.

And Phainon—froze.

Every small movement, every unconscious shift of breath, simply stilled. His entire body locked in place as if something in his mind had abruptly short-circuited, leaving him staring straight ahead as Mydei pulled back, stepping away without fanfare, without even looking to see the full aftermath of what he had just done.

“You really are easy to fluster,” Mydei mused, voice light with amusement as he turned on his heel, leaving Phainon standing there, utterly motionless.

And then he was gone.

-

Phainon stood there for longer than he would ever admit.

It wasn’t until the ambient sounds of the street shifted, people moving around him, that he forced himself to start walking, steps measured and even.

But the scene kept replaying.

Again.

And again.

The warmth lingering against his skin, phantom-like. The casual, almost careless ease of it. The words Mydei had left him with, slipping into his mind like a perfectly aimed dagger.

You really are easy to fluster.

His pace quickened.

It wasn’t often that Phainon found himself off balance. Even less often that he was caught so thoroughly off guard.

And yet.

By the time he turned a corner into a quieter street, his steps had grown sharper, more hurried, something rattling in his chest that he couldn’t quite place. Then, with a sharp inhale, he stopped.

A hand came to rest against the nearest wall, steadying himself, his head tipping forward slightly. His other hand, against his own will, rose to his face, covering his cheek as if that would somehow erase the sensation.

The heat had not faded.

He exhaled sharply, his body slouching just slightly against the wall. The kind of posture he never allowed himself.

…Damn

-

The warmth lingered longer than he expected.

Even as Mydei walked away, leaving Phainon behind, he could still feel the faint press of his lips against his cheek—the heat of it, the stunned silence that had followed. It was almost funny how easily he had turned the tables. Almost.

Yet, just as the satisfaction settled in, something else surfaced. A pause, a pull.

His steps slowed.

He had forgotten something.

The thought came unbidden, striking like a thread snapping loose from a tapestry—just subtle enough to be ignored, but persistent enough to gnaw at him. Something important.

Mydei frowned, rubbing his temple as if that might bring clarity. His mind offered nothing. Just an empty space where certainty should have been.

…Had he really been so tired?

A scoff left him as he straightened, shaking the thought away. It was probably nothing. He hadn’t slept well, had barely rested at all. If anything, he was overdue for a real night’s sleep.

Whatever it was—whatever he thought he was forgetting—it couldn’t have mattered that much.

With that, he exhaled and kept walking, letting the warmth return.

-

Weeks passed, and with each mission, Mydei felt a shift within himself. The streets of Okhema thrummed with renewed energy, the once-dim hope flickering to life as they saved more people from the chaos beyond their borders. He found himself venturing out more frequently, every outing a chance to make a difference, to carve through the darkness with a blade of light.

The elders, too, seemed galvanized. Their focus sharpened as they worked tirelessly to ensure Okhema remained a sanctuary. Mydei observed their efforts—the new protections being enacted, the city’s defenses reinforced, and the intricate network built to aid those in need. It was a tangible shift, one that made the air feel lighter, the city alive with possibility.

There was a sense of camaraderie that grew with each successful rescue. Mydei felt the warmth of gratitude in the eyes of those they brought to safety, and it ignited something within him. The fear that had once anchored him began to dissolve, replaced by a burgeoning hope that maybe, just maybe, they could rebuild what had been lost.

As he strolled through the bustling market square one afternoon, the laughter and chatter of the people filled the air, mingling with the aroma of freshly baked bread. Mydei stopped for a moment, taking in the vibrant scene. Children played in the streets, their joy infectious, while vendors called out, peddling their wares with enthusiasm. He couldn’t help but smile.

This was what they were fighting for—a future worth believing in.

And for the first time in a long while, Mydei felt the weight of his past lift, replaced by a glimmering sense of hope for the city and its people.

-

The sun hung high in the sky, casting sharp shadows over the training ground. The scent of sun-warmed earth filled the air, mingling with the distant clamor of the city beyond. Mydei stood opposite Phainon, wooden practice sword in hand, adrenaline humming through his veins. The tension between them crackled like the charged air before a storm.

“Ready to lose again?” Mydei challenged, his voice low, laced with bravado. Usually he’d use his gauntlets, but he decided he’d make an exception this time.

Phainon’s expression was bright, the hint of a smile tugging at his lips. “You’d best focus, Mydei. One victory doesn’t make you unbeatable.”

Before Mydei could fire back, Phainon lunged. Their swords clashed, the impact reverberating up Mydei’s arms. Phainon moved with the fluid grace of a predator, each strike precise, controlled. Mydei parried each blow, the thrill of the challenge surging through him. He met Phainon’s intensity with his own, dodging and weaving, matching the older warrior’s movements with an agile finesse honed through countless hours of training.

“Is that all you’ve got?” Mydei taunted, darting in closer, his breath mingling with Phainon’s for the briefest second as he feinted left and struck right.

Phainon deflected the attack, but Mydei didn’t retreat. He pressed forward, his body brushing against Phainon’s for a fleeting moment before he pivoted and landed a firm hit to his opponent’s shoulder.

Phainon stumbled back, surprise flickering in his piercing blue eyes. “Impressive,” he admitted, rolling his shoulder, but his stance remained confident, unwavering. “Let’s see if you can keep that up.”

Mydei grinned, exhilaration thrumming through him. “You’re getting slower, Phainon.” He shifted his weight, stepping in to deliver a swift kick that sent Phainon off balance. “Or maybe I’m just getting better.”

Phainon recovered swiftly, but the corner of his mouth twitched in reluctant admiration. “Just a lucky shot.”

“Lucky? Please.” Mydei spun, bringing his sword down in a decisive arc. At the last moment, Phainon twisted to block, but Mydei’s footwork was too quick. In a final calculated maneuver, he knocked Phainon’s weapon from his grip.

Silence stretched between them, broken only by the sound of their heavy breathing. Mydei stood over Phainon, victorious, his smirk triumphant.

Phainon exhaled a laugh, warm despite his defeat. “You’ve improved.” He wiped a hand over his face, shaking his head. “I’ll give you that.”

Mydei extended a hand, his fingers brushing against Phainon’s as he helped him to his feet. Their eyes met, and for a moment, the world around them faded.

The bond forged through competition and camaraderie thrummed between them, thick as the summer heat.

“Next time,” Phainon murmured, voice low, steady. “I won’t go easy on you.”

Mydei’s grin widened. “Wouldn’t have it any other way.”

-

The night sky stretched infinitely above them, a vast expanse of darkness punctuated by constellations that shimmered like scattered embers. A gentle breeze whispered through the tall grass, carrying the crisp scent of earth and the lingering traces of rain from earlier that evening. Mydei and Phainon sat on a quiet hillside, far from the remnants of the city, where ruin and memory tangled into one indistinguishable blur. Here, in the hush of the night, there were no echoes of the past, no burdens pressing upon their shoulders—only the steady rhythm of the wind and the weight of unspoken thoughts hanging in the air between them.

Mydei lay back, propped on his elbows, his gaze fixed on the endless stretch of stars. He had always looked up at the sky and wondered what it would feel like to drift among them, weightless, untethered, free. The cool breeze tousled his hair, and for a fleeting moment, he felt lighter, as if the heaviness in his chest had momentarily lifted.

Beside him, Phainon sat cross-legged, his presence a quiet contradiction— both a comfort and a reminder of all the things Mydei could not quite put

into words. The faint silver glow of the moon illuminated his face, casting sharp lines over soft expressions, highlighting the intensity in his gaze even as he looked up at the same stars.

“Do you ever wonder what’s out there?” Phainon mused, his voice breaking the stillness, low and contemplative, as if the question had been resting on his tongue for some time.

Mydei’s tone remained dry. “Only when I’m bored.”

Phainon turned to him then, his expression thoughtful. “Boredom is a luxury,” he murmured, the corners of his mouth twitching slightly, almost amused, but not quite.

Mydei chuckled, the sound rougher than he expected, as though laughter had become something foreign to him. “Is that so?” he asked, shifting his weight onto one elbow as he glanced at Phainon. “I’d say boredom is a necessity when you have nothing else to occupy your mind.”

Phainon tilted his head slightly, considering. Then, with quiet certainty, he replied, “You’re starting to sounding like you have everything figured out.”

“Hardly.” Mydei exhaled, shaking his head as he turned back to the sky. The stars seemed distant, but constant—unchanging in a world where nothing else ever stayed the same. “I’m just trying to find some peace, that’s all.”

For a moment, neither of them spoke. The weight of their past—of choices made and fates entwined—hung thick in the air, unspoken yet ever-present. And yet, despite it all, Mydei allowed himself to shift just slightly, just enough that his shoulder brushed against Phainon’s. A small gesture, a quiet concession.

“Peace isn’t something you find,” Phainon said at last, his voice softer now, reflective. “It’s something you create.”

Mydei scoffed, though there was no real bite to it. “Then I suppose I’m not very good at creating things.”

Phainon’s gaze remained steady, unwavering. “Seems to me you’re doing all right.”

The words unsettled something in Mydei, stirred something long buried beneath layers of cynicism and guarded silence. He wasn’t sure what to do with them, wasn’t sure how to accept them without picking them apart. Instead, he let the silence stretch, let himself sink into the quiet between them, let himself remember what it felt like—this closeness, this warmth, this lingering tether between two people who had fought both against and for each other.

“Do you think things will get better?” The question escaped before Mydei could second-guess himself, slipping into the space between them like a whispered uncertainty.

Phainon’s answer came without hesitation. “Better? Or just different?” He glanced at Mydei, his voice steady. “The world will always change. It’s what you choose to do with that change that matters.”

Mydei let out a short, humorless laugh. “Easy for you to say. You thrive on change. You revel in it.”

“And you survive in its wake,” Phainon countered, eyes glinting with something almost like admiration. “You’ve always had that strength.”

Strength. The word felt heavy, felt like something Mydei wasn’t sure he deserved. The world had taken so much from him, carved him into something unrecognizable, and yet, here he was, beneath the stars, leaning into something he didn’t quite understand but couldn’t bring himself to pull away from.

“You know,” he said at last, his voice effortlessly cool despite the steady beat of his pulse, “I’ve never been one for sharing. The spotlight was never mine to begin with—I never wanted it. The shadows have always been more accommodating.”

Phainon smiled, a slow, knowing thing. “Then maybe it’s time you stepped into the light.”

Mydei arched a brow. “I doubt it would suit me.”

“Funny. I don’t recall you ever lingering on the sidelines.” There was a challenge in Phainon’s gaze now, a flicker of something dangerous and familiar and far too tempting.

And just like that, something in Mydei shifted. The way Phainon looked at him, the way he always looked at him—steady, unyielding, seeing past every wall Mydei had carefully constructed—made something inside him stir.

“Maybe I just need a little push,” Mydei murmured.

Phainon leaned in slightly, their shoulders pressing closer. “What kind of push?”

Mydei turned his head, and suddenly, they were close—so close that he could see the flicker of moonlight in Phainon’s eyes, could feel the warmth of his breath against his skin. The air between them crackled, electric, charged with something neither of them had ever dared to name.

And then Mydei moved, just slightly, just enough.

The kiss was hesitant at first, a tentative press of lips that tasted of uncertainty and quiet longing. But then Phainon responded, deepening it, threading his fingers into Mydei’s hair and pulling him in as if anchoring him there, as if grounding them both in this moment, beneath this sky.

When they finally broke apart, foreheads resting together, breath mingling in the cool night air, Phainon smirked. “Better?”

Mydei exhaled a small, breathy laugh, something real, something new. “Maybe,” he admitted, his voice softer than he meant it to be. “I suppose I’ll have to see.”

And above them, the stars shone on—silent witnesses to a moment neither of them would ever forget.

-

The garden was a sanctuary, a quiet refuge from the chaos that so often shadowed their lives. Mydei and Phainon strolled along the winding paths, surrounded by a lush tapestry of colors and scents, each bloom breathing life into the air. A gentle breeze wove through the leaves, carrying the perfume of roses, lavender, and jasmine, blending into something intoxicatingly serene. The world outside the garden walls felt distant, inconsequential. Here, there was only the soft rustle of petals, the whisper of wind, and the measured rhythm of their steps against the stone path.

Mydei’s gaze drifted over the myriad of blossoms, lingering on a patch of roses in full bloom. Their deep crimson petals gleamed under the waning sunlight, rich and velvety. He plucked one, its stem still adorned with a few sharp thorns, and turned to Phainon with an unreadable expression. With a casual flick of his wrist, he held it out. “Here, take this.”

Phainon arched a brow, his gaze flickering between Mydei and the flower. “You’re not serious, are you?”

“Why wouldn’t I be?” Mydei asked, his tone laced with indifference. “It’s just a rose.”

Phainon hesitated, his fingers twitching slightly. “Right. And you’re not making fun of me?”

Mydei remained deadpan, though a glimmer of amusement lurked in his eyes. “Not at all.”

For a moment, Phainon simply looked at him, as if trying to decipher the deeper meaning beneath Mydei’s words. Then, with an exaggerated sigh, Mydei stepped past him, feigning impatience. “Are you going to stand there all day, or are you going to keep up?”

Phainon exhaled, shaking his head, but before he followed, he reached out and plucked the rose from Mydei’s grasp. Its weight was unexpected, heavier than he anticipated, as if it carried something unspoken. “You’re impossible,” he muttered, watching as Mydei merely shrugged and kept walking.

They wandered deeper into the garden, past beds of violets and lilies, trailing fingers over the cool stone of a low wall. The atmosphere was thick with something unspoken, a tension neither of them dared to name. Phainon examined the rose in his hand, twirling it thoughtfully between his fingers. “Do you think flowers actually mean anything?” he mused after a while. “Like the way people say they do?”

Mydei hummed, considering. “Maybe. But meanings change, depending on the person.” He gestured vaguely to the garden around them. “A rose could mean love or it could mean loss. A daisy could mean innocence or it could mean naivety.” He paused, then shot Phainon a sidelong glance. “Depends on how you take it.”

Phainon felt something twist in his chest at the words. He covered it with a question. “And what am I supposed to take from you handing me a rose, then?”

Mydei’s lips curved into an enigmatic smile. “That’s up to you.”

Phainon huffed a quiet laugh, shaking his head before abruptly kneeling to pluck a small flower with deep purple petals. Without hesitation, he held it out to Mydei. “Then here. Take this.”

Mydei arched a brow as he studied the offering. “What is it?”

“Just a flower,” Phainon said, mirroring Mydei’s earlier words. “What does it matter?”

Mydei took the flower, turning it between his fingers with mild curiosity. Then his expression shifted into something amused. “Ah. This one symbolizes deception.” He lifted his gaze to Phainon, voice lilting with teasing delight. “Interesting choice.”

Phainon faltered. “Deception?”

“Mm.” Mydei twirled the flower lazily. “Didn’t take you for the type to hand me something so dubious.”

Phainon ran a hand through his hair, suddenly regretting his choice. “I… I didn’t know that’s what it meant.”

Mydei let out a short chuckle, the sound light but filled with something unreadable. “It’s fine. I’ll keep it.” With a quiet smirk, he tucked the small flower behind his ear. The deep purple petals stood out starkly against his blonde hair, an ironic crown of falsehoods. “After all, it’s just a flower.”

Phainon let out a slow breath, watching him carefully. Mydei had a way of making everything feel like it carried more weight than it should—every word, every glance, every careless gift. He wasn’t sure what to do with that thought.

They reached a stone fountain, the soft trickle of water filling the space between them. Mydei rested a hand against the cool surface, his fingers tracing patterns on the weathered stone. His expression had turned contemplative, a rare softness etching into his features. Phainon studied him for a long moment before finally breaking the silence. “What’s on your mind?”

Mydei’s response was slow, deliberate. “Nothing. Just… enjoying the moment.”

Phainon nodded, sensing the lie but not calling him on it. Instead, he leaned against the fountain beside him, letting the warm breeze ruffle his hair. The silence stretched, neither awkward nor uncomfortable, just a space in which both could exist without pretense.

After a while, Mydei turned to Phainon, his eyes glinting with something unspoken. “Thanks for the flower, even if it’s a deceptive one.”

Phainon met his gaze, and for a fleeting second, something heavy hung between them, unacknowledged but undeniably present. “You’re welcome,” he replied, voice steady. “Just don’t let it go to your head.”

Mydei chuckled, a low, warm sound that made something in Phainon’s chest tighten. “You should be more worried about yourself, Phainon.”

The laughter that followed was rare and unguarded, mingling with the rustling leaves and the distant chirping of crickets. As the sun dipped below the horizon, casting the garden in hues of gold and violet, Mydei absentmindedly touched the flower still resting behind his ear.

A silent reminder. A lingering question.

In the midst of the blooms, they stood side by side, each lost in thought yet bound together by something unspoken, something neither of them was quite ready to name.
