The night stretched quiet around them, the air tinged with the scent of damp earth and the distant promise of rain. The path they followed was uneven, broken in places by the stubborn roots of old trees, but neither of them seemed to mind. The mission had gone well—better than most. No missteps. No unexpected losses. No bitter weight pressing against their ribs, reminding them of what they could have done differently.

For once, Mydei felt something close to lightness. Not quite peace, not entirely at ease, but as if the weight he carried had lessened, even if only for a moment. His breath came easier. The tension in his shoulders, so familiar it often felt like a part of him, had loosened just enough to be noticeable. He wasn’t sure how long it would last, but he didn’t question it. He simply let himself exist in the moment.

Ahead of him, Phainon walked with an easy, unhurried stride, hands tucked behind his head. His posture was loose, the kind of relaxed that suggested he was either deep in thought or thinking about nothing at all. Eventually, he glanced back.

“You’re quiet,” he noted.

“You say that as if it’s unusual.”

Phainon huffed a soft laugh. “Not unusual. Just different.”

Mydei didn’t answer, but he also didn’t refute the statement. Maybe it was different. Maybe, just for tonight, he didn’t feel the need to fill the silence with sharp edges and distance.

They continued on, the sound of their footsteps blending with the rustling of leaves in the breeze. The city loomed in the distance, its glow muted but constant, a reminder of where they had come from and where they would return.

The path dipped slightly, rough with cracks and hidden hazards. Phainon, ever careless, caught his foot on an exposed root. There was a startled curse, a sharp lurch forward—

Mydei moved before thinking. His hand shot out, gripping Phainon’s wrist in a firm, instinctive hold. He pulled him back upright with practiced ease, steady as ever.

For a moment, neither of them spoke.

Phainon blinked, looking down at Mydei’s hand still wrapped around his wrist. Then up at him, eyes glinting with something unreadable. “Oh? Didn’t take you for the chivalrous type.”

Mydei released him immediately, expression impassive. “I’d rather not have to explain why you cracked your skull open on a walk.”

Phainon grinned, rubbing the back of his head. “Admit it. You’d miss me.”

Mydei was already walking again. “I’d miss the quiet more.”

Phainon let out a low, exaggerated sigh, falling into step beside him once more. “Truly, your heart knows no bounds.”

The banter came easy. Familiar. It was strange, in its own way—how much they had endured together, how often they had fought both side by side and against each other, yet somehow, they had settled into something steady. Not unbreakable, but resilient.

They talked about small things after that. The mission. The city. A few dry remarks from Mydei about Phainon’s questionable self-preservation instincts. It felt… normal, almost. The kind of normal that didn’t need to be picked apart.

Then Phainon, careless as ever, said something he didn’t think twice about.

“Besides, you’re always dreaming about it anyway.”

Mydei stopped walking.

The shift was immediate. Subtle, but absolute.

The lightness he had felt only moments ago vanished, replaced by something sharp, unyielding. The air turned cold, or maybe it was just the way silence suddenly stretched between them, no longer easy or comfortable but heavy, weighted with unspoken things.

Phainon, who had already taken another step forward, noticed too late. He turned back, confusion flickering across his face—then realization.

Mydei’s expression hadn’t changed much. No visible anger. No immediate outburst. But there was a stillness to him now, deliberate and unmoving. The kind of stillness that came before something dangerous.

His voice, when it came, was quiet. Unshaken.

“How do you know that?”

Phainon stilled.

The space between them, once filled with conversation and warmth, stretched wide and unfamiliar.

He didn’t answer right away.

Didn’t joke. Didn’t brush it off with a grin or some deflective remark.

And that, more than anything, set Mydei further on edge.

His gaze was steady, unreadable, but there was something underneath it now. Something simmering.

Phainon exhaled, slow.

He could lie.

Or he could tell the truth.

Either way, the night was no longer quiet.

Phainon didn’t move. Didn’t shift his weight, didn’t look away, didn’t even fidget the way he usually did when faced with something uncomfortable. He simply stood there, watching Mydei with an unreadable expression.

Then, slow as anything, he tilted his head. “What are you talking about?”

The words were easy. Too easy.

Mydei’s fingers curled into a loose fist at his side. “You know exactly what I’m talking about.”

Phainon blinked, brows furrowing just slightly, like someone trying to make sense of a misplaced accusation. “You lost me.”

Something cold settled in Mydei’s chest.

It wasn’t the first time he had seen Phainon lie. It wasn’t even the best lie Phainon had ever told. But it was the way he said it—the way he delivered the words with such casual certainty, as if the problem wasn’t what he had let slip, but rather that Mydei had misunderstood him.

“You mentioned my dream,” Mydei said, voice measured. “How do you know about it?”

Phainon huffed, shaking his head with a bemused smile. “A dream? Mydei, I don’t know what you—”

“Don’t.”

The amusement vanished.

It wasn’t often that Mydei’s tone hardened like that, not with him. Phainon might have laughed if it were anyone else. Might have called him dramatic, teased him for taking things so seriously. But Mydei wasn’t just serious. He was looking at him like he was waiting for something—for a misstep, an admission, an opening.

Phainon let out a soft breath, hands slipping into his pockets. “Alright,” he said. “Say I did mention a dream. What’s the big deal?”

Mydei didn’t answer.

“People talk in their sleep all the time,” Phainon continued. “Maybe I heard something. Maybe you said something and forgot.”

It was a trap of a statement—carefully constructed, delicately placed. A path for Mydei to follow, a way to explain it to himself without forcing Phainon to admit anything. If he latched onto it, if he let himself believe it, then the weight of suspicion would lessen. The uncertainty would linger, sure, but uncertainty was manageable.

But Mydei didn’t take the bait.

“That’s not how I dream.”

Phainon made a thoughtful noise. “You sure?”

Mydei’s jaw tightened. “Yes.”

Phainon held his gaze for a long moment, then sighed, shaking his head like this was some kind of mild inconvenience. “Gods, Mydei, you’re acting like I’ve committed some kind of crime.”

“You’re avoiding the question.”

Phainon’s lips twitched. “Maybe I just don’t like being interrogated over something that doesn’t matter.”

“It matters.”

A pause. A shift.

For the first time since this conversation began, something flickered across Phainon’s face. Something fleeting but sharp, like the glint of a blade catching the light before vanishing back into shadow.

Then it was gone, replaced with that same easy carelessness. “Fine. You’re convinced I know something? Then tell me—what exactly do you think I know?”

And there it was. The final push.

Because if Mydei answered, if he gave Phainon even the smallest thread of speculation, then Phainon could untangle it. Could twist it just enough to make Mydei question himself.

Because doubt, after all, was easier to live with than certainty.

And Phainon was very, very good at making people doubt.

The silence between them thickened, heavy and charged, stretching like an unseen tether Mydei refused to sever. He felt the weight of Phainon’s gaze —steady, unwavering, patient in a way that made his skin prickle. It was the same look Phainon always wore when he was shifting the ground beneath Mydei’s feet, making him question whether he had been standing on solid earth to begin with.

Phainon exhaled softly, a sound almost too light for the tension between them. His expression softened, that usual glimmer in his eyes flickering like a candle in a draft. “You really think I’d just dig around in your mind like that?” he asked, voice warm, almost wounded. “Come on, Mydei. You know me better than that.”

Mydei clenched his jaw. “Then why did you bring it up?” His voice was steadier than he felt. “What do you know about my dreams?”

Phainon tilted his head slightly, as if considering the question with some great care, and then—just like that—he stepped closer. Not enough to be aggressive, not enough to be obvious, but enough that Mydei could feel the faint heat radiating from him, the scent of smoke and something unplaceable curling in the crisp night air.

“You,” Phainon spoke resolutely, like the answer should have been obvious. “You’re the one with the vivid imagination, Mydei. You always have been.” His voice turned almost fond, a note of indulgence threading through it. “I thought you’d appreciate a little mysticism, that’s all. We all have dreams. We all talk about them sometimes.” He gave a half-shrug. “It’s not a big deal.”

A slow, creeping pressure settled over Mydei’s chest.

Not a big deal.

The words pressed against the inside of his skull, chafing, irritating. That was exactly the trick, wasn’t it? Make him feel like the problem. Make him question why he was even pushing this.

“I don’t talk about them,” Mydei said, voice edged.

Phainon sighed, shaking his head like Mydei was being difficult. “Not out loud, maybe. But I know you, Mydei.” His voice softened further, becoming something dangerously gentle, something that could slip into the cracks of Mydei’s resolve if he let it. “And if something’s bothering you that much, I want to help.”

Mydei’s fists curled at his sides. “I never asked you to help.”

“You never have to.”

The words were so effortlessly smooth, so laced with quiet sincerity, that for half a second, Mydei almost believed them.

But the doubt was still there, gnawing at the edges of his mind.

Phainon must have sensed it, because he suddenly leaned in—close enough that Mydei felt the whisper of his breath against his skin, close enough that it would have looked, to any outsider, like something intimate instead of a battlefield of words.

“If I knew something, I’d tell you,” Phainon said, so quiet it barely carried between them. “I would never hide anything from you.”

Mydei’s breath caught.

“We’re in this together, right?” Phainon continued, voice like velvet, warm and steady. “You’re safe with me.” He reached out, brushing his fingers over the edge of Mydei’s sleeve—not quite touching him fully, but enough for Mydei to feel the weight of the gesture. “So why do you still seem so anxious?”

Mydei forced himself to breathe. He tried to keep the logic in his head, tried to cling to it like an anchor, but Phainon’s words wrapped around him like a net, made to comfort, made to bind.

“I just…” He exhaled, trying to clear the haze in his thoughts. “It’s unsettling. You shouldn’t know about my dreams.”

Phainon hummed, tilting his head as if he were puzzled by the very notion. “Why not?” he asked. “They’re a part of you, aren’t they? And I care about you, Mydei.” His voice dipped lower, nearly a whisper. “Maybe you’re just afraid of what you dream about.”

Mydei stiffened.

Phainon smiled, soft and knowing. “Maybe you’re afraid to share it with me.”

“I’m not—”

“And that’s okay,” Phainon interrupted smoothly. “We can explore it together.” His fingers ghosted against Mydei’s wrist, the touch light enough to make Mydei’s pulse jump. “You don’t have to shut me out.”

Mydei swallowed, his throat dry. “You’re making this sound like I’m the one at fault here.”

“Not at fault,” Phainon corrected, shaking his head. “Just… guarded. You always have been.” His thumb brushed lightly over Mydei’s knuckles, his voice lowering to something almost reverent. “But I can’t help you if you don’t let me. Let me in, Mydei.” His gaze softened, full of something that almost looked like devotion. “You’re not alone.”

Mydei’s mind swayed, uncertainty lacing through him like poison in the bloodstream.

Trust isn’t a light switch, Phainon had said once. It’s a dance.

Mydei’s heart was still hammering against his ribs, but there was something almost lulling about Phainon’s voice, about the warmth that pressed against the cold places inside him. It felt… safe.

And yet, wasn’t that the most dangerous part?

His breath hitched. He took a step back, forcing space between them. “No,” he said, shaking his head as he tried to clear his thoughts. “You’re not getting away with this.” He forced himself to meet Phainon’s gaze, steady despite the storm inside him. “How do you know about my dreams?”

Phainon’s expression faltered, just for a fraction of a second.

And in that heartbeat of silence, the warmth between them cooled.

Then, just as quickly, the smile returned—softer this time, almost regretful. “You’re still so fixated on this,” he stated. “What do you think I’m hiding?”

Mydei exhaled sharply. “I don’t know,” he admitted. “But you’re not telling me the truth.”

Phainon studied him, searching his face, and for a moment, something unreadable flickered in his expression. Then he sighed, running a hand through his hair. “I just—” He hesitated, shaking his head. “I don’t want you to think I’d ever hurt you.”

“You’re dodging the question.”

“No, I’m trying to make you see reason.” Phainon’s voice was softer now, gentler. “I don’t want to fight with you, Mydei.” He took a step forward again, his presence pressing into Mydei’s space like a tide returning to shore. “I want to give you something.”

Mydei blinked, thrown by the shift. “What?”

Phainon smiled, slipping a hand into his coat. “A gift.” His eyes met Mydei’s, dark and steady. “Something to remind you that I’m always looking out for you.”

The words settled deep in Mydei’s chest, like a stone thrown into still water.

Phainon held out his hand.

“Here,” he reached out. “Take it.”

And despite everything, despite the doubt clawing at his thoughts, Mydei found himself hesitating.

Because even now, after all of this—part of him still wanted to believe.

Mydei hesitated, his eyes flickering between Phainon’s outstretched hand and the unreadable expression on his face.

“A gift,” Mydei repeated slowly.

Phainon only nodded, gaze patient, unwavering.

There was nothing in his hand. No trinket, no charm, no object that could explain the weight of his words. Just the steady, open invitation of his palm —waiting.

Mydei exhaled sharply. “You can’t be serious.”

Phainon’s lips curved into a knowing smile. “Oh, but I am.”

And somehow, that was worse.

Mydei’s fingers twitched at his side. This was stupid. This was a trick. This was—

Warmth.

Before he fully realized what he was doing, Mydei reached out and clasped Phainon’s hand.

The touch was grounding, solid, and yet it sent an immediate shiver through him. Not from cold, but from something deeper, something that curled around his ribs like unseen vines. Phainon’s fingers flexed slightly, a satisfied hum slipping from him as if this—this—was what he had been waiting for all along.

Mydei’s throat tightened.

The weight of it, the significance—

A sudden, loud crack split through the air.

Mydei flinched violently, ripping his hand away as his head snapped toward the source of the noise. His heart pounded against his ribs, the rush of instinct overtaking the haze Phainon had been weaving around him.

“What was that?” he demanded, his voice sharp.

Phainon let out a slow, measured sigh, rolling his shoulders like he had just been rudely interrupted from a pleasant conversation. “Tsk.” He glanced off to the side, barely concerned. “That was too early.”

Mydei’s stomach twisted. “Too early for what?”

Phainon turned back to him, his expression unreadable, but there was a flicker of something behind his eyes—something calculating, something knowing.

“Oh, don’t worry about it,” he said lightly, waving a hand. “Just a bit of bad timing, that’s all.”

Mydei’s breath felt too shallow. His pulse still raced from the noise, but now something else coiled beneath his skin—a different kind of tension, a gnawing uncertainty that had Phainon’s name written all over it.

His hands clenched at his sides. “Phainon,” he said carefully, “what was too early?”

Phainon’s smile was slow, almost lazy.

He didn’t answer.

The silence that followed was different this time. Not heavy with tension, not charged with unspoken challenges—just quiet.

Phainon’s usual ease, his ever-present glibness, was absent. He didn’t answer. Didn’t joke. Didn’t deflect.

Mydei narrowed his eyes. “Phainon.”

Still nothing.

Phainon stood there, gaze idly drifting past Mydei, past the trees, past whatever had made the noise. Like he hadn’t heard him. Or maybe like he had and just wasn’t interested in playing along anymore.

That set Mydei’s nerves on edge more than any clever evasion ever could.

He took a step closer, voice lowering. “You said too early—too early for what?”

Phainon hummed softly. Not in amusement. Not in interest. Just… a sound. Thoughtful.

“You’re doing that thing again,” Mydei pressed, eyes flickering over him, searching for the crack in his mask. “Where you pretend I didn’t say something.”

Phainon finally turned his gaze back to him, unreadable. “Am I?”

Mydei clenched his jaw. “Yes.”

Silence.

For the first time in a long time, it felt like Phainon wasn’t guiding the conversation, wasn’t leading him into some tangled web of half-truths and distractions. No, this time, he was just waiting.

For what, Mydei couldn’t tell.

And that? That was somehow worse.

Phainon tilted his head slightly, considering Mydei with a gaze that was neither dismissive nor entirely present.

Then—so casually it almost felt accidental—he spoke.

“You always get like this when Okhema is involved.”

The words landed like a physical blow.

Mydei went still.

Something inside him—something instinctive, something primal—lurched at the statement, like a trap had just been sprung beneath his feet. His breath caught, the rhythm of his heartbeat stuttering violently before slamming into overdrive.

“What did you just say?” His voice barely carried, hoarse with the weight of his own dread.

Phainon’s expression didn’t shift.

For a moment, Mydei wondered if he had imagined it—if the words hadn’t been spoken at all, if he was only hearing the things his fear wanted him to.

But no.

Phainon was watching him.

Watching him too closely.

Mydei felt the pit open beneath him, an abyss of terrible understanding that he refused to acknowledge. He shook his head, trying to steady himself.

“Phainon,” he said, sharper this time. “What the hell does that mean?”

Phainon didn’t answer.

The silence rang louder than any explosion, louder than the noise that had broken through the night, louder than Mydei’s own pulse roaring in his ears.

And then—

A flicker.

Not on Phainon’s face, but in his posture. Something infinitesimal. A shift. A second’s hesitation that Mydei almost missed.

Almost.

Something was wrong.

Something was so wrong.

And Mydei knew—deep in the marrow of his bones, in the instincts that screamed at him to move, to run, to go—that he wasn’t ready for the answer.

But he had to know.

He turned.

And then he was running.

The ground blurred beneath him, the wind biting against his skin as his feet pounded forward, carrying him faster than thought, faster than reason. His

body moved on instinct, his mind barely keeping up as the distance between him and the city closed at a terrifying pace.

Please no. Please no. Please no.

The sky over Okhema wasn’t right.

Smoke curled like blackened fingers into the night, staining the stars. An eerie glow pulsed beyond the city walls, flickering and violent.

Mydei pushed forward, his breath ragged, his muscles burning.

And then—

He reached the gates.

His steps faltered.

His stomach lurched.

The sacred city—

The holy, untouchable city—

Had been razed to the ground.

The streets were awash in blood, slick and dark beneath the dim light. Buildings, once pristine and unmarred, had collapsed into ruin, their skeletal remains jutting against the sky like broken ribs. The scent of burning flesh choked the air, thick and cloying.

Bodies.

So many bodies.

They were scattered haphazardly—some slumped against crumbling walls, some collapsed mid-step, their expressions frozen in terror and agony. The devastation was total.

Something inside Mydei cracked.

His legs buckled, and he barely caught himself before he hit the ground. His lungs seized, his vision tunneling. The weight of the destruction pressed against him, suffocating, consuming.

His hands—he didn’t remember lifting them—were shaking. Trembling violently, his fingers curling into claws, trying to grasp something— anything—that would make this not real.

A sound.

A strangled, ragged breath.

It took Mydei too long to realize it had come from him.

He was drowning.

His chest seized, his thoughts spiraling, everything folding inward as panic consumed him whole. His vision blurred at the edges, his pulse a deafening roar. His body would not move.

And then—

A shadow at the edge of his vision.

A figure.

Standing amidst the wreckage.

Unmoving. Unbothered.

Watching.

Mydei didn’t have to turn to know who it was.

He didn’t want to.

But he did.

Phainon stood just beyond the carnage, his posture languid, his expression unreadable.

Not alarmed. Not surprised.

Just looking at him.

Like he had been waiting for this.

Like he had known exactly what Mydei would find.

Terror sank its teeth deep into Mydei’s chest.

His breath hitched, sharp and shallow, his vision tilting at the edges. The panic—before, it had been suffocating, unbearable.

But now?

Now it was nothing compared to the weight of understanding.

Phainon knew.

Phainon had always known.

And still—

Still, he smiled.

Soft.

Gentle.

Like he pitied him.

Like this had always been inevitable.

And Mydei broke.

The world had shattered for him.

One moment, Mydei had been standing before Phainon, questioning him, pushing at the edges of his silence, and the next—

This.

Okhema was gone.

How did it come to this?

The sacred city had been gutted from the inside out, its once-pristine streets now a grotesque tableau of ruin and death. Mydei barely processed the sequence of his own actions—one second, he had been running, breath tearing through his throat, and now he stood in the middle of something unspeakable.

Blood coated the stones in thick, congealing pools, the scent of iron so strong it clung to the back of his throat. Some bodies were barely recognizable—ripped apart, limbs torn from sockets, flesh twisted into something unholy. Others remained whole but disturbingly still, their eyes fixed open in frozen horror, the last moments of their lives preserved in expressions that would never change.

A child lay just a few feet from him, small hands still clutching the fabric of a tattered doll, its face smeared in red. Mydei couldn't look away from the way her body curled inward, like she had tried to make herself smaller, as if that could have saved her.

His stomach twisted violently. His knees buckled.

How did this happen?

One moment—he had been standing there, arguing. Just talking. And then —

He couldn't breathe. His mind reeled, trying to bridge the impossible gap between then and now. Between the quiet conversation and the smell of burning flesh. Between Phainon’s infuriating half-truths and the pieces of people scattered across the ground.

His breath came in short, sharp bursts. His vision swam. His hands were shaking so violently that he could barely feel them, numb and distant. He knew—he knew—he was losing control, slipping under the weight of it, drowning in it, and yet he couldn't stop.

He barely registered the soft sigh behind him.

“Tsk.”

The sound was mild, almost indulgent, as if this were nothing more than an inconvenience. “Much too early…” he repeated.

Mydei flinched. He turned, his body stiff with unspent terror, and found Phainon standing there—just standing, unbothered, untouched by the horror unfolding before them.

Phainon’s gaze swept over the carnage, unreadable. Then, with the same mild irritation, he muttered, “This is why I didn’t want this to happen so soon.”

The words didn’t make sense. None of this made sense. Mydei wanted to demand answers, wanted to grab him by the collar and shake him, force him to explain, but he couldn’t make his body move. Could barely make his lungs work.

Phainon exhaled again, more thoughtful this time, then turned his attention back to Mydei.

His lips curled into something resembling a smile. “Do you want to walk somewhere else?” he asked, voice soft, as if suggesting they take a stroll through a garden and not a slaughterhouse.

Something inside Mydei snapped.

His stomach twisted again, a violent churn of nausea and disbelief. He could barely see through the static crawling at the edges of his vision. The bodies, the smell, the ruin—his chest hurt, his ribs locking up, trapping the air in his lungs until the edges of his world blurred.

This wasn’t real.

This couldn’t be real.

Phainon stepped closer, his presence unnervingly steady against Mydei’s unraveling world. His eyes—sharp and knowing—softened slightly.

“I have a gift for you,” he spoke, voice dipped in something intimate, something meant to soothe. “Something rare. Something precious.”

Mydei barely processed the words. His ears were ringing.

Phainon tilted his head, patient, undeterred. “I’m offering you the coreflame of Mnestia.” His voice was slow, deliberate, as if he were explaining something sacred. “Algaea’s own power. The essence of romance itself.”

It took Mydei a second to register what he was saying.

Then another to process it.

The coreflame of Mnestia.

His mind latched onto the words, trying to make sense of them, trying to slot them into the same reality where Okhema was in ruins and Phainon was standing before him with a lovesick expression.

Romance.

Here. Now. With blood still soaking his boots.

Mydei’s stomach turned again, and suddenly, violently, he shoved Phainon back.

Phainon barely moved. He didn’t stumble. Didn’t even react beyond the slight shift in weight.

But something in his expression cooled.

Not anger. Not disappointment.

Just a quiet, knowing patience, as if this was always how it was going to go.

As if Mydei was being difficult, but not unpredictably so.

Phainon smiled again—smaller now, less indulgent.

And he waited.

Mydei’s breath shuddered as he backed away, his legs weak beneath him. The taste of bile clung to the back of his throat, the sheer, overwhelming wrongness of it all pressing down on his chest like a vice.

The blood, the bodies, the absolute desecration of Okhema—it was everywhere. He couldn’t escape it, couldn’t blink without seeing the grotesque display carved into the ruins of what had once been holy ground.

But Phainon…

Phainon was untouched.

He stepped toward him with the same casual ease as if this were nothing more than a stroll through the gardens, his expression still gentle, still unbearably soft, like he wasn’t surrounded by the horror he had caused.

“Stop being difficult,” Phainon scolded, his voice almost chiding, but still laced with that infuriating, almost affectionate patience. “You’re trembling.”

Mydei flinched as Phainon reached out, fingertips brushing against his cheek, light as a whisper. His skin crawled at the touch, and he jerked back violently, his heart hammering like a war drum.

Why was he acting like this? Why was he speaking so gently when Mydei could hardly breathe past the grief suffocating him?

His throat clenched. His voice had abandoned him.

But he had to say it. He had to force himself to say it.

Swallowing against the sheer terror constricting his chest, Mydei managed a breathless whisper:

“You did it.”

A statement, not a question. The truth laid bare between them.

Phainon didn’t deny it.

Instead, he exhaled, tilting his head, regarding Mydei with something almost wistful. “I really didn’t want this to happen so soon,” he admitted, sighing as if this was an inconvenience rather than a massacre. “I told you. Too hasty.”

A sick, horrible crack nearly split Mydei’s ribs.

His hands clenched into fists, nails digging into his palms. His body screamed at him to run, but the weight of what he was seeing, of what Phainon had done, pinned him in place.

His breath hitched, broken, as his next question rasped from his throat.

“Why?”

His voice wavered, raw with disbelief. His chest ached. “Why didn’t you —” His lips trembled. “Why didn’t you get rid of me too?”

Phainon’s gaze softened, and that was somehow the worst part.

“Oh, Mydei.” He reached for him again, but this time, Mydei recoiled so fast he nearly tripped over his own feet.

Phainon let his hand drop, unbothered. Instead, he smiled, slow and knowing.

“I have something else for you,” he said smoothly, shifting the conversation as if Mydei hadn’t just accused him of slaughter.

And then, in his palm—

A circular flame.

Faint, flickering, but undeniably alive.

The sight of it sent a bolt of terror straight down Mydei’s spine.

Even before Phainon spoke, he knew what it was.

A Titan’s coreflame.

Not just any.

Nikador’s.

Titan of Fury and Strife.

A relic of a god Mydei’s people had once worshipped before he fell to madness.

Mydei’s entire body locked.

The coreflame flickered in Phainon’s palm, casting faint, eerie light against the carnage surrounding them. Mydei couldn’t take his eyes off it. The heat of it gnawed at the air, ancient and waiting.

Phainon didn’t move, didn’t speak. He only watched him, patient. Expectant.

Mydei’s breath hitched.

“No.”

His voice was barely above a whisper, but it was firm. It had to be.

He would not take that coreflame.

Phainon’s expression didn’t change, but something in the air did.

It tightened.

It pressed down on Mydei’s ribs, his lungs, as if the world itself had leaned in closer to listen.

And then—

A sigh.

Long, weary, slow.

Phainon ran a hand through his hair, his fingers dragging slightly. “See, this,” he mumbled to himself, “is exactly why I wanted to do this the easy way.”

Mydei’s stomach twisted.

Before he could move, before he could even breathe—

Phainon stepped forward.

Faster than Mydei could react.

And the moment Phainon reached him, the world shattered.

Pain exploded through his body.

A force slammed into his chest, searing and unrelenting, sending him crashing into the blood-soaked ground.

His head spun. His vision blurred. His breath caught in his throat, and—oh.

This was bad.

This was—this was worse than anything he’d ever felt.

Phainon knelt beside him, slow and deliberate, like he had all the time in the world. His fingers grazed Mydei’s cheek, tilting his face upward with unbearable gentleness.

“Mydei,” he whispered, voice soft, but dangerously fraying at the edges. “You know I don’t like being cruel.”

A fresh wave of pain lanced through him as Phainon pressed a hand against his ribs. A hum of energy coursed from his fingertips, scalding beneath Mydei’s skin.

“But you,” Phainon continued, his voice still achingly tender, “are making this so very difficult.”

Mydei wheezed, his body screaming as something inside him cracked.

It didn’t matter.

He was immortal.
